title: CDP1802 Family
description: RCA's radiation-hardened CMOS CPU. Used in spacecraft and early hobbyist computers.

title: 6502 Family
description: Elegant 8-bit architecture with a small instruction set. Skills transfer directly between C64, NES, and more.

title: 65C816 Family
description: 16-bit evolution of the 6502. Native mode adds 16-bit registers while maintaining compatibility.

title: 6800 Family
description: Motorola's first 8-bit CPU and its 6801/6803 successors. A single-supply design that seeded a generation of home and embedded micros.

title: 68000 Family
description: 16/32-bit hybrid with orthogonal design. More registers, more addressing modes, more power.

title: 6809 Family
description: Motorola's advanced 8-bit CPU with orthogonal design. Position-independent code and powerful addressing.

title: 8080 Family
description: Intel's pioneering 8-bit CPU that started the microcomputer revolution. The ancestor of the Z80.

title: ARM Family
description: Acorn's RISC revolution. Clean, efficient instruction set that now powers most mobile devices.

title: CP1610 Family
description: General Instrument's 16-bit CPU. Powered the Intellivision's advanced graphics.

title: F8 Family
description: Fairchild's innovative multi-chip CPU. First processor in a programmable home console.

title: Hudson HuC6280
description: Hudson's extended 65C02 in the PC Engine. Adds block transfers, port writes, and MMU mapping instructions — a 6502 descendant with its own encodings.

title: MCS-48 Family
description: Intel's early microcontroller with built-in RAM and I/O. Simple but capable.

title: MIPS Family
description: Classic RISC architecture. Powered PlayStation, N64, and PS2 with elegant simplicity.

title: SuperH SH-2 Family
description: Hitachi's 32-bit RISC CPU. Dual processors powered the Saturn's complex architecture.

title: SuperH SH-4 Family
description: Advanced SuperH with FPU and 3D support. The brain behind Dreamcast's impressive graphics.

title: Sharp SM83
description: Sharp's Z80-flavoured core in the Game Boy. An 8080-style register file with Z80 syntax, but its own instruction encoding — not Z80-compatible.

title: TLCS-900 Family
description: Toshiba's 16-bit CPU family. Z80 heritage with modern enhancements for handhelds.

title: TMS9900 Family
description: Texas Instruments' 16-bit CPU with workspace registers. Unique architecture, ahead of its time.

title: V810 Family
description: NEC's 32-bit RISC CPU. Low power design used in Nintendo's experimental consoles.

title: x86 Family
description: Intel's dominant architecture from PC to present. CISC design with backwards compatibility.

title: Z80 Family
description: Extended 8080 instruction set with more registers. The heart of British home computing and handhelds.

title: Brick Basher
description: A Breakout clone teaching ball physics, paddle control, and power-up systems.

title: Catacombs
description: Explore a large scrolling dungeon and manage what you carry, with music playing under the action.

title: Deephold
description: A top-down adventure with inventory, NPCs, quests, and disk save/load.

title: Hornet
description: A multi-sprite action game teaching sprite multiplexing beyond hardware limits.

title: Knuckle
description: A one-on-one fighting game with hitboxes, combos, and special moves.

title: Maelstrom
description: The integration game — scroll, multiplex, music and logic all inside one stable 50Hz frame.

title: Maze Raider
description: A Pac-Man style maze chase teaching custom character sets, tile-based maps, and pathfinding AI.

title: Meet the Machine
description: The assembly on-ramp. Before you build a game, meet the 6510 and the Commodore 64 one idea at a time — registers, memory, the screen, decisions, loops — until the machine stops feeling like magic.

title: Assemble and Run
description: Write a few lines of assembly, turn them into a program with a build step, run it on the C64, and watch the border change colour. Meet the loop you'll use all course — and the idea that makes the C64 the C64.

title: LDA Is Not LET
description: Meet the registers — the three physical 8-bit stores inside the 6510. Send a value from A into X and back again, and watch the border prove it made the trip. And learn why 'load' comes in three flavours.

title: Everything Is a Number
description: A byte has no type. Discover that 65, $41, the letter 'A' and the bit-pattern %01000001 are one and the same byte — and meet hex, the way you'll read bytes from here on.

title: A Street of Numbered Boxes
description: Meet memory — one long street of numbered boxes, each holding a byte. Store a byte at an address and read it back, the same round-trip you used for registers, now through RAM.

title: The Screen Is Memory
description: The big one. Discover that the screen is just a stretch of the same memory street — poke a byte to $0400 and a character appears. No PRINT, no magic: a box on screen holds one character code, and the chip draws it.

title: Colour Is a Separate Map
description: Find out where colour lives — a second map at $D800, one byte per cell, completely apart from the characters. Colour a cell with a single byte, and meet the C64's own take on the attribute grid.

title: Test, Then Jump
description: There's no IF on the 6510. Learn how the machine makes decisions instead — compare a value, which sets a flag, then branch on that flag. Build your own IF, and write your first labels.

title: The Machine Can Hear You
description: Read the joystick the honest way — read a port, isolate one bit, branch on it. Push the stick and watch the border react, every pass of the loop. The first time the machine answers to you.

title: A Finger on the Boxes
description: Stop baking the address into every instruction. Meet indexed addressing — X as a finger you slide along the memory street, writing as it goes — the idea behind every loop that fills the screen.

title: The Counted Loop
description: Hand the repetition to the machine. Load a count, run the body, step on, and branch back until you've done them all — one loop fills a whole row where last unit you stepped by hand.

title: Call, Return, and a Stack You Can See
description: Package a job into a subroutine you can call from anywhere — and watch where the machine remembers its way back: the stack, sitting in plain memory you can read.

title: Adding and Taking Away
description: The most ordinary thing of all, finally: maths. adc and sbc on a value — and the carry flag the 6510 makes you mind: clear it before you add, set it before you subtract.

title: Working With Bits
description: Change one bit without disturbing the rest. Meet ora, and and eor — set, clear and flip individual bits — the everyday way to throw a single switch in a byte.

title: Bigger Than a Byte
description: A byte stops at 255 — too small for an address. The 6510 has no 16-bit registers, so you hold a big number as two bytes and add it by hand, low byte first — and the carry flag becomes the bridge between them.

title: The Machine Speaks Back
description: Unit 8 taught the machine to hear you. This one teaches it to answer. The SID is the C64's three-voice synthesiser — set a voice's pitch, its envelope, and the volume, open the gate, and the chip holds the note on its own while your code does nothing.

title: The Machine Trusts You
description: The last unit, and the most important. There's no error message, no bounds check, no guard rail — the machine does exactly what you wrote, even when you're wrong. Learn to debug by observing, not by reading errors.

title: Mega Blaster
description: A Turrican-style run'n'gun with multi-directional scrolling and vehicle transformations.

title: Night Raid
description: A Scramble-style side-scroller teaching terrain collision and resource management.

title: Platform Panic
description: A single-screen platformer teaching gravity, jump physics, and platform collision.

title: Raster Rider
description: A racing game with pseudo-3D road using advanced raster effects.

title: SID Symphony
description: A music player ticking under a running game — interrupt-driven SID music on the raster IRQ.

title: Starfield
description: Build a single-screen space shooter from scratch in 6510 assembly — from a blank screen to a commercial-quality C64 game, one technique at a time.

title: Ship on Screen
description: Put a hardware sprite on screen with the VIC-II — the first piece of your first C64 game, built from a blank screen up.

title: Joystick Movement
description: Wrap the ship in a game loop and read the joystick through the CIA chip, so pushing the stick moves the ship — the moment the program becomes a game.

title: Screen Edges
description: Push the ship to the right and it wraps off the screen. Add a ninth X bit and boundary clamping so it reaches the full width and stops cleanly at every edge.

title: Fire Button Shoots
description: Read the fire button and launch a bullet from the ship — then make the shot spawn correctly wherever the ship is, using the ninth X bit from the last unit.

title: Laser Sound
description: Configure a SID voice and gate it on each shot, so firing makes a sharp laser 'pew' — your first taste of the C64's sound hardware.

title: Enemy Appears
description: Add a third sprite that moves on its own — a green enemy that drifts down the screen and keeps coming, respawning in a new column each time it leaves.

title: Direct Hit
description: Make the bullet and enemy notice each other — software collision by comparing coordinates on both axes, with the unsigned-distance trick and a ninth-bit guard.

title: Explosion
description: Sell the hit — flash the enemy white with a frame-counter freeze, then fire an explosion on the SID's second voice while the laser still rings.

title: Scoring Points
description: Write a score to screen RAM — character output and colour RAM for the readout, then BCD arithmetic and nybble extraction to count each hit.

title: Enemy Waves
description: Turn one enemy into a wave — parallel arrays and indexed addressing drive several enemies from a single loop, with the Y register and a spawn subroutine doing the repetitive work.

title: Player Death
description: Make the ship killable — detect enemy-on-ship collision, freeze the game with a game-over flag, and play a death tone on the SID's third and final voice.

title: Game Over
description: Tell the player it's over and let them try again — print GAME OVER into screen RAM with a text subroutine, then restart the whole game on a press of fire.

title: Three Lives
description: Soften the one-hit ending — give the player three lives, a counter that ticks down on each hit and respawns the ship, with game over held back until the last life is gone.

title: Life Lost Flash
description: Make losing a life fair — a border flash marks each hit and doubles as a short window of invulnerability, so a respawn can't die on the spot.

title: Starfield
description: Fill the empty space — draw a scrolling starfield straight into screen RAM with indirect indexed addressing, then split it into three depths moving at three speeds.

title: Title Screen
description: Turn the program into a finished game — a title screen and a three-state machine (title, playing, game over) that opens, plays, ends, and loops back to the start.

title: The Curve
description: Starfield works; nothing escalates. A wave counter, a speed table and a live fall speed put a difficulty curve in the game; a SID jingle gives the title a voice; and a dwell on both ends of the loop lets the endings land. Then the winnability gate does its work: the turret park — park under the lane, hold fire, never lose — is closed with a real LFSR spawn, full-field 9-bit enemies, and a hunt that leaves no square safe. And finally the game gets a curve worth playing: the swarm grows from three enemies to six over the waves, the hunt tightens late, and a four-digit score can hold a long game.

title: Strata
description: An advanced side-scrolling shooter with multi-layer parallax, R-Type/Gradius style.

title: Tumbledown
description: An isometric adventure game teaching 3D projection and depth sorting.

title: Velocity
description: A horizontal scrolling runner introducing VIC-II hardware scrolling.

title: Bleeper
description: The C64 plays a tone-and-colour sequence and you repeat it from the keyboard — one panel longer every round. Meet the SID chip as a voice, an array as a growing memory, and GET as the way to read the player's echo and check it, press by press.

title: Light and Bleep
description: Bleeper's whole vocabulary is a panel that lights and sounds at once. Draw a colour block in screen memory, flash it white for a beat, and fire a SID note at the same moment. Colour and sound, locked together — the atom the whole game is built from.

title: Four Panels, Four Notes
description: One panel becomes four — red, cyan, green, yellow — each with its own pitch. The flash-and-tone code moves into a GOSUB routine you call by panel number, so the same six lines light any panel. That reusable routine is the engine of the whole game.

title: A Sequence from an Array
description: A game needs a sequence. Store a list of panels in an array, then walk it with a loop, flashing and bleeping each in turn. The sequence is data now, not code — the machine plays back whatever the array holds.

title: One More Each Round
description: A fixed sequence is a performance; a growing one is a game. Each round, add a random panel to the array and replay the whole thing from the start. The chain lengthens by one every time — the escalation at the heart of Simon.

title: Your Turn
description: Now the player plays. After the sequence, read their echo a key at a time with GET, light the panel they press, and check each one against the array. A right echo wins; a wrong press ends it with a harsh tone. This is the moment Bleeper becomes a game you can lose.

title: How Far Can You Hold?
description: Put it together: rounds that grow, an echo checked each round, a score that's just the length you held, and a key to play again. Number the panels so the player knows the keys. Your finished Bleeper — the SID, an array, and live input as one game.

title: Dropzone
description: Fly a lander down through gravity and set it on the pad — too fast and you crash, and your fuel is running out. The capstone of Volume 1: a real-time physics game where velocity accumulates in a plain variable, thrust fights gravity, and one clean touchdown is the whole reward.

title: A Falling Dot
description: Every lander game starts with something that falls. Hold an altitude in a variable, increase it each loop, and draw the lander at the row it points to — erase-move-draw, falling on its own whether you act or not. The continuous loop that drives every real-time game.

title: Gravity Pulls
description: A constant fall has no weight. Add velocity as its own variable and let gravity grow it every loop — the lander starts slow and speeds up, just like a real drop. This is the physics at the heart of the game: velocity that accumulates over time.

title: Thrust Pushes Back
description: Gravity has it all its own way — until now. Read a key inside the loop, and when it's pressed, shrink the velocity. Press to slow the fall; release and gravity takes over. Two forces on one variable: the game exists the moment you can fight back.

title: The Landing Pad
description: The lander needs somewhere to come down. Draw a ground line across the foot of the screen and a coloured pad in its middle — the one safe place to land, marked by colour, not a label. Now the descent has a target.

title: Soft or Hard
description: Reaching the pad isn't the same as landing on it. Check the speed at the moment of contact: slow enough is a soft landing, too fast is a crash. Now how you flew the last few rows is the whole game — and each ending gets its own screen.

title: Fuel — The Squeeze
description: Free thrust means braking all the way down. Add a fuel store that each burn spends, shown in the readout — and when it runs dry, the thruster dies and you coast on whatever speed you have. Finite fuel turns the descent into a negotiation. The finished Dropzone, and the end of Volume 1.

title: Meet C64 BASIC
description: The Commodore 64 BASIC on-ramp. Before you build a game, learn to write, run, edit and debug Commodore BASIC for real — and meet the screen, colour, sound and joystick that, on the C64, you reach by writing straight to the chips.

title: You Type the Whole Word
description: Type your first line of Commodore BASIC, run it, and read what the C64 prints back. Meet the keyboard where you spell each word out — and the type-run loop you'll use all primer.

title: The Line Number Is an Address
description: Edit a program by its line numbers — replace a line by reusing its number, slip a new line into a gap, delete one, and LIST them in order. Then meet the C64's full-screen editor, where you change a line in place.

title: PRINT, and Its Punctuation
description: Give PRINT its punctuation — join with a semicolon, line things up in 10-column zones with a comma — then clear the screen the C64 way, with PRINT CHR$(147), and start the title card you'll grow all primer.

title: LET, and the First Two Letters
description: Give the program a memory: LET names a box that holds a value. Meet the C64's naming rules — strings end in $, and the surprise that only the first two letters of a name count, so CASH and CARD are the same box.

title: INPUT — the Program Listens
description: Let the person at the keyboard fill a variable. INPUT stops the program, prints a prompt and a ?, waits for what's typed, and stores it — text into a $ box, numbers into a plain one.

title: IF / THEN, the C64 Way
description: Let the program decide. IF tests a condition; THEN runs the rest of the line only when it holds. The C64 has no ELSE — so two-way choices are two IFs, one per outcome.

title: FOR / NEXT Counts For You
description: Repeat a thing a fixed number of times without retyping it. FOR sets a counter and its range; NEXT sends the loop round again; STEP changes how the counter moves — even backwards, for a countdown.

title: GOTO, GOSUB, and the Game Loop
description: Jump and repeat. GOTO sends the program to a line; the endless loop is its game-shaped form. GOSUB calls a named job and RETURN comes back. RND picks a secret, and the guessing loop ties it all together.

title: The Screen Is Memory
description: Meet the C64's defining trick: the screen is just memory. POKE a screen code into an address from 1024 onward and a character appears there — no PRINT, no cursor. An address formula puts it anywhere.

title: Colour Lives Somewhere Else
description: Every character cell has a second byte that nobody mentioned yet: its colour, stored in a separate block of memory at 55296. Set the border and background too, and the screen finally has the colours you choose.

title: The Machine Can Sing
description: C64 BASIC has no sound keyword at all — because sound here isn't a word, it's a chip. The SID lives in memory at 54272, and a handful of POKEs give it a note, a voice, and a sound that moves while your program runs.

title: Reading the Joystick
description: Input on the C64 is another PEEK. The joystick port is memory at 56320: read it and each direction is one bit, cleared when the stick is pushed. Decode the bits with AND, and a ball moves under your hand.

title: A Shape That Moves
description: Give a shape a life of its own. The animation loop is erase, move, draw, repeat — and a direction variable you flip at the edges makes a ball bounce. Meet the flicker that sends C64 game-writers to assembly.

title: Keeping Your Work
description: A program lives in RAM and vanishes when the power goes off. The disk drive keeps it: SAVE writes your program to disk, LOAD brings it back, and the directory shows what's there. The save-and-reload cycle every C64 session is built on.

title: When It's Wrong
description: The C64's error messages are terse, but each one names the problem and points to the line. SYNTAX ERROR, UNDEF'D STATEMENT, ILLEGAL QUANTITY — read them as directions, not scolding, and you can fix anything you write.

title: Oracle
description: Ask the machine a yes/no question and it answers — and you never know which answer is coming. Meet RND as a decision-maker, a string array as a memory of replies, a thinking pause that builds suspense, and colour that gives each answer a mood.

title: Ask the Oracle
description: The Oracle's whole shape in four lines: the machine takes a question with INPUT, and gives an answer. For now the answer is always YES — but ask, then answer, is the ceremony everything else hangs on.

title: The Oracle Chooses
description: Replace the one fixed answer with one of two, picked at random. RND rolls a number, ON…GOTO branches on it, and the player stops knowing which answer is coming — that gap is chance.

title: A List of Answers
description: Two answers aren't enough. Store eight in a string array, then use RND as an index to reach in and pull one out — one PRINT line that can speak any of them.

title: The Oracle Thinks
description: An answer that arrives instantly feels cheap. Add a thinking pause — a delay loop with a SID tone humming for its length — and the answer means more because you waited for it. That's suspense.

title: Mood in Colour
description: The Oracle should look like it feels something. Give each answer a mood — yes, no, maybe — and shift the colour to match before it prints. The player reads the feeling before the words.

title: Ask Again
description: Right now the Oracle answers once and stops. Close the loop — clear the screen and GOTO back to the question — and it becomes something you consult, not something you run. Your finished Oracle.

title: Reflex
description: The screen flashes white at a moment you can't predict — how fast can you hit a key? Meet the C64's jiffy clock, learn GET for an instant keypress, and turn raw timing into a verdict on the player's speed.

title: The Flash
description: Reflex begins with a signal. Hold the screen black, wait a beat, then flash it white — the moment the player reacts to. One register does it, and a timing loop sets the wait.

title: An Unknown Wait
description: A fixed beat can be learnt, and a reaction test you can predict is no test. Make the wait a different length every run with RND — now the flash always catches you off guard.

title: Timing the Press
description: The flash catches you out — but how fast did you answer? Meet TI, the C64's built-in clock, ticking sixty times a second. Reset it at the flash, read it at the keypress, and you have a time.

title: Catch It Instantly
description: INPUT makes the player press RETURN — two actions where a reaction test wants one. GET catches a single keypress the moment it lands, no RETURN at all. The timing finally feels honest.

title: Jiffies and Seconds
description: Sixty-one jiffies is precise but means little to a human. Divide by 60 and you have seconds — the unit we think in. One line of arithmetic turns the clock's count into a time a person reads at a glance.

title: How Fast Are You?
description: A time is a number; a verdict is a game. Read the jiffies and rate them — LIGHTNING, QUICK, OK, SLOW — then catch the player who jumps the gun before the flash. Your finished Reflex.

title: Rover
description: Steer a rover around a maze with the joystick, in real time — it stops dead at walls and scores when it rolls over a pickup. Meet PEEK(56320) for the stick, erase-move-draw for movement, and look-ahead collision: PEEK the cell you're about to enter to know what you'd hit before you hit it.

title: Place the Rover
description: Before the rover can move, it has to exist. Hold its position in two variables and draw it with two POKEs — a bright block in screen memory, its colour alongside. The whole game starts from this: the rover is just two numbers and two pokes.

title: Drive It with the Stick
description: Open a loop that reads the joystick on every pass, decode the direction, and move the rover — erase the old block, draw the new one. PEEK(56320), an AND to pick the bit, two POKEs. The first time the machine answers you in real time.

title: Walls That Stop You
description: An open screen lets the rover wander off the edge. Draw a maze of walls, then before each move, PEEK the cell the rover is about to enter — if it's a wall, cancel the step. The world pushes back, and a border wall keeps the rover in bounds for free.

title: Pickups and Score
description: Scatter pickups in a second colour, then teach the look-ahead PEEK a new trick: tell wall from pickup from empty by the character code it reads. Roll over a pickup, collect it, and the score climbs on a status row that never disturbs the maze.

title: Clear the Board
description: A game needs an ending. Count the pickups at the start, count them down as they're collected, and when the last one's gone, break the loop and show ALL CLEAR with the final score. The session gets a shape: enter, clear, done.

title: Make It a Game
description: Give Rover a front door. A title screen with the rover's name and a fire-to-start — read fire with (J AND 16) — turns the program into a game someone can pick up and play. Your finished Rover, ready to drive.

title: Safe Cracker
description: The C64 hides a code; you close in on it, guess by guess, the safe answering higher or lower and the screen warming as you near it — but your guesses are numbered. Meet the loop-with-a-goal: a loop that ends in a win or a loss, the structure under every game from here on.

title: Pick a Secret
description: Every guessing game needs a secret. Make the machine choose a hidden code between 1 and 100 with RND, and print it just this once to prove it lands in range. The number you'll spend the rest of the game hunting starts here.

title: Take a Guess
description: Now hide the secret and let the player put a number against it. INPUT takes their guess, a single IF weighs it against the code — cracked, or not. The first real contest between player and machine.

title: Higher or Lower
description: A wrong guess should teach something. Add two comparisons — is the guess below the code, or above it? — and a miss becomes a direction. This is the clue that turns blind guessing into deduction.

title: Loop Until Cracked
description: One clue isn't enough — the player needs to keep guessing. Wrap the guess in a loop that runs until the safe opens. This is the loop-with-a-goal: not a FOR that counts to a number, but a loop that ends when something specific happens.

title: Colour the Feedback
description: Words are slow; colour is instant. Make the background warm red when the guess is too high and cool blue when it's too low, behind a safe drawn on screen. The player reads the safe's mood before they read a word — colour carrying meaning, not decoration.

title: A Stake That Runs Out
description: A game you can't lose isn't a game. Give the safe a fixed number of tries: count each guess, and when they run out before the crack, the safe locks. Now the loop ends two ways — win or lose — and the guess count is the clock. Your finished Safe Cracker.

title: Skyline
description: Your first C64 program: build a city by writing straight to the screen. POKE blocks into screen memory, light the windows from colour memory, randomise the towers, and set the hour with two registers — a cityscape that composes itself.

title: One Block on the Screen
description: Skyline starts with a single block, placed exactly where you send it. Clear the screen, work out the address with 1024 + R*40 + C, POKE the block, and POKE its colour into the matching cell at 55296.

title: A Tower
description: One block is a brick; a loop is a building. A FOR loop counting up a fixed column POKEs a block at each row, turning one block into a tower of any height.

title: A Row of Towers
description: Wrap the tower in a second loop. An outer FOR steps the column across the screen while the inner FOR raises a tower at each — nested loops turn one tower into a skyline.

title: Lights in the Windows
description: Colour memory stops being a flat wash. As each tower goes up, some cells get a bright window colour against the tower's body — same coordinate, different byte — and the skyline comes alive.

title: No Two Cities Alike
description: Bring in RND. Randomise each tower's height and light each window on a coin-flip, and the program produces more than you typed — run it twice, get two different skylines.

title: Sunset
description: Two registers set the hour. POKE the background for the sky and the border for the frame, add a soft SID tone as each tower tops out, and the black screen becomes a city at dusk — your finished Skyline.

title: Tally
description: Roll two dice a thousand times, count every total, and watch a bell curve rise out of pure randomness. Meet numeric arrays as counters and the screen as a chart — the first time the machine draws a shape you never told it to.

title: A Die Roll
description: Tally begins with a single die. You met RND in Oracle picking answers; here the same command rolls a 1 to 6. Roll it ten times in a loop and watch the faces fall — the raw material the whole game is built from.

title: Two Dice, One Total
description: One die is fair. Roll two and add them, and the total — 2 to 12 — is not. Sevens crowd the middle, twos and twelves are rare. The lopsidedness you'll spend the rest of the game explaining starts here.

title: Counting the Totals
description: Counting totals by eye doesn't scale. Meet the array — eleven counters in one named structure — and use the dice total itself as the index. One line tallies any roll, no chain of IFs. Twenty rolls in, the shape is still ragged.

title: A Thousand Rolls
description: Twenty rolls were too ragged to trust. Change one number — 20 to 1000 — and the bell stops hiding. The counts climb, 7 pulls ahead, the edges stay low, and a clear shape emerges from pure chance. That's the law of large numbers.

title: The Bell in Bars
description: A column of figures isn't a picture. Walk the array and POKE each count as a bar of solid blocks straight to the screen — scaled to fit, on black, labelled beneath. The bell you read in numbers becomes a bell you can see.

title: You Set the Rolls
description: Hand the run count to the player. One INPUT, one FOR loop driven by it, and the same chart — but now you can roll 10 and see a ragged guess, or 1000 and see a clean bell. Watching randomness become a picture is the whole design lesson. Your finished Tally.

title: Getting Started with C64 Development
description: Set up your tools for Commodore 64 programming.

title: Block Drop
description: Falling blocks puzzle with rotation logic and two-player competition.

title: Bounce Back
description: Breakout clone with ball physics, power-ups, and double-buffered display.

title: Crate Stack
description: Single-screen platformer with gravity physics and Blitter Objects.

title: Dungeon Doors
description: Flip-screen dungeon exploration with persistent state and save/load.

title: Getting Started with AMOS
description: Set up AMOS Professional on an emulated Amiga, then type and run your first program.

title: Knight Watch
description: Hold the arena under waves of foes — SAM sampled audio and AMOS Music as a system.

title: Meet AMOS
description: The AMOS on-ramp. AMOS is the Amiga's own game-making language — sprites, sound, and smooth movement built right in. Learn it one idea at a time, from your first PRINT to a shape you can steer, until making a game feels like something you can just do.

title: Type and Run
description: Everything starts here: type a program into the AMOS editor, press one key, and watch it run. Before you can make anything, you need the loop of writing, running, and seeing the result — so let's make the Amiga say hello.

title: Print and the Screen
description: Your first program put one line of text near the top-left and left it at that. Now you take charge of the screen: clear it to a colour of your choosing, and place text exactly where you want it with Locate. Two small commands, and the whole screen becomes yours to arrange.

title: Variables and Types
description: So far every Print has shown text you typed straight into the program. Variables let the program hold a value under a name — a score, a player's name — and change it as it runs. You meet the two kinds AMOS cares about, the number and the string, and the small mark that tells them apart.

title: If, Then, Else
description: A program that does the same thing every time isn't much of a game. Decisions are what make it react: check a value, and do one thing when it's true, another when it isn't. You meet If, Else and End If, and the comparisons that drive them.

title: Loops
description: Computers are tireless at repeating things, and a loop is how you ask. Count from one number to another and run the same lines each time round, with a counter you can use as you go. One small block does the work of five Print lines — or five hundred.

title: Procedures
description: When you find yourself writing the same lines twice, give them a name instead. A procedure bundles a chunk of work under a label you choose, so you can run it whenever you need it by writing the name. It's how programs stay readable as they grow.

title: Open a Screen
description: Until now you've printed onto the screen AMOS handed you. Now you make your own — choosing its size, how many colours it can show, and whether it's low or high resolution. One command, and you've got a display built to your spec to draw on.

title: Colour and the Palette
description: Your screen shows 16 colours — but which 16? You choose them. Mix your own shades from red, green and blue, drop them into numbered slots, and pick which slot the text is drawn in. This is where the screen starts to look like yours.

title: Drawing and Shapes
description: Text is one thing; now you draw. Dots, lines, outlined boxes, filled bars and circles go straight onto the screen at the pixel coordinates you name, in the colours you mixed. This is the raw material every game's graphics are built from.

title: Your First Bob
description: Shapes you draw stay put. A bob is different: a graphic object you place by number, move with a single command, and reposition as often as you like. Make one, drop it on screen, and meet the thing every moving sprite in your game will be built from.

title: The Frame Loop
description: A game is a loop that runs fifty times a second: move things a little, wait for the screen to refresh, repeat. Put your bob inside one and nudge its position each time round, and it stops sitting still and starts to glide. This loop is the heartbeat under every game ever made.

title: Reading the Player
description: A bob that moves on its own is a demo. Read the joystick inside the frame loop and let the player decide which way it goes, and it becomes a game. Four little questions each frame — pushed left? right? up? down? — turn input into motion.

title: AMAL: Movement That Runs Itself
description: You've moved a bob by hand, frame by frame. AMAL lets you describe a movement once and hand it to AMOS to run on its own — in the background, fifty times a second, while your program gets on with everything else. It's the Amiga's secret weapon for smooth motion.

title: Bumping Into Things
description: Catch, hit, pick up, crash — every one of those is two things touching. AMOS can tell you the moment one bob overlaps another with a single test. Drop it into your frame loop and your game gains consequences: the point where moving pictures turn into something you can win or lose.

title: AMOS Makes a Sound
description: A game you can't hear is half a game. AMOS comes with sound effects built in — an explosion, a laser, a bell — each a single word you drop in wherever something happens. Give your hits and pickups a noise, and the screen comes alive.

title: Keeping Your Work
description: Everything you type lives in the Amiga's memory — and memory forgets the moment you switch off. Saving writes your program to disk so it survives, ready to load and carry on tomorrow. It's the least glamorous habit in programming and the one that saves you the most heartache.

title: The AMOS Way
description: Look back at the whole primer in one short program, and at how much AMOS quietly did for you. A bob gliding under a title is a handful of lines here — and a small mountain of work on a bare machine. That gap is the whole point of AMOS, and where you go next.

title: Nomad
description: The AMOS capstone — an arcade-adventure with progression, mixed AI and a full save.

title: Scroll Quest
description: Side-scrolling platformer showing AMOS's capabilities and limitations.

title: Space Swarm
description: Fixed-screen space shooter with enemy formations and wave progression.

title: Star Catcher
description: Catch falling stars using AMOS sprite handling — your introduction to Amiga game development.

title: Warren
description: Pac-Man style maze game with ghost AI personalities and AMOS Banks.

title: Ascension: The Guru Meditation
description: An epic action-adventure capstone combining all Amiga techniques into a commercial-quality game.

title: Ascent
description: A single-screen platformer teaching gravity, jump physics, and BOB animation.

title: Brawler
description: A side-scrolling beat 'em up with Y-depth sorting and two-player cooperative action.

title: How the Copper Works
description: A between-games interval, built as a demo — drive the Copper DMA by hand and watch it paint the screen one scanline at a time.

title: Crypt
description: A flip-screen top-down dungeon explorer with room transitions and inventory.

title: Echoes of the Ancients
description: A Metroidvania with connected world exploration, ability-gating, and multi-disk support.

title: Flock
description: Get the daft flock home. A sheep-crossing arcade game built on hardware sprites — steer one sheep at a time across the lane and the stream, fill the fold, and mind the duck.

title: The Farmyard
description: Compose the playfield: the Copper paints the farmyard's bands from above, and one bitplane plays fence, footbridge and lane markings — recoloured per band.

title: The Sheep
description: The first hardware sprite: a white sheep standing in the field. Denise overlays her on the farmyard for free — sprite data is a list of words, her position is two more.

title: Steering
description: The joystick arrives. Read the stick when a hop is available, move the sheep in 8-pixel steps, rewrite the sprite's POS/CTL — position is data, and now the player owns it.

title: The Amble
description: Two pictures of the same sheep and a pointer that alternates between them on every hop. Animation is choosing which data the sprite channel fetches — nothing more.

title: The Tractor
description: The first sprite nobody steers. A red tractor crosses the lane on a fixed, learnable loop — deterministic traffic is the skill this whole game is built on.

title: Squashed
description: CLXDAT arrives — the hardware that watches every sprite and reports what touched what. Sheep meets tractor, the bit goes up, and Flock becomes a game.

title: The Flock in Hand
description: The flock is finite: five sheep, shown as icons on a HUD strip at the foot of the screen. Each loss takes one. When the strip empties, the field empties too.

title: Busy Lanes
description: The cart and the Land Rover join the tractor — three speeds, two directions, one data-driven mover, and a collision mask that watches every lane at once.

title: The Fold
description: Somewhere to arrive: reach an empty pen and she's safe for good — a white resident in the fold, drawn on the scene's new second bitplane. Fill all five and the level is won.

title: Keeping Score
description: The HUD strip's second job: +5 for surviving the road, +25 for a sheep safely home — one binary word, peeled into decimal digits with DIVU and stamped in a glyph font.

title: A Soft Baa
description: Paula speaks: one looping square wave, and three farmyard sounds made of nothing but pitch, volume and time — a baa on the hop, a squelch for a loss, a rising bleat at the pen.

title: The Stream
description: The rule flips: in the water, the only safe place is aboard a drifting hay bale — one collision latch carrying two laws, a forgiving landing, and a phantom vertical blank that nearly sank the ride.

title: The Duck
description: A second ferry paddles the other way — and dips under to feed on a cycle you can learn. The platform becomes the hazard, and the vanishing trick costs no new death code at all: no pixels, no evidence.

title: The Cow
description: The farmyard's biggest resident takes the verge — half a pixel a frame of patient, unstoppable bulk. The mover learns fixed-point fractions, the last sprite pair fills up, and one forgotten invitation tells on itself.

title: The Black Sheep
description: An occasional black sheep brings a bonus and a quicker stride. A stored seed, player timing and palette changes give the next sheep a different role.

title: The Nervous Sheep
description: Time pressure without a clock on the screen: stand still too long mid-crossing and she trembles, frets aloud, and finally bolts — three involuntary hops with the stick ignored. Pressure that only ever lands on the shepherd who stops.

title: The Title
description: FLOCK over the farmyard, Baa Baa Black Sheep on Paula, press fire to begin — and underneath it the state machine every finished game runs on: title, play, won, lost, and back round for one more go.

title: The Whole Flock Home
description: The finale: a level table that quickens the lanes, hurries the duck and frays her nerves; a shepherd's bonus for a clean flock; and a feel pass on the hop itself. Eighteen units, one finished game.

title: Fortress
description: An isometric action-adventure with 3D projection and block puzzle mechanics.

title: Gobble
description: A Pac-Man style maze game with ghost AI personalities and power-up mechanics.

title: Highway
description: A pseudo-3D racing game with Copper road effects and split-screen multiplayer.

title: Meet the Machine
description: The assembly on-ramp. Before you build a game, meet the 68000 and the Amiga's custom chips one idea at a time — MOVE, registers, the bitmap screen, the Copper, the Blitter — until the machine stops feeling like magic.

title: Assemble and Run
description: Write a little 68000 assembly, build it into a bootable floppy, run it on the Amiga, and watch the screen fill with red. Meet the build loop you'll use all course — and the harness a 16-bit machine needs before it shows a single colour.

title: MOVE Is the Verb
description: Meet the 68000's workhorse. Where 8-bit machines had separate load and store, the 68000 has one instruction — MOVE — that carries a value from almost anywhere to almost anywhere. Use it to drive the colour from the CPU.

title: Bytes, Words and Longs
description: The idea that makes the 68000 a 16/32-bit machine: a value can be a byte, a word, or a long — 8, 16 or 32 bits — and you choose the size on every move. Carry a colour out of a 32-bit long.

title: A Register for Every Job
description: Meet the 68000's register file: eight data registers for values and maths, eight address registers for pointers — sixteen in all, far more elbow room than an 8-bit chip's two or three.

title: A Vast Street of Memory
description: Meet the 68000's enormous address space — millions of numbered boxes, each holding a byte. Store a colour out in memory and read it back, the same round-trip you ran through registers, now through RAM.

title: The Screen Is a Bitmap
description: The picture is a map of bits in memory. Each bit is one pixel — 1 lights it, 0 leaves it dark. Point the display at a stretch of Chip RAM, set some bits, and watch them become a block on the glass.

title: Colour and the Copper
description: Open the box we've leaned on since Unit 1. The Copper is a tiny co-processor that runs in step with the video beam, changing the hardware mid-screen — and with two instructions it paints a band of colours the CPU never touches.

title: Test, Then Branch
description: A program that can't make a decision can't do much. The 68000 has no IF — instead you compare two values, which sets the flags, then branch on a flag. That pair, CMP and Bcc, is every IF you'll ever write.

title: The Vertical Blank
description: Poll the Amiga’s beam position to pace a small colour update, distinguish a frame from vertical blanking, and discover why a late loop can miss its turn.

title: Reading the Player
description: Input is just memory you read instead of write. The left mouse button lives in one bit of a chip register — and it reads backwards, 0 for held and 1 for up. Test that bit every frame and the screen answers to a human hand.

title: Pointers and the Address Registers
description: An address register holds an address, not a number — and with brackets, (a0) means "the box a0 points at". Add the + and reading also steps the pointer on. Walk a pointer along a table and you can process a list of anything.

title: The Counted Loop
description: Doing a thing a hundred times shouldn't mean writing it a hundred times. DBRA is the 68000's count-and-loop instruction: it decrements a register and branches back until it runs past zero. One short loop replaces a wall of repeated lines.

title: Call, Return, and the Stack
description: A subroutine is a job you write once and call from anywhere. BSR jumps to it and quietly remembers the way back on the stack; RTS reads that note and returns. Together they let code call code — the foundation every program is built on.

title: Adding and Taking Away
description: Arithmetic is two instructions: ADD and SUB. They work on a size you choose, and they leave the flags set for a branch to read. Master the size suffix and the carry between sizes and you've got the maths every program runs on.

title: Working With Bits
description: Sometimes a value isn't a number — it's a row of independent switches. AND, OR and EOR work on those switches: OR turns bits on, AND clears the ones outside a mask, EOR flips them. This is how you pack flags and read hardware registers.

title: The Blitter Moves It
description: Everything so far has been the 68000 alone. The Blitter is a chip built for one job — shifting blocks of graphics through memory far faster than the CPU can. You point it at a source, a destination, and a size, and it moves the block while the CPU does something else.

title: A Sprite of Your Own
description: A sprite is a small picture the hardware draws over the background, on its own, wherever you point it. No bitplane, no blitting — you hand the chips a shape and a position and they put it on the glass and keep it there. This is how you make a player.

title: Paula Makes a Sound
description: The last custom chip is the one you hear. Paula plays sound by reading a sample — a list of numbers describing a waveform — straight out of memory. Hand her the sample, set how loud and how fast, switch on her DMA, and she plays it on her own, forever.

title: The Machine Trusts You
description: The last unit, and the most important. There's no error message, no bounds check, no guard rail — the 68000 does exactly what you wrote, even when you're wrong. Learn to debug by observing, not by reading errors.

title: Onslaught
description: A vertical scrolling shooter with bullet patterns and a full MOD soundtrack.

title: Parallax
description: A horizontal parallax shooter — the quintessential Amiga showcase with dual playfield scrolling.

title: Shatter Point
description: A Breakout clone teaching ball physics, Copper gradients, and Paula sample playback.

title: Wanderer
description: A scrolling platformer with large world exploration and parallax backgrounds.

title: Ballistic
description: Turn-based artillery over destructible terrain — the Scorched Earth tradition, with the Blitter as the mechanic.

title: Getting Started with Blitz BASIC
description: Set up Blitz BASIC on an emulated Amiga, then type, compile, and run your first program.

title: Meet Blitz
description: The compiled-BASIC on-ramp. Blitz BASIC 2 is the language the Amiga scene shipped real games in — Worms and Skidmarks among them. It looks like BASIC and runs like C. Learn it one idea at a time, from your first compile to graphics that fly.

title: Type, Compile, Run
description: Everything in Blitz starts with one loop: type a program, compile it, run it. That compile step is the whole point — Blitz turns your BASIC into a native Amiga program that runs at full speed. Let's go round the loop once and make the machine say hello.

title: Amiga Mode and Blitz Mode
description: Blitz can run your program two ways. Amiga mode plays nicely with the operating system — windows, the mouse pointer, multitasking. Blitz mode switches all that off and hands your program the whole machine, for graphics that run flat out. Knowing which mode you're in is the key to everything fast.

title: Variables and Blitz's Types
description: Most BASICs hide how a number is stored. Blitz doesn't — it lets you choose, because it's working close to the machine. A byte, a word, a long: each holds a different range, and picking the right one is part of writing fast, lean code. Here's the idea, and the surprise when a number doesn't fit.

title: Decisions, Loops, and the Frame
description: The control flow every game runs on: repeat work with a loop, branch on a decision with If, and meet VWait — the command that paces a Blitz program to the screen's 50-times-a-second beat. The skeleton of every game loop, in compiled Blitz.

title: Many Things at Once
description: Here's why the scene reached for Blitz. Put eighty objects in the frame loop, move every one of them each frame, and compiled Blitz draws the lot smoothly at full speed — the thing an interpreted BASIC can't keep up with. This is the headline trick of the whole language.

title: Slices and the Display
description: A slice is Blitz's description of a region of the screen — how tall, how many colours, what resolution. The power is that you can have more than one, carving the display into independent bands. It's something the Amiga's normal screens make hard, and it's pure Blitz mode.

title: Shapes
description: Boxes and circles are fine, but a game is made of pictures — and you don't want to redraw them line by line every time. A shape is a picture grabbed into memory once, ready to stamp down anywhere, as many times as you like. It's the building block every sprite and tile is made from.

title: Blitting
description: Stamping a shape is one thing; moving it is another. To animate a shape you redraw it each frame in a new place — and erase where it was, or it smears. Meet the Blit family, the no-trail trick, and why a shape must stay on its bitmap.

title: Reading the Joystick
description: A moving picture becomes a game the moment the player is steering it. Blitz reads the joystick with two plain functions that hand you a direction as a number — push right, get +1; push left, get -1; let go, get 0. Wire those numbers to a shape's position and the player is in control.

title: Animating a Shape
description: A single shape that slides around is a token. Swap between several shapes as it moves and it comes alive — a walking figure, a spinning coin, a pulsing power-up. Animation is just showing a different frame every so often, and you already have every piece you need.

title: Bumping Into Things
description: Objects that pass through each other aren't a game yet — a game needs consequence. Blitz answers the question 'are these two shapes touching?' with a single function, ShapesHit, that returns true the instant they overlap. That one test is the seed of every hit, catch, pickup and crash there is.

title: Smooth Scrolling
description: Every great Amiga game scrolls — a world wider than the screen, sliding past pixel by pixel. The trick isn't redrawing fast; it's drawing a bitmap bigger than the display and letting the hardware slide a window across it. Blitz hands you that window directly.

title: Reaching the Hardware
description: AMOS keeps the machine at arm's length. Blitz hands you the chips. The Amiga's colours don't live in your picture — they live in registers, and you can rewrite them directly, every frame. Change the registers and the picture changes colour without a single pixel being redrawn. That's colour cycling, and it's your first real touch of the metal.

title: Hardware Sprites
description: Every moving thing so far has been the blitter copying pixels into your picture — clear, redraw, repeat. The Amiga has another way: eight hardware sprites the chips overlay and move for you, floating above the bitmap without ever touching it. No Cls, no Blit. This is the chip feature AMOS hides most completely.

title: The Blitz Way
description: Look back at the whole primer in one program — two dozen objects, all moving at once, every part of it built by your own hand. Where AMOS did the work for you, Blitz handed you the parts and the speed to use them. That's the Blitz way — one of two roads into Amiga game-making, and the one that shipped one of the biggest games the Amiga ever saw.

title: Skyfire
description: A parallax shoot-'em-up at full speed — dual-playfield layers feeding off compiled Blitz.

title: Slipstream
description: The Blitz capstone — a multi-layer racer/action game that ties every Blitz power together.

title: Star Drift
description: A horizontal shooter reaching past the picture — hardware sprites over a Copper-split background.

title: Getting Started with Amiga Development
description: Set up your tools for Amiga 68000 assembly programming.

title: Game Feel
description: Explore how controls, movement, feedback and recovery shape the experience of playing.

title: Maths for Games
description: Explore the maths behind chance, direction and movement through experiments you can change.

title: Roll a die
description: Generate twelve numbered rolls of a six-sided die.

title: Keep the tallies
description: Keep six array entries that account for every roll.

title: Compare shares
description: Read proportions without losing the exact counts.

title: Watch the distribution
description: Watch a fixed-scale chart change as rolls arrive.

title: Compare experiments
description: Repeat, extend and compare samples, then save the complete experiment.

title: Find the angle to a target
The Basics
description: What a program is, before any machine or language: instructions in order, a way to show things, a place to remember, and a way to ask.

title: A Program Is Instructions
description: A program is a list of instructions. The computer does each one in turn, exactly as you wrote it.

title: One Thing After Another
description: Give the computer several instructions and it does them in order. That order matters as much as the instructions do.

title: Showing Your Work
description: Output is not only fixed words. A program can show a value it worked out, and join text and values together.

title: A Place to Remember
description: A variable is a named box that holds a value, so a program can keep it, use it, and change it.

title: Asking the Player
description: The program asks whoever is using it, and does something different depending on the answer.

title: Counting in Twos
description: How a machine counts: binary, hex, two bytes together, and a minus sign made of nothing but switches.

title: Ten Fingers, Two Wires
description: Why we count in tens and the machine counts in twos, and how a row of switches spells an ordinary number.

title: Four Bits at a Time
description: Hex gives each half of a byte a single symbol, so the writing still shows you the switches.

title: Two Bytes Together
description: A byte stops at 255. Put two side by side and you can count to 65535, which is why that number is all over these machines.

title: A Minus With No Minus Sign
description: How a row of switches stands for a negative number, and why that turns subtraction into ordinary addition.

title: Decisions
description: A program that reacts: test a value, choose between paths, keep a yes or no in a box, and join questions together.

title: Making a Choice
description: A program that decides: test a value, and do something only if the test passes.

title: One or the Other
description: Two paths from one question: do this, or else do that. And a chain of questions when there are more than two answers.

title: A Yes You Can Keep
description: The answer to a question is a value. Put it in a box and the program can remember it, carry it about, and act on it later.

title: Asking Two Things at Once
description: Join questions together with AND, OR and NOT, so one test can ask about more than one thing.

title: From Source to Silicon
description: How source becomes instructions, what translation costs, and how to investigate performance.

title: The Program Is Not What Runs
description: You write words. The processor only ever sees numbers. Something has to stand between them, and the interesting question is when it does its work.

title: Translating As You Go
description: Read a line, work out what it means, do it. Then do all of that again the next time the same line comes round.

title: Translating Once
description: Turn the whole program into numbers before it runs, then get out of the way. The thinnest translator that does this fits in eight lines, and you are about to write it.

title: What Speed Costs You
description: Assembly gives us more control over instructions, but also more responsibility. We compare diagnostics, detail and portability.

title: Put It on the Clock
description: Choose a question, measure comparable work, and check that a faster result still does the right job.

title: Gates and the Adder
description: The same truth tables, built out of wire, and then wired into something that adds. This is where a machine stops being magic.

title: The Same Table, Drawn
description: A gate is a truth table with wires. Set the inputs and the output follows, row by row.

title: The Half Adder
description: Adding two bits needs two answers. One of them is XOR and the other is AND, which means you have already built it.

title: The Full Adder and the Ripple
description: Give the adder a third input and chain the carries together, and you can add numbers of any size out of nothing but gates.

title: Repeating
description: Three kinds of loop: a set number of times, until something happens, and only while something holds. The second one is the shape of every game.

title: Doing It Again
description: A loop repeats work without writing it out over and over, a set number of times, with a counter you can use as it goes.

title: Until You Get It
description: The loop that runs until something happens, rather than a set number of times. It is the shape of every game.

title: Checking Before You Start
description: A loop that asks its question first, so the work can happen no times at all.

title: Structure
description: Lists, jobs with names, jobs that take a value and hand one back, and the one skill that separates getting it done from getting stuck.

title: A Box That Holds Many
description: A list is one name holding a row of values, and a loop can walk along it.

title: A Job With a Name
description: Give a piece of work a name, write it once, and call it whenever you need it.

title: Telling a Job What to Work On
description: A job that takes a value and hands one back, so one job can do a whole family of things.

title: When It's Wrong
description: The most useful skill there is: finding out why a program misbehaves by looking at what it did, not by guessing.

title: Truth Tables
description: A way to write down every case a question can have, so you can see that two different-looking tests are the same test.

title: True and False
description: A question has exactly two answers, so you can write down every case there is and stop guessing.

title: Both, Either, Different
description: Two questions make four cases. AND, OR and XOR are three of the ways of answering them.

title: Two Guards, One Guard
description: A truth table can prove that a tangled test and a plain one behave identically, which lets you swap one for the other.

title: Working It Out
description: The computer does arithmetic on values it did not have when you wrote the program, grows a box from its own value, and decides what to do with a leftover.

title: Working It Out
description: The computer works a new value out from what you give it, following a fixed order you can steer with brackets.

title: A Box That Grows From Itself
description: One line puts a box's own value back into it, larger. It is the counter behind every score, timer and life count.

title: When It Doesn't Divide Evenly
description: Seven does not split into twos. What you do with the part left over is a question every program has to answer.

title: Working the Bits
description: The tools that change a byte one switch at a time, slide the whole row, turn a letter into a number, and carry a fraction on a machine that only counts in whole steps.

title: Switch by Switch
description: Four tools that work a byte one switch at a time, to keep some bits, force others on, and flip the ones you choose.

title: Slide the Whole Row
description: Shifting slides every bit sideways at once, which is the machine's quickest way to multiply and divide by two.

title: A Letter Is a Number
description: The machine holds nothing but numbers, so a letter is a number too. Which number is an agreement, and the agreement has a pattern in it.

title: Numbers That Aren't Whole
description: A machine that counts in whole steps still has to carry half a pixel. The flexible answer is to let the point float, and it is never exact.

title: Nailing the Point Down
description: Fix the point at an agreed scale and a fraction becomes an ordinary whole number, which the machine adds at full speed.

title: Crate Escape
description: A single-screen platformer teaching gravity, jump physics, and platform collision detection.

title: Crypt Crawler
description: A flip-screen dungeon explorer — the ancestor to Zelda-style games.

title: Dash
description: A single screen, a character you steer, a hazard that sweeps, three coins to gather. Your first finishable NES game in 6502 assembly — built one technique at a time on the NMI game loop, from a blank screen to a title, two levels, sound and a win.

title: See Your Character
description: Build a complete NES cartridge from scratch — iNES header, PPU warmup, palette, and sprite data. A running figure appears on screen.

title: Controller Input
description: Read the NES controller with the strobe-and-serial protocol. AND masks test individual buttons, BEQ branches on the result. The figure walks left and right.

title: Jump
description: The A button launches the player upward. Gravity pulls them back down. Signed velocity, two's complement arithmetic, and the core verb of every platformer.

title: Obstacle
description: A diamond-shaped obstacle scrolls across the floor. SEC/SBC moves it left each frame. Bounding box collision detects the hit. Jump or get knocked back.

title: Jump Sound
description: The APU's pulse channel gives the jump a voice. Four register writes set the duty cycle, volume, pitch, and sweep — a rising chirp that silences itself.

title: Background Tiles
description: The nametable fills the screen with tiles from CHR-ROM. Write tile indices via $2006/$2007, set colours with the attribute table. The world becomes visible.

title: Platform Collision
description: The game reads the level data to detect what tile is below the player's feet. A floating platform proves the system — platforms become real.

title: Wall Collision
description: Horizontal tile checks prevent the player from walking through solid tiles. A wall on the ground proves the system — the player must jump over it.

title: Collectible Items
description: Three coin sprites appear around the level. A subroutine checks whether the player overlaps each one — the first use of JSR and RTS.

title: Score Display
description: Collecting a coin increments a score variable. The NMI handler writes the digit to the nametable every frame — the first VBlank update.

title: Collect Sound
description: Collecting a coin plays a short, bright note on the APU triangle channel. Three register writes produce a sound that makes every pickup feel rewarding.

title: Hazard Tiles
description: Spike tiles on the ground damage the player on contact. The tile collision code now distinguishes between tile types — not just solid or empty, but safe or dangerous.

title: Three Lives
description: The player starts with three lives. Each spike hit or obstacle collision costs one. Run out and the game freezes. A shared damage subroutine keeps the logic clean.

title: Game Over Screen
description: When all three lives are gone, GAME OVER appears on screen. Letter tiles in CHR-ROM spell the message. A one-shot flag ensures the NMI handler writes it exactly once.

title: Title Screen + Restart
description: A state machine drives the game through three states: title, playing, and game over. Press Start to begin. Die and press Start to return to the title. The game is now a complete loop.

title: Integration + Polish
description: A two-frame running animation brings the player to life. Sprites hide cleanly on game over. A boundary check prevents Y wrap-around. Phase 1 is complete.

title: The Last Yard
description: A win that means something: collect every coin and the level turns over — coins return, the obstacle quickens from a speed table, an L digit joins the HUD. A tiny pulse-channel sequencer gives the title a tune and both endings a voice. The game becomes a loop with a curve.

title: Echoes of Eponium
description: A Metroidvania with connected world, ability-gating, and MMC3 mapper features.

title: Fangs for the Memory
description: A Snake game with a pun, teaching ring buffers and self-collision.

title: Fracture Point
description: A Breakout clone teaching ball physics and background tile manipulation.

title: Gridlock
description: A falling blocks puzzle teaching piece rotation and line clearing.

title: Ion Trail
description: A side-scrolling shooter in Gradius territory with weapon upgrades.

title: Iron Assault
description: A Contra-style run 'n' gun with multi-directional shooting and co-op.

title: Meet the Machine
description: The assembly on-ramp. Before you build a game, meet the 6502 and the Nintendo Entertainment System one idea at a time — registers, memory, the PPU, palettes, decisions, loops — until the console stops feeling like magic.

title: Assemble and Run
description: Edit, assemble and run your first NES program in this page with Asm198x. Change one instruction, turn the screen blue, and download your own cartridge.

title: LDA Is Not LET
description: Meet the registers — the three physical 8-bit stores inside the 2A03. Send a value from A into X and back again, and watch the screen prove it made the trip. And learn why 'load' comes in three flavours.

title: Everything Is a Number
description: A byte has no type. Discover that 65, $41, the letter 'A' and the bit-pattern %01000001 are one and the same byte — and meet hex, the way you'll read bytes from here on.

title: A Street of Numbered Boxes
description: Meet memory — a street of numbered boxes, each holding a byte. Store a byte at an address and read it back, the same round-trip you used for registers. And learn why the NES's street is far shorter than you'd guess.

title: The Screen Is Behind a Window
description: The big one. The harness has been writing your colour through a little two-register window all along — and that same window reaches the screen itself. Aim it at the nametable, write a tile, turn the picture on, and a block appears.

title: Colour Lives in a Palette
description: Open up the stage light. On the NES, a tile's colour isn't stored with the tile — it lives in a separate little table, and the tile only points at it. Change the palette and the same block changes colour, with no touch to the screen at all.

title: Where the Shapes Come From
description: The last mystery in the harness. Tile 1 has been a 'solid block' only because of sixteen bytes of CHR ROM — a tiny picture. Edit those bytes and the block becomes whatever you draw. Here, a heart.

title: Test, Then Jump
description: There's no IF on the 6502. Learn how the machine makes decisions instead — compare a value, which sets a flag, then branch on that flag. Build your own IF, and write your first labels.

title: The Machine Has a Heartbeat
description: Use a short NMI handler for one visible update, preserve interrupted state, and distinguish a frame from the VBlank transfer window.

title: The Joypad in Your Hand
description: Read the NES controller the honest way — strobe it, shift the buttons out one at a time, isolate the one you care about, and branch on it. Hold A and watch the screen react, every pass of the loop.

title: A Finger on the Boxes
description: Stop baking the value into every instruction. Meet indexed addressing — X as a finger you rest on one entry of a table and slide along — the idea behind every lookup, message and animation a game does.

title: The Counted Loop
description: Hand the repetition to the machine. Load a count, run the body, step on, and branch back until you've done them all — and the PPU's auto-stepping port turns one short loop into a whole row across the screen.

title: Call, Return, and a Stack You Can See
description: Package a job into a subroutine you can call from anywhere — and watch where the machine remembers its way back: the stack, sitting in plain memory you can read.

title: Adding and Taking Away
description: The most ordinary thing of all, finally: maths. adc and sbc on a value — and the carry flag the 6502 makes you mind: clear it before you add, set it before you subtract.

title: Working With Bits
description: Change one bit without disturbing the rest. Meet ora, and and eor — set, clear and flip individual bits — the everyday way to throw a single switch in a byte.

title: Bigger Than a Byte
description: A byte stops at 255 — too small for an address. The 6502 has no 16-bit registers, so you hold a big number as two bytes and add it by hand, low byte first — and the carry flag becomes the bridge between them.

title: The Machine Speaks Back
description: Unit 10 taught the machine to hear you. This one teaches it to answer. The NES has a sound chip — the APU — built into the same 2A03 as the CPU. Set up a pulse channel, switch it on, and it holds the note on its own while your code does nothing.

title: The Machine Trusts You
description: The last unit, and the most important. There's no error message, no bounds check, no guard rail — the machine does exactly what you wrote, even when you're wrong. Learn to debug by observing, not by reading errors.

title: Pavement Justice
description: A side-scrolling beat 'em up with Y-depth sorting and combo systems.

title: Pellet Panic
description: A Pac-Man style maze game with ghost AI personalities.

title: Pixel Plains
description: A side-scrolling platformer introducing NES hardware scrolling.

title: Requiem for a Mapper
description: An action-adventure epic combining all NES techniques into a commercial-quality capstone.

title: Tarmac Terror
description: A pseudo-3D racing game with sprite scaling and split-screen multiplayer.

title: Thunder Run
description: A vertical scrolling shooter with MMC1 mapper and extended graphics.

title: Getting Started with NES Development
description: Set up your tools for NES 6502 assembly programming.

title: Deepdelve
description: A single-screen platformer in the Manic Miner tradition — tile-map collision, jump physics and deadly hazards.

title: Gloaming
description: Dusk in a small square. Light every lamp before the dark catches you. The first complete game you finish in assembly — and at the end, your build matches the shipped game byte for byte.

title: The Empty Square
description: Build the town square in three runnable steps — hold the border black, wipe the pixel canvas, wash in dark cobbles and frame them in blue walls — one attribute byte per cell, the screen itself the map.

title: The Cobbles and the Brick
description: Write the bitmap under the attributes — meet the Spectrum's famous screen layout, blit an 8-byte texture into every ground cell, then let the map itself decide where the brick goes.

title: The Lamplighter
description: Draw the game's first character — eight bytes of figure blitted like any texture, his position held as data, and his own attribute colour to lift him out of the dark.

title: The Heartbeat
description: Replace the idle spin with a frame-locked loop — IM 1, EI, and HALT beat once per 50 Hz frame — then build a one-line probe to watch the pulse, and take it out again.

title: Reading the Keys
description: Fill the loop's INPUT stage: select a keyboard half-row through port $FE, read it with IN A,(C), test the active-low bits — and the lamplighter glows the instant a direction key goes down.

title: One Step
description: The four keys become four directions: propose a target cell, clamp it to the map, then move — first without erasing (he smears), then with the naive erase (the floor pays). Honest movement, with its costs on show.

title: Taming the Key
description: Pay the WAY-TOO-FAST debt: a combined any-key scan, a countdown timer that gates the step, and a release re-arm — so a tap is one step, instantly, and a hold is a stride at a chosen pace.

title: Save and Restore
description: Repay the gouge: a nine-byte buffer remembers what the lamplighter stands on — eight bitmap rows and an attribute — and the move becomes a dance with a strict order: restore, step, save, draw.

title: Walls
description: The map gets opinions: two brick buildings arrive as rectangle data, walk on as paint you can ghost through — then wall_at bit-tests the target cell's attribute, and everything brick turns solid at once.

title: Edges
description: Retire the scaffold: prove the numeric clamp is dead code by moving its fence where you can see it, then delete it whole — the square's own walls are the boundary, and the movement core converges with the finished game, byte for byte.

title: The Lamps
description: The game's first real objects: an unlit lantern glyph, drawn once the direct way — then eight of them scattered from a data table, standing on walkable floor, and surviving the lamplighter's passage untouched.

title: Light It
description: Give crossing a lamp its consequence — the obvious way first, painting the screen, and the light won't stay. Then the real way: edit the lamp's nine bytes while the buffer holds them, and restore paints it back lit, permanently.

title: The Tally
description: Give the game a score you read at a glance: eight pip cells on the HUD ledge that's been waiting since Unit 2, one byte counting lit lamps, and a hook in the single line where cold becomes lit.

title: The Square Warms
description: Progress becomes atmosphere: the frame's colour stops being a constant and becomes a nine-entry ramp indexed by lit_count — dusk stone, warming mortar, a bright glow, and gold at eight — repainted at the same event that warms a pip.

title: The Night Is Held
description: The game learns to end: printing with the Spectrum's own ROM font — demonstrated on a claim nobody earned — then a game_state byte, a gated loop, and a win check that fires the frame the eighth lamp lights. THE NIGHT IS HELD.

title: The Draught
description: The dark gets its agent: a second cell sprite on the lamplighter's own engine, hunting him with one compare-and-step rule that reads as intent — ghosting through stone, tangling buffers on contact, and finally taught to stop at his side.

title: Lives, and the Fall of Night
description: Price the touch: three ember pips, a lose_life that respawns him through the same dance as any move — and the playtest lesson built wrong first: without the wisp's recoil, the night strip-mines every life in under a second.

title: A Small Sound
description: The beeper is one bit on one port, toggled by hand — and from it, three voices: a rising blip when a lamp catches, a fanfare for the night held, a settling sting for the fall. The machine clears its throat.

title: The Title
description: The game gets a front door: GLOAMING on a black void, PRESS SPACE, a dusk chime — built hardwired first, then done properly: the boot-time setup becomes init_game, and beginning becomes a thing the game can do, not just a thing that happens once.

title: Again
description: The last arrow: win or lose, SPACE returns you to a title that remembers your best night — what persists, what's reborn, and an input lock to make every transition deliberate. The state machine closes and the module converges on the shipped game — and then the winnability gate does its job: two bugs the proof found, a tie that steals a win and a wall that kills, closed for good.

title: Greypeak
description: An isometric arcade-adventure in the Knight Lore tradition, built on Y-sorted depth rendering.

title: Hard Rain
description: A run-and-gun with bosses, state-machine enemy AI and multi-directional action.

title: Lamplight
description: A single-screen collect-and-dodge: light every lamp while a creature stalks the room — your first masked sprite, drawn cleanly over the background.

title: Meet Assembly
description: Edit and run Z80 code, draw and move a character, and investigate faults across eight interactive lessons.

title: Change the border
description: Write a Z80 instruction, assemble it, and make a visible prediction.

title: A byte becomes pixels
description: Follow a byte from a labelled memory address through register A to the screen.

title: Build an eight-row shape
description: Draw a small image and discover why neighbouring screen rows are not neighbouring bytes.

title: Draw with a counted loop
description: Keep the picture, turn its patterns into data, and follow eight real screen writes through a Z80 loop.

title: Call a drawing routine
description: Draw twice with one routine, follow CALL and RET, and check what a routine needs and changes.

title: Move your character
description: Read O and P, keep a position in RAM, and erase and redraw a character within bounds.

title: Give movement a clock
description: Hold a direction, count frame interrupts, and change movement speed without changing the machine’s clock.

title: Find the first wrong step
description: Investigate a movement fault: reproduce it, test a hypothesis, inspect a decision, then repair and retest.

title: Meet the Machine
description: The assembly on-ramp. Before you build a game, meet the Z80 and the Spectrum one idea at a time — registers, memory, the screen, decisions, loops — until the machine stops feeling like magic.

title: Assemble and Run
description: Write three lines of assembly, turn them into a program with a build step, run it on the Spectrum, and watch the border change colour. Meet the loop you'll use all course.

title: LD Is Not LET
description: Meet the registers — the handful of physical, 8-bit stores inside the CPU. Move a value from A into B and back again, and watch the border prove it made the trip.

title: Everything Is a Number
description: A byte has no type. Discover that 65, $41, the letter 'A' and the bit-pattern %01000001 are one and the same byte — and meet hex, the way you'll read bytes from here on.
