title: A Street of Numbered Boxes
description: Meet memory — one long street of numbered boxes, each holding a byte. Store a byte at an address and read it back, the same round-trip you used for registers, now through RAM.

title: The Screen Is Memory
description: The big one. Discover that the screen is just a stretch of the same memory street — poke a byte to $4000 and pixels light up. No PLOT, no magic: the bits in the byte are the dots on the glass.

title: Colour Is a Separate Map
description: Find out where colour lives — a second map at $5800, one packed byte per cell, completely apart from the pixels. Colour a whole cell with a single byte and never touch a pixel.

title: Test, Then Jump
description: There's no IF on the Z80. Learn how the machine makes decisions instead — compare a value, which sets a flag, then jump on that flag. Build your own IF, and write your first labels.

title: The Machine Can Hear You
description: Read the keyboard the hard, honest way — pick a half-row, read a port, test one bit. Hold a key and watch the border react, every frame. The first time the machine answers to you.

title: A Finger on the Boxes
description: Stop baking addresses into instructions. Meet the pointer — HL as a finger you move along the memory street, writing as it goes — the idea behind every loop that fills the screen.

title: Counting Toward Zero
description: Hand the repetition to the machine. Load a count into B, and DJNZ runs the body that many times — one loop fills a whole row where last unit you stepped by hand.

title: Call, Return, and a Stack You Can See
description: Package a job into a subroutine you can call from anywhere — and watch where the machine remembers its way back: the stack, sitting in plain memory you can read.

title: Adding and Taking Away
description: The most ordinary thing of all, finally: maths. inc, dec, add and sub on a value — and the carry flag, the machine's way of telling you a byte just overflowed.

title: Working With Bits
description: Change one bit without disturbing the rest. Meet and, or and xor — clear, set and flip individual bits — the everyday way to flip a single flag like an attribute's BRIGHT.

title: Bigger Than a Byte
description: A byte stops at 255 — too small for an address. See how registers pair up into 16-bit numbers, and use add hl, de to step a pointer by more than one, the way a game walks down a wall.

title: The Machine Speaks Back
description: The 48K Spectrum has no sound chip. Sound is the CPU's own job: flip one bit of one port to push the speaker, wait, flip it back, wait — over and over. That square wave is the tone, and the CPU does nothing else while it plays. On this machine, you are the sound chip.

title: The Machine Trusts You
description: The last beat, and the most important. There's no error message, no bounds check, no guard rail — the machine does exactly what you wrote, even when you're wrong. Learn to debug by observing, not by reading errors.

title: Meteor Storm
description: Build a timed Z80 dodging game from pixels, independent objects and a measured update loop.

title: Carry a pixel into the next byte
Find a pixel in Spectrum memory
Give the interrupt a small job
Put steering on the frame clock
Distinguish a hit from a near miss
Walk the pool and reuse a slot
Make a storm with an end
Turn a score into readable digits
Keep the best time and score
Nibble Run
description: A maze chase: clear the dots before the hunters reach you, with chase AI and power-up states.

title: Ricochet
description: A bat-and-ball game built on smooth pre-shifted sprite motion and pixel-perfect collision.

title: Shadowkeep
description: Explore a darkened keep room by room — a place of many rooms, built on the engine you finish in The Long Night. The first game in Spectrum assembly you don't finish in an afternoon.

title: A Hooded Figure
description: Shadowkeep begins where The Long Night ended — the same engine, a new face. Design a hooded thief as eight bytes and stand him, alone, in the cold blue dark of the keep.

title: The First Hall
description: The thief stood on flat blue. A keep is made of stone, and stone has shade. Meet dithering — mixing two colours in the bitmap to get the shades between them — and build the keep's first room: a dark slate floor inside lit stone walls.

title: A Place to Move
description: Set the thief walking the hall. It's almost all Gloaming — keyboard, cell-step movement, save/restore, wall collision — with two keep-specific twists: the save buffer now carries dithered stone, and a wall is known by its light.

title: The Keep's Hand
description: One bordered box was baked into the code. The keep needs many shapes, so we describe a room as data: a tile palette, and a room map you can read as a picture in the source. The reward — pillars, and a thief who walks between them.

title: The Room Graph
description: One room is a picture; a keep is many pictures and a sense of which lies through each door. Build the room table — each room's map plus its four edge-links — and let the thief walk through a doorway into a second room.

title: Through the Doorway
description: Unit 5's room travel was a teleport to the centre. Make it a step: leave by one edge and arrive at the opposite edge of the next room, at the same height, mid-stride — so the flick reads as walking through a doorway.

title: The Hero Remembers
description: Each room is redrawn from its template every time you enter, so the keep forgets everything. Move the rooms into RAM, let the thief chalk his route as he goes, and watch the marks survive leaving and returning. The keep gains a memory.

title: Three Rooms
description: The flick-screen engine is complete — graph, doorways, memory. Now build a keep with it: three connected rooms, each with its own character, doors lined up so the whole thing reads as one place to explore. No new code, all design.

title: The Keep's Gold
description: Three rooms you can wander, and nothing to do in them. Scatter gold through the keep, let the thief lift each coin as he steps on it, and make the last one matter: collect them all and the keep stands.

title: Something in the Dark
description: The keep has never had anyone in it but you. Give it a second figure — a Warden, drawn the same way as the thief, with its own private patch of screen to save and restore — and set it walking a slow, fixed route of its own.

title: Join the Sleepers
description: The Warden walks, but it cannot touch you. Give its touch a consequence — the one the keep has lacked since the first room — and the Place stops being a walk and becomes a game: step where it steps, and you join the sleepers.

title: A Warden for Every Room
description: One Warden in one room is a demo. Turn the Warden into data — a table with a line per room — so every room instantiates its own patrol on the coins' ground, and the whole keep, at last, is a game.

title: Light and Shadow
description: The keep is a finished game — but lit like a warehouse, every cell the same cold blue. Hang a torch and let the dithering you met in Unit 2 become lighting: pick each floor cell's shade by its distance from the flame, so a pool of light fades into the dark.

title: Furnishings
description: A lit room is still a bare room. Add the things light falls on — a statue, banners, a scatter of rubble — as tiles in the palette. Bright ones you walk around, dim ones you walk over, and the keep starts to feel inhabited.

title: Mood through Constraint
description: The lighting engine is built; now compose with it. Give each room its own falloff — one byte — so the Hall reads as a broad lit chamber and the Vault as a near-black crypt lit only at the altar. Same two colours, same dither; restraint is the technique.

title: A Keep with Character
description: Compose the whole keep as one place. Let a room hold more than one torch — each floor cell lit by its nearest flame — and use that with per-room falloff to give every chamber its own character from one coherent toolset.

title: Footsteps and Doors
description: The keep's events already sound — coins chime, victory flourishes, capture tolls. What's missing is the sound of the place itself. From the same one-bit beeper, add a footfall under every step and a falling creak at every door: sound as place, not as feedback.

title: A Theme in One Voice
description: Write music on one bit. Turn the note-table into a tune the title loops while it waits — pitch/duration pairs driving the beep primitive — and compose a short, solemn theme in D minor. One voice, no harmony: the melody carries the whole mood alone, and the keypress is never swallowed.

title: Stand or Sleep
description: Everything is here — the game plays, sounds, lights and sings. This unit seals it: a hand-pixelled crown of stone over the title, and the course's own proof met head-on — a run to each ending, THE KEEP STANDS and THE KEEP SLEEPS, both reachable, both real. And the proof earns its keep: driven to the edge, it catches a tie that read a won game as a lost one — the same ordering bug that hid in Gloaming and The Long Night — and closes it.

title: Skyhawk
description: A horizontal shooter that puts many masked sprites on screen and scrolls the world smoothly in software.

title: Spectral Legacy
description: The commercial-quality capstone combining all techniques with professional distribution.

title: Starfall
description: A 128K vertical shooter with AY music and dense bullet patterns.

title: The Long Night
description: The night fights back. Pools of claimed light, a tendril of creeping dark, a grudge-bearing hunter and a five-watch night with a dawn at the end — built by upgrading the finished Gloaming, byte for byte, exactly as it happened.

title: The Dark Seeks the Light
description: The hunt generalises: a Manhattan scan over every lit lamp — and your own flame — replaces the single-target chase, and the wisp learns to take back what you lit, using your own saved-under trick against you.

title: It Carries Its Prize Home
description: Behaviour needs rhythm, not just rules: a one-byte mode flag gives the wisp a cycle — hunt, snuff, withdraw, rest — and every theft buys the lamplighter a window he can plan inside.

title: The Pools of Light
description: Claimed ground: every lit lamp warms the eight cells around it, rebuilt from lamp truth after every change — and the restore-both-movers discipline that keeps two sprites honest while the world recolours under them.

title: The Tendril
description: The night takes territory: every cell the wisp crosses turns to solid, impassable dark, held in a fixed-length ring buffer whose oldest claim always releases — no permanent walls, by construction — plus the two gap bugs the real build hit, and their fixes.

title: The Night Bears Grudges
description: The eraser problem: greedy-nearest camps your work, so the night learns to reclaim the ground it lost first — a lit-order queue replaces the Manhattan scan, and the sharpest design lesson in the module gets its name.

title: The Night Deepens
description: One dusk becomes a five-watch night: the run/watch state split, a win screen that deepens instead of ending, escalation as two data tables and a corner probe — and a small lie in the lives display, caught and fixed.

title: Dawn Breaks
description: A run needs an ending you can reach: the fifth watch held becomes the true win — a new state, the morning's own screen, and a blocking ceremony that sweeps the square gold row by row.

title: The Dusk Bells
description: The title's one-shot chime becomes a real tune — and a tune changes the input contract of every screen that returns to the title. Deaf rests, listening rests, a latched keypress, and the snuff finally finds its voice.

title: Your Longest Night
description: What deserves to survive changed: the best-lives row becomes the watches you survived — a replacement, not an addition, and the only unit whose diff removes working code from the game you inherited.

title: The Dawn Phrase
description: Motif discipline: the dawn gets its own voice — dusk's bell answered and reversed — auditioned by ear from three candidates in notation. Your build is the shipped game, byte for byte — and then the winnability gate does its work: a fifth-watch tie that denied the dawn, and a wall that killed through the wisp, both inherited from Gloaming's engine, both closed.

title: Wyrmhold
description: A sprawling arcade-adventure — a large interconnected world with inventory and a save system.

title: Sinclair BASIC reference lessons
description: Explore individual Spectrum BASIC commands, the keyboard, graphics, sound, saving and debugging.

title: The Keyboard Types Words
description: Type your first Sinclair BASIC line, run it, and read the report the Spectrum prints back. Meet the keyboard that types whole words from a single key — and the type-run loop you'll use all primer.

title: The Line Number Is an Address
description: Edit a program by its line numbers — replace a line by reusing its number, slip a new line into a gap, delete one, and LIST them in order. The number is the line's address, and that is the whole of editing.

title: PRINT, Properly
description: Give PRINT its punctuation — join text and numbers with a semicolon, line them up in columns with a comma, break a line with an apostrophe — then clear the screen with CLS and start the title card you'll grow all primer.

title: LET, and What You May Name
description: Store a value in a named box with LET, use it, and change it — then meet the Spectrum's own rule: numeric names can be long, but a text variable must be a single letter plus a dollar sign. See name$ fail, and learn why.

title: INPUT — the Program Listens
description: Make the program wait for the person at the keyboard. INPUT reads what they type into a variable — text into a single-letter dollar name, numbers into a numeric one — the first time the program responds to you, not just itself.

title: IF / THEN, the Spectrum Way
description: Make the program decide. IF ... THEN acts only when a condition holds — and Sinclair BASIC has operators of its own: <> for not-equal, AND and OR that are logical not bitwise, and no ELSE, so you write a second IF.

title: FOR / NEXT Counts For You
description: Repeat a block a set number of times without copying a single line. FOR ... NEXT counts from one number to another, hands you the count as a variable you can use, and counts backwards too with STEP.

title: GO TO, GO SUB, and the Game Loop
description: Build the loop every game runs on — keep asking until the player wins — with GO TO. Package a job and call it from anywhere with GO SUB and RETURN. And let the computer pick a secret number with RND.

title: The Screen Is a Grid
description: Place text anywhere with PRINT AT. The Spectrum's screen is a grid 32 columns wide and 24 rows tall, addressed from the top-left — so you can put a label in a corner, the centre, or wherever the layout needs it. The title card finds its spot.

title: Colour, and Text in Many Colours
description: Turn a grey screen into a Spectrum screen. INK, PAPER and BORDER set the colours; BRIGHT and FLASH add punch; and a loop that changes INK per letter paints text in every colour at once. The title card gets its palette.

title: The Machine Can Sing
description: Make a sound in one line. BEEP plays a note — you give it a length and a pitch — and a FOR loop turns a row of notes into a rising fanfare. The title card gets its voice.

title: Drawing With Light
description: Draw shapes, not just text. PLOT lights a pixel, DRAW runs a line from it, CIRCLE draws a circle — on a finer grid than the character one, measured from the bottom-left. A frame goes round the title card.

title: Making It Move
description: Bring the title card to life. Animation is draw, wait, erase, move, repeat — built from a loop, PRINT AT, and a pause, with nothing new to learn. And in the flicker of it, you'll see exactly why the Spectrum's legends wrote their games in assembly.

title: Keeping Your Work
description: A program you can't keep isn't yours yet. SAVE stores your program so it survives the machine switching off; LOAD brings it back. On a real Spectrum that's tape; in an emulator it's a file — but the words are the same.

title: When It's Wrong
description: The skill that separates getting it done from getting stuck. The Spectrum tells you how every program stopped — a code, a message, and the line. Read the report, read the state, and find out why; don't guess. The debugging mindset, as the primer's last lesson.

title: Brick Bash
description: Catch a pixel ball, aim its return and clear eighteen bricks.

title: Draw below the character grid
description: Draw and toggle a four-pixel ball while distinguishing pixel and character coordinates.

title: Send the ball bouncing
description: Propose and reflect a move before changing the ball on screen.

title: Put the paddle under your control
description: Build a rounded character paddle and attach the ball until serving.

title: Catch the falling ball
description: Use horizontal overlap to catch a falling two-pixel ball.

title: Break one brick
description: Separate a brick picture, its rectangle and its stored live state.

title: Give the wall an address
description: Inspect wall addresses, gaps and removed bricks before returning to play.

title: Break the whole wall
description: Connect the moving ball to a three-by-six wall of destructible bricks.

title: Aim with the paddle
description: Choose a left, vertical or right return from paddle contact.

title: Finish the round
description: Add instructions and check every start, retry and exit path.

title: Keep the game
description: Save and cold-load the complete eighteen-brick game.

title: Bright Spark
description: Build a four-panel memory game: store an order, play its signals, compare the player's response and grow a sixteen-round challenge.

title: Four choices on the screen
description: Build a labelled board from coloured character cells, then make one drawing routine serve four positions.

title: Give a choice a signal
description: Light and restore a panel, give it a note, then use the same cue routine for all four choices.

title: Remember an order
description: Store panel choices as text, find individual items and extend the order without losing its beginning.

title: Play the stored order
description: Read each stored choice, turn its digit into a panel number and play the sequence with a way to quit.

title: Let the player repeat it
description: Read one fresh valid choice, echo it, then compare a whole response with the stored order.

title: Grow a new round

description: The Spectrum's speaker has two positions. Everything anyone got out of one was made by moving between them at the right moments.

title: 48K, and Where It Goes
description: The machine is sold on 48K of memory. A useful amount of it is spoken for before your program starts.

title: Driving a C64 With No Hands
description: Automating a C64 headless for curriculum captures — five small ways the machine lies to you, and the one rule that catches them all: trust the machine's own state, not your eyes.

title: Filming a Race Condition
description: The fixed Amiga build refused to show its own bug — because a race condition's real inputs are cycles, and everything that costs cycles is secretly an input.

title: Pin Budget, Not Design Choice
description: Every 'weird' retro peripheral decision follows from one number — how many spare pins the chipset had. Find the pin budget first, and the quirks become the only options that fit.

title: The Game That Couldn't Be Won
description: Sixteen verified curriculum units added up to an unwinnable game — a jump one pixel short of the pit. The oldest distinction in testing, sixteen pixels wide and four months old.

title: The Sheep That Slid Off the Hay Bale
description: A pixel-every-nine-frames drift in an Amiga game turns out to be a torn longword read of the beam position — and the forty-year-old confirm-read idiom that fixes it.

title: The Slate That Came Out Blue
description: A dithered dark-slate checkerboard came out of the video encoder as flat bright blue. The culprit — 4:2:0 chroma subsampling — is a codec quietly doing the eye's job at the wrong scale.

title: What Attribute Clash Actually Taught
description: The Spectrum's one-colour-per-8×8-cell limit is its signature look — and the Ultimate 'proof' that you could do great sprites in a single cell is a myth. What the constraint really taught.

title: What You're Allowed to Call Things
description: Sinclair BASIC forbids a multi-letter string variable; the C64 treats 'speed' and 'spell' as the same variable. Neither naming rule is arbitrary — each is the interpreter's memory model, leaking through.

title: White Is the Colour of Not Yet
description: A headless Amiga capture came back blank and silent — a dead copper, a crashed program, broken past doubt. It was none of those. The machine hadn't finished booting.

title: The register is the bitfield
description: On the ZX Spectrum one byte to port $FE drives the border, speaker and tape at once — so you mask bits to set them. Where chmod 755 and packed flags come from.

title: Why the bytes come out backwards
description: The 6502 stores the low byte first, the 68000 the high byte first. Watch both side by side and see where garbled hex dumps and htons() come from.

title: Mario moves in fractions of a pixel
description: The NES has no floating point. Mario's momentum is 8.8 fixed-point — the same trick that keeps money in whole cents instead of a drifting float.

title: What a switch actually compiles to
description: A switch doesn't test your value — it uses it as an index to jump. The Z80 shows exactly what your compiler does, and why dense cases win.

title: The fastest function is the one you already ran
description: On the 68000 a multiply costs up to seventy cycles and sine doesn't exist — so you precompute a table and read it forever. Memoisation, demoscene-style.

title: A pointer is just an address you stored somewhere
description: Pointers feel abstract until a 6502 strips them bare — two bytes holding an address, and one addressing mode that goes and reads it.

title: Why everything is a power of two
description: The Z80 has no multiply instruction, so it lays bare why a power-of-two size makes modulo free — and why hash tables get rounded to 1,024.

title: Racing the beam
description: The NES has no framebuffer: the beam paints one scanline at a time, so all video work happens in vblank — where VSync, tearing and double buffering come from.

title: Code that rewrites itself
description: On the 6502 code was just bytes in RAM, so a program could rewrite its own instructions — the ancestor of every JIT and runtime codegen.

title: Why your structs have holes in them
description: On the 68000 a misaligned word read traps, it doesn't run slow. Struct padding is the silicon keeping every field on a legal even address.

title: Why there's a chip that does nothing but move memory
description: The Amiga's Blitter was a coprocessor that did nothing but move memory — and it's where 'offload the bulk work to dedicated hardware' begins.

title: "Stack overflow" is a real place
description: On the 68000 the stack is just the A7 register walking down through RAM — making stack frames, recursion's cost and 'stack overflow' all literal.

title: When 255 + 1 = 0
description: On a 6502, 255 + 1 = 0 and $80 is both 128 and −128. The byte quirks that look like language bugs are two's complement out in the open.

title: Why "unroll your loops" is real advice
description: On a 6502 the loop is not free — it's instructions that run every iteration. Count the cycles by hand and 'unroll your loops' stops being folklore.

title: Numeric Display

title: Progress Bar (BASIC)

title: Seven-Segment Digits (BASIC)

title: Alan Turing describes the Turing machine
description: Turing's theoretical 'universal machine' establishes the mathematical foundations of computation, defining what it means to compute.

title: World War II begins in Europe
description: Germany invades Poland, triggering a global conflict that will accelerate computing research through military necessity.

title: Colossus begins codebreaking at Bletchley Park
description: The world's first programmable electronic computer enters service breaking Nazi codes, though its existence remains secret for decades.

title: ENIAC becomes operational
description: The Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, the first general-purpose electronic computer, begins operation at the University of Pennsylvania.

title: World War II ends
description: The deadliest conflict in human history concludes, leaving behind technological advances that will reshape civilian life.

title: The transistor is invented at Bell Labs
description: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley invent the transistor, the tiny switch that will replace vacuum tubes and enable modern electronics.

title: OXO: the first graphical video game
description: Alexander Douglas creates OXO (noughts and crosses) for his Cambridge PhD thesis, the earliest known game with a visual display.

title: First fully transistorised computer built
description: The TRADIC, built by Bell Labs for the US Air Force, becomes the first computer to use transistors instead of vacuum tubes throughout.

title: The integrated circuit is invented
description: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments creates the first integrated circuit, putting multiple transistors on a single chip and launching the microelectronics revolution.

title: Yuri Gagarin becomes first human in space
description: Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin orbits Earth aboard Vostok 1, winning a major victory in the Space Race and inspiring a generation.

title: President Kennedy assassinated
description: The assassination of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas shocks the world and marks a turning point in American political culture.

title: Apollo 11 Moon landing
description: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin become the first humans to walk on the Moon, watched by an estimated 600 million people worldwide.

title: Intel releases the 4004 microprocessor
description: The first commercially available microprocessor launches, putting a complete CPU on a single chip and making personal computing possible.

title: OPEC oil embargo triggers energy crisis
description: Arab oil producers embargo Western nations, quadrupling oil prices and triggering a global recession that reshapes the world economy.

title: Fall of Saigon ends Vietnam War
description: North Vietnamese forces capture Saigon, ending two decades of American involvement in Vietnam and reshaping US foreign policy.

title: Star Wars released
description: George Lucas's space opera transforms cinema, creates the modern blockbuster, and inspires a generation of game developers.

title: Sony Walkman launches
description: The portable cassette player creates a new category of personal electronics and demonstrates the appeal of technology you carry with you.

title: John Lennon murdered
description: The murder of former Beatle John Lennon outside his New York apartment marks the end of an era and sparks global mourning.

title: IBM PC launched
description: IBM's entry into personal computing legitimises the market and establishes the architecture that dominates business computing for decades.

title: MTV begins broadcasting
description: Music Television launches with 'Video Killed the Radio Star,' creating a new visual medium that transforms pop culture and advertising.

title: Apple Macintosh launched
description: Apple's Macintosh introduces the graphical user interface to mass audiences, heralded by the iconic '1984' Super Bowl advertisement.

title: Live Aid concerts
description: Simultaneous concerts in London and Philadelphia raise over £100 million for Ethiopian famine relief, watched by 1.9 billion people.

title: Space Shuttle Challenger disaster
description: The Space Shuttle Challenger breaks apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew members and halting the US space programme.

title: Chernobyl nuclear disaster
description: An explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear plant in Soviet Ukraine becomes the worst nuclear accident in history, with global repercussions.

title: Black Monday stock market crash
description: Stock markets around the world crash, with the Dow Jones falling 22.6% in a single day—the largest one-day percentage decline in history.

title: Berlin Wall falls
description: East Germany opens the Berlin Wall, symbolically ending the Cold War division of Europe and beginning German reunification.

title: Tiananmen Square protests suppressed
description: Chinese military forces suppress pro-democracy protests in Beijing, with the iconic 'Tank Man' image broadcast worldwide.

title: Soviet Union dissolves
description: The Soviet Union officially dissolves after 69 years, ending the Cold War and reshaping global politics and economics.

title: World Wide Web goes public
description: Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web project goes public, laying the foundation for the internet as we know it today.

title: Nelson Mandela elected President of South Africa
description: Nelson Mandela becomes South Africa's first Black president after the country's first fully democratic election, ending apartheid.

title: Princess Diana dies in Paris crash
description: The death of Diana, Princess of Wales, in a Paris car crash triggers unprecedented global mourning and media coverage.

title: Y2K preparations reach fever pitch
description: The world prepares for potential computer chaos as the year 2000 approaches, highlighting society's dependence on software.

title: September 11 attacks reshape the world
description: Terrorist attacks on the United States trigger wars, surveillance expansion, and a fundamental shift in global politics and technology.

title: Facebook launches from a Harvard dorm room
description: Mark Zuckerberg's social network begins its rise to become the dominant platform connecting billions of people worldwide.

title: Apple launches the iPhone
description: Steve Jobs unveils a device that combines phone, music player, and internet communicator, launching the smartphone revolution.

title: Global financial crisis erupts
description: The collapse of Lehman Brothers triggers the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression, reshaping economies worldwide.

title: Minecraft begins its blocky conquest
description: Markus 'Notch' Persson releases an early version of Minecraft, a game that will become one of the best-selling of all time.

title: Steve Jobs dies
description: Apple's co-founder and visionary leader dies of pancreatic cancer at 56, ending an era of personal computing.

title: Kickstarter transforms game funding
description: Double Fine Adventure raises $3.3 million on Kickstarter, proving crowdfunding can revive genres abandoned by publishers.

title: Pokémon GO sends millions into the streets
description: Niantic's augmented reality game becomes a global phenomenon, briefly making mobile gaming a shared outdoor experience.

title: Nintendo Switch blurs home and portable gaming
description: Nintendo's hybrid console succeeds where Wii U failed, proving there's still a market for dedicated gaming hardware.

title: COVID-19 pandemic transforms daily life
description: A global pandemic forces billions indoors, accelerating digital transformation and making gaming more central to social connection.

title: ChatGPT sparks the AI revolution
description: OpenAI releases ChatGPT, bringing large language models to the mainstream and triggering a race to integrate AI into everything.

title: Retro gaming reaches mainstream acceptance
description: Classic gaming moves from niche hobby to mainstream culture, with official re-releases, preservation efforts, and record auction prices.

title: The Caverns: time to escape
description: Build a small world where the order of a turn makes its warnings useful.

title: Cipher: letters that remember
description: Build a word game whose revealed letters, unused alphabet and mistakes agree.

title: Dash — a finishable NES game
description: The NES track's on-ramp: steer a runner, time a jump over the sweep, collect three coins to turn the level. Seventeen units from a blank screen to a cartridge, all driven off the NMI loop.

title: Dice Roller: watch a sample form
description: Build a live probability experiment with counts, shares and comparable samples.

title: All four launch machines have a game you can finish
description: Spectrum, C64, Amiga and NES each now open with a complete game, built one technique at a time — a title screen, a win and a loss, the lot. Not a demo: a small game you can play to the end.

title: Locksmith: count each digit once
description: Build a four-digit deduction game in nine Spectrum BASIC lessons.

title: Aim a shot. Feel the difference.
description: Six interactive maths lessons explore aiming and fixed-point movement, with a new Game Feel playground alongside them.

title: Meet Assembly: predict, run, inspect
description: Eight interactive lessons connect Z80 instructions to pixels, movement and debugging.

title: Meet BASIC: from a greeting to your first story
description: Four new Spectrum BASIC lessons take you from your first instruction to a story you can change, save and share.

title: Meteor Storm: pixels, objects and a race against time
description: Build a Spectrum assembly game through 24 lessons with editable code and live machine inspection.

title: Night Patrol: read the guard
description: Build a BASIC stealth game with corner scans, cover and a file to bring home.

title: Quickstep: plan beyond the next gap
description: Build a six-lane Spectrum BASIC crossing through ten lessons, from a single moving lane to buffered controls.

title: The shipped games learned to be lost
description: A pass over every finished game to make sure each has real stakes — a win you earn and a loss you can genuinely hit. Flock now shows both its endings, and a couple of latent bugs that quietly made games un-losable are closed.

title: Three in a Row: read the opponent
description: Build a Spectrum BASIC opponent, inspect its decisions and discover a fork it misses.

title: Yearfall: a budget that remembers
description: Build a settlement whose food, land and population carry the consequences into later years.

subtitle: The C64 bible

title: The Complete Spectrum ROM Disassembly
description: Ian Logan and Frank O'Hara's 1983 Melbourne House book listed every byte of the ZX Spectrum ROM with commentary — turning the machine's most important 16 KB from a black box into a documented library. It was the fourth book in a run that started on the ZX80, and it is still the reference forty years on.
subtitle: Sinclair's 16 KB, printed and annotated line by line

title: Computer Battlegames
description: Usborne's 1982 type-in book featuring Hangman and other games that introduced countless children to programming.
subtitle: The book that launched a million programmers

title: Machine Code for Beginners
description: Usborne's remarkable 1983 book that taught assembly language to children through colourful illustrations.
subtitle: Assembly language made accessible

title: Mastering Machine Code on Your ZX Spectrum
description: Toni Baker's 1983 classic that taught a generation of Spectrum owners to program in Z80 assembly language.
subtitle: The definitive Spectrum assembly guide

title: Usborne computing books
description: Usborne Publishing's home-computer book series, launched in 1982, taught BASIC, machine code, and game-making to British children in colourful, cartoon-illustrated paperbacks priced under £3. Titles like Computer Spacegames, Machine Code for Beginners, and Write Your Own Adventure Programs sold in the millions, defined an entire generation's expectation of what 'a programming book' looked like, and were re-released as free PDFs in 2016. The explicit pedagogical bar the Code198x BASIC track is calibrated against.
subtitle: The illustrated children's programming books that taught Britain to code

title: Aminet
description: The massive FTP archive that preserved Amiga software, art, music, and demos - one of the largest software repositories of its era and a crucial preservation resource for the platform.
subtitle: The Amiga archive

title: BBS Door Games
description: Turn-based multiplayer games that ran on bulletin board systems, allowing multiple callers to compete asynchronously before broadband internet made real-time online gaming possible.
subtitle: Multiplayer before the internet

title: BBS Scene
description: Bulletin Board Systems connected computer enthusiasts before the internet, enabling file sharing, messaging, and online gaming through dial-up modems.
subtitle: Pre-internet communities

title: The Chiptune Scene
description: The chiptune scene transformed the bleeps and bloops of gaming hardware into a recognised musical genre, with dedicated composers, festivals, and a global community.
subtitle: When game music became an art form

title: Crack Intros
description: Crack intros—screens added to pirated software announcing the cracking group—evolved from simple text into elaborate technical showcases that birthed the demo scene.
subtitle: Piracy's unexpected art form

title: Cracking Scene
description: The cracking scene transformed software piracy into a competitive culture that trained generations of programmers and directly spawned the demo scene.
subtitle: Where the scene began

title: Demo Parties
description: Demo parties brought programmers, musicians, and artists together for weekend competitions, creating the demo scene's most celebrated works and lifelong friendships.
subtitle: Where the scene gathers

title: Demo Scene
description: The demo scene emerged from crack intros into a global subculture where programmers, artists and musicians make real-time audiovisual productions, competing to get more out of a machine than its designers ever demonstrated.
subtitle: Art from hardware limits

title: The Rise of Esports
description: Competitive gaming evolved from Space Invaders tournaments to million-dollar leagues, turning players into athletes and gaming into spectator sport.
subtitle: From arcade high scores to professional gaming

title: Fan Translations
description: Fan translations brought Japanese RPGs and other games to English-speaking audiences, enabling players to experience titles that publishers never officially localised.

title: Fighting Game Community
description: The Fighting Game Community developed from arcade competition into a global grassroots movement with its own culture, terminology, and major tournament circuit.
subtitle: The FGC

title: LAN Parties

title: Ludum Dare
description: Ludum Dare is the world's longest-running online game jam, challenging developers to create complete games in 48 or 72 hours around a community-voted theme.

title: Modding

title: Speedrunning
description: Speedrunning transformed game completion into competitive sport, with players exploiting glitches and perfecting routes to achieve seemingly impossible times.
subtitle: Racing against time

title: Total Conversions
description: Total conversions replaced everything in a game—art, sound, gameplay—creating entirely new experiences on existing engines, sometimes rivalling commercial releases in scope.
subtitle: Complete game overhauls

title: 3D Realms
description: 3D Realms created Duke Nukem and pioneered shareware distribution, building a gaming empire from the shareware model before the infamous Duke Nukem Forever development saga.
subtitle: Duke Nukem creators

title: Acclaim Entertainment
description: Acclaim built a business on licensed games, from early NES sports titles to controversial marketing, experiencing both tremendous success and eventual bankruptcy.
subtitle: Licensed game giant

title: Accolade
description: Founded by two Activision founders, and the defendant in the 1992 case that established reverse engineering for compatibility as lawful — the reason console makers cannot control who publishes for their machines.

title: Acid Software
description: Mark Sibly's New Zealand company that created Blitz Basic and developed games like Skidmarks, proving that compiled BASIC could produce commercial hits.

title: Acorn Computers
description: Acorn Computers built the BBC Micro, won hearts in British schools, and spawned ARM—the processor architecture now in billions of devices.
subtitle: The British computer pioneer

description: Acorn's own software arm, and the original publisher of Elite. Acornsoft sold games at education-machine prices to the owners of a computer sold as an educational tool — and put out the game the period press held up as the standard the industry could no longer reach.
subtitle: The label that published Elite

title: Activision
description: Founded by rebellious Atari programmers who wanted credit for their work, Activision invented third-party publishing and proved developers mattered.
subtitle: The first third-party publisher

title: Alligata Software

subtitle: Three Sizzlers in one issue, all re-releases

subtitle: Kick Off, and what happens when you change the view

title: Ape Inc.
description: Ape Inc. developed the Mother/EarthBound series under Shigesato Itoi's direction before reorganising into Creatures Inc. and becoming part of the Pokémon empire.
subtitle: Mother's creators

title: Apogee Software
description: The company that invented the modern shareware model, giving away the first episode free to sell the rest - launching Commander Keen, Duke Nukem, and publishing Wolfenstein 3D.
subtitle: Shareware pioneers

title: Argonaut Software
description: Jez San's Argonaut Software pioneered 3D graphics on home computers and co-developed Nintendo's Super FX chip, shaping console gaming's polygonal future.
subtitle: 3D before its time

title: Ariolasoft
description: A record company's software arm that held the British rights to Electronic Arts and Broderbund — the reason Marble Madness, Archon and Lode Runner arrived in UK shops with an unfamiliar name on the box.
subtitle: How American software reached Britain

title: Arkane Studios
description: Arkane Studios kept immersive sim design alive when publishers abandoned the genre, delivering Dishonored, Prey, and Deathloop while maintaining creative integrity under corporate ownership.
subtitle: Immersive sim torchbearers

title: Atari Games
description: Atari Games continued Atari's arcade legacy after the company split, creating classics like Gauntlet, Paperboy, and the Hard Drivin' series throughout the late 1980s and 1990s.
subtitle: Arcade division

title: Atari
description: Atari created the video game industry with Pong, dominated it with the 2600, and nearly destroyed it through hubris and shovelware.
subtitle: The company that started it all

title: Atlantis Software
description: A budget house of the first wave whose catalogue mixed arcade games with computerised card and board games — the £1.99 shelf where casual gaming quietly begins.
subtitle: Connect 4 at £1.99

title: Atlus
description: Atlus carved a niche with mature, challenging JRPGs through Shin Megami Tensei and Persona, building devoted audiences who appreciated darker themes and demanding gameplay.
subtitle: Demon summoners

title: Audiogenic
description: A publisher that found a niche the arcade converters ignored — proper sports simulations, cricket above all — and worked it for fifteen years across five machine generations.
subtitle: Cricket, and the long tail

title: Beam Software
description: The Australian game developer founded in 1980, creators of The Hobbit text adventure's revolutionary parser, and one of the southern hemisphere's most significant studios.
subtitle: Australian developer

title: Beau Jolly
description: A London company that made no games at all. It bought the marketing rights to other publishers' catalogues, packaged them ten at a time, and spent a quarter of a million pounds on television advertising.
subtitle: Ten games, one cassette, £9.95

title: Bemani
description: Bemani developed Konami's rhythm game empire including Beatmania, Dance Dance Revolution, and Guitar Freaks, dominating Japanese arcades through dedicated music gaming.
subtitle: Konami's music division

title: Bethesda Game Studios
description: Bethesda Game Studios created the modern open-world RPG template with Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim, delivering vast explorable worlds at the cost of technical polish.
subtitle: Open world pioneers

title: Bethesda Softworks
description: Bethesda Softworks created vast open-world RPGs with The Elder Scrolls and later acquired Fallout, building immersive sandbox worlds where player freedom trumps narrative linearity.
subtitle: Open world RPG masters

title: Beyond Software
description: The publisher of Lords of Midnight and Doomdark's Revenge, whose 'landscaping' technique put a vast explorable world on a 48K machine — before being absorbed into British Telecom's software arm.
subtitle: Landscaping the Spectrum

title: BioWare
description: BioWare defined modern Western RPGs through companion relationships, moral choices, and cinematic presentation in Baldur's Gate, Knights of the Old Republic, and Mass Effect.
subtitle: Story-driven RPGs

title: The Bitmap Brothers
description: The Bitmap Brothers combined striking metallic visual design with polished gameplay, creating Speedball 2, Xenon 2, and The Chaos Engine.
subtitle: Style meets substance

title: Black Isle Studios
description: Black Isle Studios delivered Fallout 2, Planescape: Torment, and Icewind Dale before Interplay's collapse scattered its talent across the industry.
subtitle: CRPG golden age

title: Blizzard Entertainment
description: Blizzard Entertainment built an empire on exceptionally polished games, from Warcraft and StarCraft to Diablo and World of Warcraft, defining genres through refinement rather than invention.
subtitle: Polish perfected

title: BlueSky Software
description: BlueSky Software created technically impressive games for Sega platforms, including Vectorman and its sequel, showcasing the Mega Drive's capabilities in its twilight years.
subtitle: Vectorman developers

title: Brøderbund
description: Brøderbund published landmark titles including Prince of Persia, Lode Runner, and Carmen Sandiego, maintaining high quality standards across games and educational software.
subtitle: Quality software publisher

title: Bubble Bus Software
description: A Kent publisher whose fortunes rested on one programmer, Stephen Crow, and one game — Starquake, a 500-room exploration platformer that was still being called an 8-bit classic years after the machines it ran on were obsolete.
subtitle: 87 High Street, Tonbridge

title: Bug-Byte
description: Founded in May 1980 by two Liverpool chemistry students, Bug-Byte was one of the first British software houses of any size — publishing for the Acorn Atom and the ZX81 in parallel, shipping the ZX81's best-regarded assembler, and putting out Matthew Smith's Manic Miner in 1983. It also lost its staff twice: to Imagine in January 1983 and to Software Projects a year later. It went into receivership in June 1985.
subtitle: Liverpool's first software house, and the one everyone else walked out of

title: Bullfrog Productions
description: Bullfrog Productions created Populous, Theme Park, and Dungeon Keeper, pioneering god games and business simulations under Peter Molyneux's direction.
subtitle: God game inventors

title: Bungie
description: Bungie created Marathon, defined console FPS with Halo, and pioneered live-service gaming with Destiny, evolving from indie Mac developer to industry giant.
subtitle: From Mac shooters to console dominance

title: Camelot Software Planning
description: Camelot Software Planning created the Shining Force series for Sega before becoming Nintendo's premier sports game developer with Mario Golf and Mario Tennis.
subtitle: Tactical RPG pioneers

title: Capcom
description: Japanese developer Capcom created Street Fighter, Mega Man, Resident Evil, and countless arcade classics, shaping gaming for decades.
subtitle: From arcade to empire

title: Cascade Games
description: The Leeds company behind Cassette 50 — fifty games on one tape for £9.95, on a dozen incompatible machines, with a calculator watch thrown in. The most famous bad deal in British home computing.
subtitle: Fifty games and a free watch

title: Cavedog Entertainment
description: Cavedog Entertainment created Total Annihilation, pushing RTS toward unprecedented scale before parent company GT Interactive's collapse ended the studio's promising trajectory.
subtitle: Total ambition

title: CentreSoft
description: Geoff and Anne Brown started distributing games from a Halesowen office with milk crates for chairs in 1983. CentreSoft became Britain's largest games distributor, and its credit line is what made U.S. Gold possible a year later.
subtitle: The Halesowen distributor that grew a publisher

title: Chunsoft
description: Chunsoft developed Dragon Quest's early entries and created the Mystery Dungeon roguelike series before merging to form Spike Chunsoft.
subtitle: Mystery Dungeon creators

title: Cinemaware
description: Cinemaware pioneered cinematic gaming with Defender of the Crown and It Came from the Desert, combining Hollywood production values with varied gameplay in ambitious multimedia experiences.
subtitle: Interactive movies

title: Clickteam
description: The company founded by François Lionet after AMOS, creating Klik & Play, The Games Factory, and Fusion - continuing the mission of accessible game development.
subtitle: Game creation evolved

title: Climax Entertainment
description: Climax Entertainment crafted distinctive action-adventures with isometric perspectives, creating Landstalker and its spiritual successors across multiple Sega platforms.
subtitle: Isometric adventure specialists

title: Cloanto
description: The Italian software company that legally owns and preserves the classic Commodore and Amiga system ROMs, distributing them through Amiga Forever and C64 Forever.
subtitle: Keepers of the Commodore and Amiga ROMs

title: Codemasters
description: Codemasters, founded in 1986 by brothers Richard and David Darling after they left Mastertronic, became the British budget-games scene's most successful publisher of the late 1980s — home to the Oliver Twins' Dizzy franchise, the Simulator series, and the Game Genie console-cheat device. The company survived the 8-bit transition, grew into a major PC and console publisher in the 1990s and 2000s, and was acquired by Electronic Arts in 2021 for $1.2 billion.
subtitle: From £1.99 cassettes to Formula 1 — the Darling brothers' four-decade trajectory

title: Commodore
description: From typewriter repair to the best-selling computer ever, Commodore's C64 and Amiga defined home computing for millions.
subtitle: Computers for the masses, not the classes

title: Compile
description: Compile created the Puyo Puyo puzzle phenomenon and developed acclaimed shoot-em-ups including Zanac and Aleste, before financial troubles led to their closure and IP sales.
subtitle: Puyo Puyo and shooters

title: Compupress
description: Compupress published Computer για Όλους, then spun Pixel out of it in October 1983 on the strength of a reader questionnaire, and added PC Master in 1989. Both surviving titles in this library are its, under the same publisher, Nikos Manousos, across at least six years.
subtitle: The Athens publisher behind Greece's computer press

title: Core Design
description: Core Design created Lara Croft and Tomb Raider, defining 3D action-adventure before annual sequels and franchise fatigue led to the series leaving their hands.
subtitle: Tomb Raider creators

title: Creatures Inc.
description: Creatures Inc. co-owns the Pokémon franchise alongside Nintendo and Game Freak, developing spin-off games and managing the trading card game.
subtitle: Pokémon's third pillar

title: Criterion Games
description: Criterion Games pioneered spectacular crash physics with Burnout before taking over Need for Speed, demonstrating technical innovation in arcade racing.
subtitle: Burnout's architects

title: CRL Group
description: CRL spent its first years buying properties it could put on a cassette inlay — the Magic Roundabout, Gerry Anderson, a Jeff Wayne record. When it wanted Blade Runner and could not trace the film rights, it licensed the Vangelis soundtrack instead and shipped a game of the score. The BBFC certificates that made it famous came from the same instinct, and Clement Chambers defended them on a point of law.
subtitle: The licence chasers who accidentally invented games censorship

title: Cyan
description: Cyan created Myst and its sequels, pioneering contemplative puzzle design and CD-ROM gaming before continuing to explore mysterious worlds through decades of development.
subtitle: Myst creators

title: Data East
description: Data East developed diverse arcade games from BurgerTime's food-based platforming to Bad Dudes' action brawling, creating memorable experiences across multiple genres.
subtitle: Arcade variety

title: Daze
description: A small British distributor that carried French, German and Finnish Amiga games into UK shops in the mid-nineties — the last working version of the import route that ran through the whole era.
subtitle: The route continental games took in

title: Delphine Software
description: French studio Delphine Software created *Another World* and *Flashback*, games that elevated interactive storytelling through rotoscoped animation and cinematic presentation.
subtitle: Cinematic ambition

title: Denton Designs
description: Formed in September 1984 by five ex-Imagine staff in Liverpool's medical district, Denton Designs ran as a co-operative facilities house and produced Shadowfire, Frankie Goes to Hollywood, The Great Escape and Where Time Stood Still.
subtitle: Five people who walked out of Imagine's collapse and kept working

title: Design Design
description: A Manchester house with a jokey authorial voice and a serious technical reputation, whose 1986 compilation Working Backwards was sold as 'the first concept album' — four games including one that had never been released, on the shelf at Woolworth.
subtitle: The first computer game concept album

title: The Designers Republic
description: The Designers Republic brought graphic design credibility to gaming through WipEout's visual identity, proving games could be culturally cool through aesthetic sophistication.
subtitle: Gaming's graphic identity

title: Devolver Digital
description: Devolver Digital built a publishing identity around distinctive indie games and anarchic marketing, championing developers while mocking industry conventions.
subtitle: Indie's wild card

title: DICE
description: Digital Illusions CE, the Swedish studio with demo scene roots that created the Battlefield series, Mirror's Edge, and became one of gaming's most technically accomplished developers.
subtitle: Swedish scene to Battlefield

title: DISMAC
description: DISMAC began on 25 January 1973 selling imported calculators, moved to making them, and by 1981 was selling the D-8000 — which Micro Sistemas called the first Brazilian personal computer. Its commercial director gave that magazine's first issue the clearest account this library holds of why Brazilian machines were built the way they were.
subtitle: From imported calculators to a Brazilian personal computer

title: DMA Design
description: DMA Design emerged from Dundee, Scotland to create Lemmings' puzzle innovation and Grand Theft Auto's open-world crime gameplay, later becoming Rockstar North.
subtitle: From Lemmings to GTA

title: Domark
description: Domark is remembered for licences — Bond, Star Wars, Trivial Pursuit — but it began with Eureka!, an original 250K adventure devised by Ian Livingstone, programmed by Hungarians working for Andromeda, and sold on a secret telephone number worth £25,000 to whoever found it first. It sold 50,000 copies in Britain.
subtitle: Started with £25,000 hidden in a game written behind the Iron Curtain

title: Dragon Data
description: The Welsh computer company that produced the Dragon 32 and 64 from 1982-1984, bringing 6809-based computing to the UK market before folding due to competition.
subtitle: Welsh computer company

title: Durell Software
description: A quantity surveyor who left the Oxford Regional Health Authority because he was bored built one of the most consistently well-reviewed publishers of the Spectrum era from an attic in Somerset — and trained its programmers on games it never released.
subtitle: An Oric on a desk in Taunton

title: EA Sports
description: EA Sports dominated sports gaming through aggressive licensing, annual releases, and franchises covering every major sport, building a multi-billion dollar business.
subtitle: It's in the game

title: Edizioni Hobby
description: Edizioni Hobby s.r.l. of Via della Spiga, Milan, published Italian editions of Zzap! from May 1986 and The Games Machine from September 1988, both under licence from Newsfield of Ludlow. Both titles passed to Xenia Edizioni in September 1991, the year Newsfield collapsed.
subtitle: The Milanese publisher that licensed Newsfield's magazines for Italy

title: Eidos Interactive
description: British publisher Eidos rose to prominence with *Tomb Raider* and became a major force in 1990s gaming before acquisition by Square Enix.
subtitle: Lara Croft's keepers

title: Electric Dreams Software
description: A UK imprint run out of Activision's Wellingborough operation, holding Sega licences and publishing Spindizzy — a game that took a year to build and swept every format award going.
subtitle: Activision's British label

title: Electronic Arts
description: Trip Hawkins founded Electronic Arts with a revolutionary idea: treat game developers like artists and put their names on the box.
subtitle: We see farther

title: Elite Systems
description: Steve Wilcox's Walsall publisher won Amtix's Best Software House of 1986 while one of its own conversions placed third in Least Pleasing Game — the coin-op business in a single page. Elite advertised openly for contract programmers, pioneered the multi-game compilation, and put a holographic sticker on every cassette.
subtitle: Anchor House, Aldridge

title: EMAP
description: EMAP published Computer and Video Games from its first issue in 1981, Sinclair User from 1982, Commodore User and its successor CU Amiga from 1983, and later ACE and The One. Five of this Vault's magazine entries are the same company, and it had none of its own.
subtitle: The Clerkenwell publisher behind most of the magazines

title: Empire Interactive
description: A British publisher that sold tank simulations and flight sims at £34.99 while the rest of the market sold platformers at £25.99 — and priced for an audience that would pay it.
subtitle: The expensive end of the Amiga

title: Enix
description: Enix published Dragon Quest, Japan's most beloved RPG series, establishing the template for Japanese role-playing games before merging with rival Square in 2003.
subtitle: Dragon Quest's publisher

title: Ensemble Studios
description: Ensemble Studios created the Age of Empires series, delivering historical RTS excellence for Microsoft before closure in 2009 despite consistent critical and commercial success.
subtitle: Age of excellence

title: Epic Games
description: Tim Sweeney's Epic Games evolved from shareware publisher to Unreal Engine creator to *Fortnite* phenomenon, reshaping game development and distribution.
subtitle: From shareware to Fortnite

title: Epyx
description: Epyx created the Games series (Summer, Winter, California) and innovative action titles, pioneering sports compilations and establishing the joystick-waggling gameplay that defined an era.
subtitle: Games by gamers

title: Europress
description: Europress owned Database Publications, published Amiga Computing from 1988, and took CRASH and ZZAP!64 when Newsfield collapsed in 1991. Its subsidiary Europress Impact ran the acquired titles from Newsfield's own address in Ludlow rather than moving them to Cheshire. At the end of 1994 Europress sold eleven magazines to IDG.
subtitle: The Macclesfield publisher that kept CRASH in Ludlow

title: Eutechnyx
description: Eutechnyx developed racing games across multiple platforms for decades, from early motorsport titles through licensed NASCAR games before studio troubles in the 2010s.
subtitle: Racing specialists

title: Factor 5
description: Factor 5 emerged from the German demo scene to create technically stunning games—from Turrican on C64 to Star Wars: Rogue Squadron on N64.
subtitle: Technical wizards

title: Nihon Falcom
description: Nihon Falcom pioneered action RPGs with Ys and Dragon Slayer in the 1980s, maintaining independence through decades while creating sprawling interconnected worlds in the Trails series.
subtitle: Action RPG pioneers

title: Firebird
description: British Telecom's software label, set up in 1984 by its New Information Services Division — £2.50 tapes chosen from two thousand unsolicited submissions, plus the premium Rainbird imprint named after the man who ran it.
subtitle: British Telecom’s budget-to-premium powerhouse

title: Flair Software
description: A small British publisher whose games filled the CD32's final retail pack — including the one the £299 bundle was named after.
subtitle: Two of the four games in Commodore's last bundle

title: Frictional Games
description: Frictional Games proved that vulnerability creates terror, pioneering weaponless horror design with Penumbra and Amnesia that influenced an entire generation of indie developers.
subtitle: Horror through helplessness

title: FromSoftware
description: FromSoftware is a Japanese developer known for the Souls series, creating a genre of demanding action RPGs that reward patience and skill.
subtitle: Masters of challenging action RPGs

title: Frontier Developments
description: David Braben's Frontier Developments carried forward the *Elite* legacy while building simulation games and theme park management titles.
subtitle: Elite's legacy continues

title: Future Publishing
description: The UK publishing company that built an empire of gaming magazines including Amiga Format, Amiga Power, PC Gamer, and many others, becoming one of the largest gaming media companies in the world.
subtitle: Gaming magazine empire

title: Futuremark
description: Founded by Future Crew members, Futuremark turned demoscene craft into the industry-standard 3DMark benchmarks — performance tests that are, in essence, demos that keep score.
subtitle: The demo that became a benchmark

title: Galoob
description: The American toy company that distributed the Game Genie and won the landmark lawsuit against Nintendo, establishing the legality of game enhancement devices.
subtitle: Game Genie company

title: Game Freak
description: Game Freak evolved from a fan magazine into the developer of Pokémon, creating one of the world's most valuable media franchises from Satoshi Tajiri's childhood bug-collecting memories.
subtitle: Pokémon's developer

title: Gargoyle Games
description: Roy Carter and Greg Follis built a small Midlands house on literate, unhurried Spectrum adventures — Tir Na Nog, Dun Darach, Marsport — scoring 92, 97 and 95 in CRASH. Then, in 1986, they diagnosed their own commercial problem and launched a second label, Faster Than Light, to make the opposite kind of game. Its first release won Amtix's Best Shoot 'Em Up.
subtitle: Two men in Birmingham, making dense games slowly

title: GCE
description: General Consumer Electronics, the company that created the Vectrex console in 1982 before being acquired by Milton Bradley.
subtitle: Vectrex creators

title: Gilsoft
description: A pocket-money venture in South Wales that became the house behind The Quill, The Illustrator and PAW — the tools most British text adventures of the 1980s were written with.
subtitle: The Welsh Wizards of Adventure

title: Graftgold
description: Steve Turner quit his job in 1983 to write Spectrum games as ST Software, hired his friend Andrew Braybrook to handle Dragon conversions, and incorporated as Graftgold in 1984. It supplied Hewson's flagship output on both machines, signed exclusively to Telecomsoft in 1987, and lasted until 1998.
subtitle: A development house, not a publisher — and it outlasted most publishers

title: Grandslam Entertainments
description: Formerly Argus Press Software — the games label of a magazine house, and the third of three outside industries that walked into British software and found the distribution already suited them.
subtitle: A magazine publisher's software arm, renamed

title: Gremlin Graphics
description: Gremlin Graphics, founded in Sheffield in 1984 by Ian Stewart and Kevin Norburn, grew from a small Yorkshire software-shop publishing arm to one of the most consistent British mid-tier publishers of the 1980s and 1990s. The Monty Mole platformers gave the company its early identity; the Lotus Esprit Turbo Challenge series defined Amiga racing in the early 1990s; the Actua Sports series carried the brand into the PlayStation era. Acquired by Infogrames in 1999.
subtitle: Sheffield's mid-tier publisher — Monty Mole, Thing on a Spring, the Lotus trilogy, and the Actua Sports era

title: HAL Laboratory
description: HAL Laboratory created Kirby and the Super Smash Bros. series while serving as a key Nintendo partner, with future Nintendo president Satoru Iwata among its programmers.
subtitle: Kirby's home

title: Harmonix
description: Harmonix created the Western rhythm game phenomenon with Guitar Hero and Rock Band before transitioning through multiple acquisitions while maintaining their musical focus.
subtitle: Guitar Hero and Rock Band creators

title: Hello Games
description: Hello Games transformed No Man's Sky from gaming's most controversial launch into its greatest redemption story through years of silent, dedicated updates.
subtitle: From disaster to redemption

title: Hewson Consultants
description: Andrew Hewson's Hewson Consultants championed solo programmers and small teams from 1980 to 1991, publishing classics like Paradroid, Uridium, Cybernoid, and Stormlord — and putting their developers' names on the cassette covers when most publishers kept programmers anonymous.
subtitle: The publisher that put the developer's name on the box

title: Hitmaker
description: Sega's Hitmaker studio (formerly AM3) created *Crazy Taxi*, *Virtua Tennis*, and other arcade classics that defined late-1990s coin-op gaming.
subtitle: Sega's arcade innovators

title: Hudson Soft
description: Hudson Soft created Bomberman, co-developed the PC Engine/TurboGrafx-16 with NEC, and pioneered multiplayer gaming with their iconic bomb-laying franchise.
subtitle: Bomberman's creators

title: id Software
description: id Software created Commander Keen, Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, and Quake, defining PC gaming and pioneering shareware distribution.
subtitle: The house that Doom built

title: IDG
description: International Data Group bought the Europress magazine titles late in 1994 — Amiga Computing, Amiga Action and nine others — and ran them from the same Macclesfield offices under IDG Media. Europress's founder framed the deal as IDG filling the one gap in a network of 220 publications across 64 countries: Britain.
subtitle: The American publisher that bought eleven British computer magazines at the end of 1994

title: Imagine Publishing
description: Incorporated in February 2005 and publishing from Richmond Hill in Bournemouth, Imagine bought Retro Gamer out of Live Publishing's collapse that October and ran it for eleven years, until Future acquired the company in 2016.
subtitle: The Bournemouth house that rescued Retro Gamer from the receivers

title: Imagine Software
description: Imagine Software, founded in Liverpool in 1982 by Mark Butler and Dave Lawson, rose in two years to become one of Britain's most-hyped games publishers — Porsches, full-page magazine adverts, the famous Megagames Bandersnatch and Psyclapse — before collapsing spectacularly in July 1984 with the BBC's Commercial Breaks documentary crew in the office. The footage of bailiffs arriving on camera remains one of the era's most-cited business cautionary tales, and the company's fall reshaped the British games industry: Ocean acquired the brand, ex-Imagine staff founded Psygnosis, and the Liverpool scene's centre of gravity shifted permanently.
subtitle: The Liverpool publisher whose collapse was filmed live by the BBC

title: Impressions
description: A strategy house whose Amiga credits list the people who went on to build Sierra's city-building series and then Firefly's Stronghold — a design lineage still shipping thirty years later.
subtitle: The line that runs to Stronghold

title: Incentive Software
description: Incentive built Freescape, the first engine to give 8-bit home computers a genuine filled-polygon 3D world — then sold it to players as a construction kit.
subtitle: Solid 3D on an 8-bit machine

title: Infocom
description: Infocom perfected the text adventure, creating Zork, Hitchhiker's Guide, and dozens of games that proved words could be as immersive as graphics.
subtitle: Masters of interactive fiction

title: Infogrames
description: A Lyon publisher whose games reached the British press from 1986 — police procedurals and odd puzzle games among the arcade conversions, and evidence that the 8-bit era was never a national story.
subtitle: French games in British magazines

title: Insomniac Games
description: Insomniac Games created Spyro and Ratchet & Clank for PlayStation before expanding to multiplatform development with Spider-Man and other action titles.
subtitle: Spyro and Ratchet creators

title: Intelligent Systems
description: Intelligent Systems developed Fire Emblem's tactical RPG template, Advance Wars' turn-based combat, and Paper Mario's RPG adventures as a key Nintendo partner.
subtitle: Strategy specialists

title: Interplay Entertainment
description: Interplay Entertainment published defining RPGs including Baldur's Gate, Fallout, and Planescape: Torment, nurturing studios that would shape Western role-playing games.
subtitle: RPG powerhouse

title: IO Interactive
description: Danish studio IO Interactive created the *Hitman* series, defining the stealth sandbox genre with meticulous level design and dark humour.
subtitle: Masters of stealth

title: Ion Storm
description: Ion Storm's Austin studio delivered Deus Ex and Thief sequels while the Dallas office imploded around Daikatana, demonstrating how team culture matters more than resources.
subtitle: Design is law

title: Irem
description: Irem developed influential arcade games including Moon Patrol's parallax scrolling and R-Type's demanding shoot-em-up design, establishing techniques that defined their genres.
subtitle: R-Type's creators

title: Irrational Games
description: Irrational Games combined first-person gameplay with literary ambitions, creating System Shock 2 and BioShock before closing in 2014 as Ken Levine pursued smaller-scale development.
subtitle: Thinking philosophically

title: Kixx
description: U.S. Gold's budget imprint, launched in August 1988 at £2.99, whose business was selling yesterday's full-price games a second time — the model that kept British 8-bit software affordable, and profitable, into the 1990s.
subtitle: US Gold's second life for old hits

title: Kompart UK
description: The British publisher for German and Austrian developers in the mid-nineties — Blue Byte and Max Design — and the entry point for a strategy tradition that outlasted everything around it.
subtitle: How Blue Byte reached Britain

title: Konami
description: Japanese arcade pioneer Konami created Frogger, Gradius, and Castlevania, plus gaming's most famous cheat code.
subtitle: From jukeboxes to the Konami Code

title: Krisalis Software
description: A South Yorkshire house whose product was often the port and not the game — moving other people's software between machines, and taking German games to Britain and British games to the PC.
subtitle: Rotherham, and the business of conversion

title: Level 9
description: Level 9 Computing brought sophisticated text adventures to 8-bit machines, cramming Infocom-quality experiences into 48K of RAM.
subtitle: British interactive fiction pioneers

title: Lionhead Studios
description: Peter Molyneux's Lionhead Studios created Black & White and Fable, becoming synonymous with innovative game design and the gap between ambitious promises and delivered features.
subtitle: Ambition and promise

title: LJN
description: The Acclaim-owned toy company notorious for producing consistently poor licensed NES games, whose rainbow logo became a warning sign for quality-conscious gamers.
subtitle: The Rainbow of Death

title: Llamasoft
description: Founded by Jeff Minter, Llamasoft mixed arcade precision with absurd humour, mail-order hustle, and loyal fans.
subtitle: Psychedelic software from a Welsh farmhouse

title: Looking Glass Studios
description: Looking Glass Studios pioneered immersive simulations with System Shock and Thief, creating sophisticated game systems that trusted player intelligence before financial struggles closed the studio.
subtitle: Immersive sim creators

title: LucasArts
description: The legendary game studio that revolutionised adventure games with the SCUMM engine and a player-friendly design philosophy that eliminated unfair deaths and dead ends.
subtitle: The house that SCUMM built

title: Magnetic Scrolls
description: Magnetic Scrolls created the most sophisticated British text adventures—beautifully written, gorgeously illustrated, and technically advanced.
subtitle: Adventures in elegance

title: Marshall Cavendish
description: British publisher whose part-work magazines including Input taught computing to a generation through weekly collectible issues.
subtitle: Part-work publishers

title: Martech
description: A Sussex publisher that built its catalogue on personality licences — Eddie Kidd, Geoff Capes, Brian Jacks, Nigel Mansell — and made buying an audience into a business model.
subtitle: The name on the box was somebody famous

title: Mastertronic Added Dimension
description: Mastertronic's second budget tier, created when £1.99 stopped being enough to pay for an ambitious game — and the label that carried the Magic Knight adventures.
subtitle: £2.99, because £1.99 had a ceiling

title: Mastertronic
description: Mastertronic, founded in 1983 by Frank Herman, Terry Medway, Martin Alper, and Alan Sharam, built a British budget-game empire on £1.99 cassettes sold in newsagents, petrol stations, and corner shops — places traditional games publishers ignored. The model gave first-time bedroom coders a viable path to commercial release, reached audiences full-price publishers couldn't, and ultimately seeded Virgin Mastertronic and Virgin Interactive.
subtitle: The £1.99 budget label that put games in every newsagent

title: Maxis
description: Maxis created the simulation game genre with SimCity, then expanded into diverse 'Sim' titles before The Sims became one of gaming's best-selling franchises.
subtitle: Simulation pioneers

title: MECC
description: Minnesota Educational Computing Consortium created *The Oregon Trail* and pioneered educational software that taught generations of American students.
subtitle: You have died of dysentery

title: Media Molecule
description: Media Molecule pioneered user-generated content gaming with LittleBigPlanet and Dreams, proving players could become creators within commercial games.
subtitle: Play, create, share

title: Melbourne House
description: Melbourne House, founded as a book publisher in 1977 by Alfred Milgrom and Naomi Besen in Melbourne, became one of the most respected software publishers of the 8-bit era through its in-house development studio Beam Software. Britain met it as a publisher of Sinclair books: by 1981 it was advertising Ian Logan's Understanding Your ZX81 ROM, the start of a four-book run that ended with the Complete Spectrum ROM Disassembly. The Hobbit (1982) then brought literary text-adventure design to mass audiences and Way of the Exploding Fist (1985) founded the 8-bit fighting game.
subtitle: The Australian publisher that reached Britain as a book house first, and documented three Sinclair ROMs before it sold a hit game

title: MicroProse
description: MicroProse built an empire on military simulations and strategy games, publishing works by Sid Meier that defined genres for decades.
subtitle: Simulations and strategy

title: Microsoft
description: Microsoft's journey in gaming spans from MS-DOS enabling early PC games to Xbox becoming a major console platform, acquiring studios like Bethesda and Activision.
subtitle: From MS-DOS to Xbox

title: Midway
description: Midway distributed classic arcade games including Pac-Man and Galaga in the US, later creating controversial hits like Mortal Kombat that sparked industry-wide content debates.
subtitle: Arcade and controversy

title: Mikro-Gen
description: Bracknell's Wally Week comedies were among the best-reviewed Spectrum games of 1984-85 — 93, 93, 92, 91, 90. Then Mikro-Gen shipped Shadow of the Unicorn with a hardware cartridge in the box, at £15, to beat the pirates. CRASH said the price would do more damage than piracy ever could. ACE later recorded that Mikro-Gen faded away not long after.
subtitle: The company that sold you a Spectrum upgrade to play its game

title: Millennium Interactive
description: The Cambridge publisher behind James Pond and Diggers — a British attempt at the console-era mascot character, and a case study in what the Amiga's last years were spent chasing.
subtitle: Britain's try at a mascot

title: Milton Bradley
description: Board game giant Milton Bradley entered video games with the Vectrex and various licensed titles, bringing traditional gaming expertise to the digital age.
subtitle: Board games go digital

title: Mindscape
description: An American publisher whose European arm put out other people's Amiga games — a useful case study in what a publisher was for, and how invisible the role becomes in retrospect.
subtitle: Always the publisher, never the author

title: Mirrorsoft
description: Launched in November 1983 as one of twenty-five things Mirror Group Newspapers was diversifying into, Mirrorsoft began by publishing Mr Men and multiplication tables and said it was not writing games. Two years later it produced Dynamite Dan. It ended holding the European rights to Tetris when Robert Maxwell's empire collapsed underneath it.
subtitle: The newspaper that went into software, and said it would not make games

title: Mojang
description: Mojang grew from Minecraft's success into a studio acquired by Microsoft for $2.5 billion, continuing to develop the world's best-selling game under corporate ownership.
subtitle: House of blocks

title: Monolith Soft
description: Monolith Soft was founded by Xenogears veterans to pursue ambitious JRPGs, eventually becoming a Nintendo subsidiary creating Xenoblade Chronicles and supporting Zelda development.
subtitle: Xeno architects

title: MOS Technology
description: MOS Technology created the 6502 processor and the engineers who designed the SID and VIC-II—the silicon heart of the Commodore 64.
subtitle: The chip fab that changed everything

title: Motorola
description: Motorola's 68000 processor powered the Amiga, Atari ST, and Sega Mega Drive—bringing 32-bit architecture to home computers and consoles.
