description: Mega Man 2 refined everything from its predecessor, delivering tight platforming, memorable boss battles, and one of gaming's greatest soundtracks.
subtitle: Blue bomber perfected

title: Mega Man
description: Capcom's 1987 NES platformer introduced weapon-stealing mechanics and non-linear stage selection, launching one of gaming's longest franchises.
subtitle: The Blue Bomber

title: Metal Gear Solid
description: Metal Gear Solid reinvented stealth gaming with cinematic presentation, codec conversations, and fourth-wall-breaking moments that made players feel like action movie protagonists.
subtitle: Tactical espionage action

title: Metal Slug
description: Metal Slug delivered exquisitely animated run-and-gun action on Neo Geo hardware, combining Contra-style gameplay with cartoon visuals, vehicle combat, and dark military humour.
subtitle: Run-and-gun perfection

title: Metroid II: Return of Samus
description: Metroid II brought Samus's exploration to Game Boy, tasking players with exterminating the Metroid species across the labyrinthine caves of SR388.
subtitle: Handheld isolation

title: Metroid Prime
description: Retro Studios translated *Metroid*'s atmospheric exploration into first-person, creating one of the GameCube's defining experiences.
subtitle: First-person isolation

title: Metroid
description: Nintendo's atmospheric action-adventure introduced Samus Aran, non-linear exploration, and the template for an entire genre.
subtitle: Alone in the dark

title: Micro Machines
description: Codemasters' 1991 top-down racing game featuring miniature vehicles racing across household environments—breakfast tables, pool tables, and garden paths.
subtitle: Tiny cars, giant fun

title: Microsoft Flight Simulator
description: The *Flight Simulator* series set the standard for aviation simulation across four decades, from 1982's wireframes to 2020's planet-scale photorealism.
subtitle: The sky above your desk

title: Minecraft
description: Minecraft's procedural voxel world and creative freedom made it the best-selling game of all time, transforming indie development and spawning an entire genre of survival crafting games.
subtitle: Block by block

title: Missile Command
description: Missile Command captured nuclear age anxiety in game form, challenging players to defend cities against relentless ICBM attacks using limited anti-missile batteries.
subtitle: Cold War defence

title: The Secret of Monkey Island
description: The Secret of Monkey Island perfected the point-and-click adventure with witty writing, memorable characters, and puzzles that challenged without frustrating.
subtitle: Mighty pirate adventure

title: Monty on the Run
description: Gremlin's platformer took 94% in CRASH on the Spectrum, and is remembered on the C64 for Rob Hubbard's loading theme — one game, two reputations.
subtitle: Freedom for Monty

title: Moon Patrol
description: Moon Patrol introduced parallax scrolling to arcade games, creating an illusion of depth as players drove a lunar buggy across the moon's surface, jumping craters and shooting enemies.
subtitle: Parallax pioneer

title: The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind
description: Morrowind dropped players into Vvardenfell's alien landscape without hand-holding, trusting them to find their own path through a world of giant mushrooms, enslaved races, and dying gods.
subtitle: Alien world

title: Mortal Kombat
description: Mortal Kombat shocked arcades with digitised violence and fatality finishers, sparking controversy that led to the ESRB rating system while building a fighting game empire.
subtitle: Finish him

title: Myst
description: Myst dropped players onto a mysterious island with no instructions, selling millions of copies and proving that atmospheric puzzle games could find mainstream audiences.
subtitle: CD-ROM phenomenon

title: NBA Jam
description: NBA Jam abandoned basketball simulation for two-on-two arcade mayhem with impossible dunks, burning basketballs, and commentary that entered the cultural lexicon.
subtitle: Boomshakalaka

title: Nebulus
description: John Phillips' 1987 tower-climbing game created the illusion of 3D rotation on 8-bit hardware through clever programming.
subtitle: The tower that turned

title: NetHack
description: NetHack expanded Rogue's foundation into one of gaming's deepest systems, where almost everything interacts with everything else across decades of community development.
subtitle: Ascension or death

title: Neverwinter Nights
description: Neverwinter Nights shipped with a complete toolset that let players create and share their own D&D adventures, spawning a modding community that outlived the game's commercial lifespan.
subtitle: Dungeon master's toolkit

title: NHL '94
description: NHL '94 achieved sports game balance that kept players returning decades later, with responsive controls, the one-timer mechanic, and gameplay that transcended its era.
subtitle: Hockey perfection

title: Ninja Gaiden
description: Ninja Gaiden combined brutal difficulty with pioneering cutscenes, telling a revenge story through animated sequences that elevated NES storytelling.
subtitle: Cinematic action

title: No Man's Sky
description: Hello Games' No Man's Sky launched controversially incomplete but became gaming's greatest redemption story through years of free updates that delivered on original promises.
subtitle: Redemption through persistence

title: The Oregon Trail
description: The 1971 educational game that taught American children about westward expansion while killing their virtual families with disease.
subtitle: You have died of dysentery

title: Out Run
description: Sega's 1986 arcade racer combined stunning visuals, branching routes, and a Ferrari Testarossa into the definitive driving fantasy.
subtitle: Drive into the sunset

title: Outlast
description: Outlast thrust players into a nightmare asylum armed only with a camcorder, creating found-footage horror gaming that became a streaming sensation.
subtitle: Night vision nightmare

title: Pac-Man (Atari 2600)
description: The notoriously poor 1982 port of Pac-Man for the Atari 2600 that sold millions yet disappointed everyone - a cautionary tale of overproduction and compromised quality.
subtitle: The other crash catalyst

title: Pac-Man
description: Namco's 1980 maze-chase created gaming's first mascot, transcended arcades into mainstream culture, and taught the industry that characters sell.
subtitle: Gaming's first icon

title: Panzer Dragoon
description: Panzer Dragoon combined rail-shooter action with a haunting post-apocalyptic world, establishing one of the Saturn's most distinctive franchises through atmosphere and artistry.
subtitle: On dragon wings

title: Paperboy
description: Paperboy turned newspaper delivery into an obstacle course of dogs, cars, and lawn ornaments, with the unique goal of delivering papers while causing maximum property damage.
subtitle: Suburban chaos

title: Paradroid
description: Andrew Braybrook’s 1985 masterpiece blended shooter action with territory control aboard a hijacked robot freighter.
subtitle: C64 strategy welded to arcade reflexes

title: PaRappa the Rapper
description: PaRappa the Rapper pioneered the modern rhythm game with call-and-response gameplay and paper-thin visual style that influenced a generation of music games.
subtitle: I gotta believe

title: Parodius
description: Parodius parodied Konami's own shooters with penguins, octopi, and Las Vegas showgirls, combining tight Gradius gameplay with surreal Japanese humour.
subtitle: Gradius meets absurdity

title: Perfect Dark
description: Perfect Dark built on GoldenEye's foundation with simulant bots, weapon customisation, and Counter-Operative mode, pushing the N64 to its absolute limits.
subtitle: GoldenEye evolved

title: Persona
description: Persona spun off from Shin Megami Tensei to explore teenage identity through Jungian psychology, blending dungeon crawling with social simulation in modern Japanese settings.
subtitle: Face yourself

title: Phantasy Star
description: Phantasy Star brought Japanese RPG excellence to the Master System with 3D dungeons, a female protagonist, and science-fantasy storytelling that rivalled anything on Nintendo's platform.
subtitle: Sega's epic RPG

title: Pillars of Eternity
description: Obsidian Entertainment's crowdfunded *Pillars of Eternity* revived the classic isometric RPG, proving appetite remained for deep, text-heavy adventures.
subtitle: The Kickstarter resurrection

title: Pirates!
description: Sid Meier's Pirates! created open-world gaming in the 17th-century Caribbean, combining ship combat, fencing, trading, and exploration in a seamless sandbox adventure.
subtitle: Caribbean open world

title: Pitfall!
description: David Crane's jungle adventure sold four million copies, proved third-party games could be best-in-class, and defined the platformer before Mario existed.
subtitle: Swinging into history

title: Planescape: Torment
description: Planescape: Torment asked 'What can change the nature of a man?' and delivered gaming's most celebrated narrative through an immortal protagonist exploring questions of identity and mortality.
subtitle: Narrative transcendence

title: Planetfall
description: Steve Meretzky's *Planetfall* combined Infocom wit with genuine emotional impact, featuring a robot companion whose fate became gaming legend.
subtitle: Floyd's sacrifice

title: Pokémon Gold & Silver
description: Pokémon Gold and Silver expanded the formula with day/night cycles, breeding, and a post-game return to Kanto that doubled the adventure's scope.
subtitle: The perfect sequel

title: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon
description: Chunsoft's *Pokemon Mystery Dungeon* combined the roguelike dungeon crawling of *Shiren* with Pokemon collecting, creating an unexpectedly emotional series.
subtitle: Roguelike meets Pokemon

title: Pokémon Red & Blue
description: Pokémon Red and Blue created a global phenomenon through monster collection, trading via link cable, and version exclusives that made social play essential.
subtitle: Gotta catch 'em all

title: Pokemon
description: Pokemon created a global phenomenon through monster collection, strategic battling, and social trading that transcended gaming into multimedia dominance.
subtitle: Gotta catch 'em all

title: Pole Position
description: Pole Position established the behind-the-car racing perspective and sprite scaling techniques that defined racing games for a decade.
subtitle: Racing revolution

title: Pong
description: Two paddles, one ball, endless quarters—Atari's Pong proved video games could be a business and launched an industry.
subtitle: The game that started an industry

title: Populous
description: Bullfrog's Populous invented the god game genre, letting players reshape terrain and guide followers to dominance in a battle of divine powers.
subtitle: Playing god, literally

title: Prince of Persia
description: Prince of Persia pioneered fluid rotoscoped animation in games, creating a cinematic platformer where precise movement through deadly traps became an art form.
subtitle: Rotoscoped elegance

title: Pro Evolution Soccer
description: Pro Evolution Soccer prioritised gameplay authenticity over licenses, creating a football simulation beloved by purists who valued how it played over whose names appeared.
subtitle: Beautiful game simulation

title: Punch-Out!!
description: Punch-Out!! challenged players to read opponent patterns and counter with precision timing, turning boxing into a puzzle game starring the undersized Little Mac against memorable caricatured opponents.
subtitle: Pattern-based boxing

title: Puyo Puyo
description: Puyo Puyo combined falling-block puzzling with chain reaction mechanics, creating a competitive puzzle game that became a Japanese phenomenon and Sega staple.
subtitle: Chain reaction mastery

title: Puzzle Bobble
description: Puzzle Bobble transformed Bubble Bobble's dragons into a colour-matching shooter, creating an accessible puzzle format that spawned countless imitators.
subtitle: Aim and match

title: Q*bert
description: Q*bert challenged players to hop across pyramid cubes while avoiding enemies, becoming an arcade icon with distinctive visuals and synthesised swearing.
subtitle: Isometric hopping

title: Quake
description: Quake brought true 3D graphics and online multiplayer to first-person shooters, establishing the technological and competitive foundations that define the genre today.
subtitle: True 3D arrives

title: R-Type
description: Irem's 1987 shooter combined beautiful sprite art with the innovative Force pod, creating the definitive side-scrolling shooter.
subtitle: The Force is with you

title: Raiden
description: Raiden distilled vertical shooting to its essence: satisfying weapons, challenging patterns, and two-player co-op that defined arcade shooting for the early 1990s.
subtitle: Vertical shooting perfection

title: Rainbow Islands
description: Taito's 1987 sequel transformed Bub and Bob into human form, swapping bubbles for rainbows in vertical platforming perfection.
subtitle: The story of Bubble Bobble 2

title: Rampage
description: Rampage let players become giant monsters destroying cities, punching buildings, eating people, and battling the military in gleeful urban destruction.
subtitle: Monster destruction

title: Rayman
description: Rayman introduced Ubisoft's mascot through gorgeous 2D animation and challenging platforming, evolving from solo adventure to cooperative chaos.
subtitle: Limbless platforming hero

title: R.C. Pro-Am
description: R.C. Pro-Am delivered addictive isometric racing with weapons and upgrades, showcasing Rare's technical prowess on the NES with smooth scrolling and detailed graphics.
subtitle: Isometric racing

title: Command & Conquer: Red Alert
description: Red Alert reimagined World War II with Tesla coils and time travel, delivering faster gameplay and the iconic Hell March soundtrack while spawning its own beloved sub-series.
subtitle: Hell march

title: Renegade
description: Mike Lamb's conversion of Technos' beat-em-up sat at #2 for four consecutive months without ever reaching #1 — and brought street fighting to the British charts.
subtitle: Four months at number two

title: Repton
description: Superior Software's *Repton* series challenged BBC Micro owners with boulder-physics puzzles and spawned one of the platform's most beloved franchises.
subtitle: Boulder-dodging on the Beeb

title: Resident Evil
description: Resident Evil codified survival horror with fixed camera angles, limited resources, and the Spencer Mansion's interconnected puzzles, creating a genre that terrified millions.
subtitle: Survival horror defined

title: Reversi
description: Victorian board game Reversi—later trademarked as Othello—became a computer gaming staple, teaching territory control and forward thinking.
subtitle: The flip side of strategy

title: Rez
description: Tetsuya Mizuguchi's *Rez* fused rail shooting with electronic music, creating an audio-visual experience where gameplay and sound became inseparable.
subtitle: Synaesthesia in digital form

title: River City Ransom
description: River City Ransom combined side-scrolling brawling with RPG progression, letting players buy food, learn techniques, and build stats while punching through gang-controlled streets.
subtitle: Beat-em-up meets RPG

title: Road Rash
description: Road Rash combined motorcycle racing with vehicular combat, letting players punch, kick, and club opponents while tearing down Californian highways.
subtitle: Combat racing

title: Robot Odyssey
description: The Learning Company's notoriously complex 1984 puzzle game where players programmed robots to escape an underground city.
subtitle: The hardest game ever made

title: Robotron: 2084
description: Eugene Jarvis's Robotron: 2084 defined twin-stick shooting with its dual-joystick controls, relentless enemy waves, and the desperate goal of saving the last human family.
subtitle: Twin-stick perfection

title: Rock Band
description: Harmonix expanded the *Guitar Hero* concept to full bands, letting four players perform together on drums, bass, guitar, and vocals.
subtitle: Start a band in your living room

title: Rocky's Boots
description: The Learning Company's 1982 game that taught Boolean logic and circuit design to children through engaging puzzles.
subtitle: Logic gates for children

title: Rogue
description: Rogue created the roguelike genre with procedurally generated dungeons, permadeath, and ASCII graphics, establishing design principles that would influence games for decades.
subtitle: The original permadeath

title: RollerCoaster Tycoon
description: RollerCoaster Tycoon let players build elaborate theme parks with custom coasters, achieving remarkable depth through code written entirely in assembly language by one developer.
subtitle: Theme park management

title: Rolling Thunder
description: Rolling Thunder combined cover-based shooting with stylish spy aesthetics, tasking players with infiltrating enemy strongholds while managing limited ammunition.
subtitle: Stylish spy action

title: Rygar
description: Rygar combined side-scrolling action with overhead exploration sections, sending a warrior with a yo-yo-like shield weapon through mythological landscapes.
subtitle: Diskarmor warrior

title: Sabre Wulf
description: Ultimate's 1984 follow-up to Atic Atac dropped Sabreman into a 256-screen jungle, four amulet pieces to find, a Sabre Wulf that couldn't be killed — and proved the Spectrum could handle a world this size.
subtitle: Ultimate's open-world jungle adventure

title: Salamander
description: Salamander brought simultaneous two-player action to Gradius-style shooting, with direct power-ups replacing the selection bar and organic alien environments.
subtitle: Gradius goes co-op

title: Sam & Max Hit the Road
description: Sam & Max Hit the Road followed a dog detective and hyperkinetic rabbity thing across American roadside attractions, delivering surreal comedy through LucasArts' refined adventure formula.
subtitle: Freelance police

title: Samurai Shodown
description: Samurai Shodown emphasised single decisive strikes over combo chains, creating a tense, methodical fighting game set in feudal Japan with distinctive SNK artistry.
subtitle: Weapon-based precision

title: Scramble
description: Scramble established the side-scrolling shooter template with fuel management, terrain navigation, and multiple weapon types that defined the genre for decades.
subtitle: Side-scrolling pioneer

title: Secret of Mana
description: Secret of Mana delivered real-time combat with three-player co-op on SNES, combining action gameplay with RPG progression in a vibrant world of Mana and ancient civilisation.
subtitle: Action RPG harmony

title: Sega Rally Championship
description: Sega Rally Championship introduced surface-dependent handling to racing games, with tyres responding differently to asphalt, gravel, and mud in genre-defining rally action.
subtitle: Surface matters

title: Sensible Soccer
description: Sensible Software stripped football to its essence—tiny players, aftertouch, and pure competitive joy.
subtitle: Beautiful simplicity

title: Shadow of the Beast
description: Shadow of the Beast showcased the Amiga's graphical power with unprecedented parallax scrolling and atmospheric visuals, becoming a system-selling technical demonstration.
subtitle: Parallax perfection

title: Shadowfire
description: Denton Designs' 1985 squad game for Beyond replaced the text parser with icons — CRASH called it the first fully icon-driven game — and went to number one twice.
subtitle: The first game with no words

title: Shenmue
description: Shenmue created an unprecedented living world with day/night cycles, weather systems, and NPC schedules, pioneering open-world design at enormous cost to Sega.
subtitle: Living world pioneer

title: Shin Megami Tensei
description: Atlus's *Shin Megami Tensei* series offered darker, more mature JRPGs where players recruit demons, make moral choices, and navigate post-apocalyptic Tokyo.
subtitle: Negotiate with demons

title: Shining Force
description: Shining Force brought tactical RPG battles to the Mega Drive, combining Fire Emblem-style grid combat with explorable towns and a diverse army of recruitable characters.
subtitle: Tactical RPG warfare

title: Shinobi
description: Shinobi established Sega's ninja franchise with tight platforming, hostage rescue missions, and the devastating ninja magic attacks that cleared screens of enemies.
subtitle: Ninja arcade action

title: Shovel Knight
description: Yacht Club Games' 2014 action-platformer that captured the NES aesthetic perfectly while incorporating decades of design lessons.
subtitle: NES perfection, modern design

title: Silent Hill
description: Silent Hill shifted survival horror from action to atmosphere, using fog, radio static, and psychological terror to create dread that lingered long after the game ended.
subtitle: Psychological horror

title: SimCity
description: SimCity invented the city-building genre, letting players zone, build, and manage urban development while balancing budgets, traffic, and the occasional disaster.
subtitle: City building pioneer

title: Skate or Die
description: Skate or Die brought skateboard culture to home computers with five competitive events, attitude-filled presentation, and the rebellious spirit that defined 1980s skating.
subtitle: EA skateboarding

title: Skidmarks
description: Acid Software's top-down racing game that proved Blitz Basic could produce commercial hits, featuring split-screen multiplayer and satisfying physics.
subtitle: Blitz Basic racing

title: Snake Rattle 'n' Roll
description: Snake Rattle 'n' Roll challenged players to guide hungry snakes through isometric worlds, eating pellets to grow long enough to reach the exit scale.
subtitle: Isometric snake action

title: Snake
description: Pre-installed on Nokia phones, *Snake* became one of the most-played games in history, demonstrating that compelling gameplay needs minimal technology.
subtitle: Nokia's killer app

title: Sonic the Hedgehog
description: Sega's blue blur gave them a mascot, a marketing weapon, and the game that made Genesis a genuine threat to Nintendo.
subtitle: Speed kills (Nintendo's dominance)

title: Soul Calibur
description: Soul Calibur perfected 3D weapon-based fighting with eight-way movement and the Dreamcast port that many consider the greatest launch title in console history.
subtitle: A tale of souls and swords

title: Space Channel 5
description: Space Channel 5 blended rhythm gameplay with 1960s retro-futurism, creating a stylish musical experience that epitomised Dreamcast's creative experimentation.
subtitle: Up, down, up, down, chu, chu, chu

title: Space Harrier
description: Space Harrier pioneered the into-screen shooter with sprite scaling technology, sending players flying through surreal landscapes at unprecedented speed.
subtitle: Into the Fantasy Zone

title: Space Invaders
description: Taito's 1978 arcade phenomenon created the shooter genre, caused a coin shortage in Japan, and proved games could be cultural events.
subtitle: The game that conquered Earth

title: Space Quest
description: Space Quest followed hapless janitor Roger Wilco through comedic sci-fi adventures, parodying Star Trek, Star Wars, and science fiction tropes with Sierra's punishing puzzle design.
subtitle: Sci-fi comedy adventure

title: Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe
description: The Bitmap Brothers' violent future sport combined pinball physics with tactical team management.
subtitle: Ice cream! Ice cream!

title: Spellbound
description: David Jones's Magic Knight adventure put pull-down menus on a 48K Spectrum at £2.99 — and its two chart positions in the same month show exactly what a budget game was up against.
subtitle: #3 in one chart, #21 in another

title: Spelunky
description: Spelunky fused roguelike principles with platformer action, proving procedural generation and permadeath could work in real-time gameplay and inspiring a generation of roguelites.
subtitle: Roguelike platformer

title: Splatterhouse
description: Splatterhouse brought slasher film aesthetics to arcades, with a hockey-masked hero fighting through grotesque monsters in one of gaming's first explicitly horror-themed brawlers.
subtitle: Horror beat-em-up

title: Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell
description: Splinter Cell defined stealth through its light meter mechanic, putting players in darkness as Sam Fisher navigated geopolitical intrigue with lethal precision.
subtitle: Light and shadow

title: Spy Hunter
description: Spy Hunter combined vertical scrolling driving with James Bond gadgetry, letting players deploy oil slicks, smoke screens, and missiles against enemy vehicles.
subtitle: Vehicular espionage

title: Spy vs Spy
description: Spy vs Spy adapted the MAD Magazine comic strip into simultaneous split-screen gameplay where two spies set traps, searched for items, and raced to escape before each other.
subtitle: Split-screen sabotage

title: Spyro the Dragon
description: Spyro the Dragon offered open 3D worlds to explore, combining flame breath, charging attacks, and gem collecting in a family-friendly platformer that showcased PlayStation's capabilities.
subtitle: Colourful 3D platforming

title: SSX
description: SSX combined arcade snowboarding with massive tricks, vibrant presentation, and a boost system that rewarded stylish play, defining extreme sports on PlayStation 2.
subtitle: Snowboarding spectacle

title: Star Fox 64
description: Star Fox 64 delivered cinematic rail-shooter action with full voice acting, branching paths, and the first Rumble Pak support, creating an endlessly quotable Nintendo classic.
subtitle: Do a barrel roll

title: Star Fox
description: Nintendo's 1993 SNES rail shooter that used the custom Super FX chip to bring filled polygon 3D to consoles, created in partnership with Argonaut.
subtitle: Super FX revolution

title: Star Raiders
description: Atari's groundbreaking 1979 space combat game that defined the genre and demonstrated what the Atari 400/800 could achieve.
subtitle: The first space combat simulator

title: StarCraft
description: StarCraft delivered three radically different factions in perfect balance, creating an esports phenomenon that dominated competitive gaming for over a decade.
subtitle: Asymmetric RTS perfection

title: Starglider
description: Argonaut's 1986 3D combat flight game that brought filled polygon graphics to home computers, establishing the studio's reputation for technical wizardry.
subtitle: Filled polygons on 8-bit

title: Stormlord
description: Raffaele Cecco's 1989 Hewson game, and the only one in this Vault whose construction was documented month by month in a magazine column as it happened. CRASH gave it 91%; Sinclair User gave it 71%.
subtitle: Built in public, one diary entry at a time

title: Street Fighter II
description: Street Fighter II created the competitive fighting game genre, revitalised arcades, and sparked console wars as Sega and Nintendo fought for the best port.
subtitle: The fighting game revolution

title: Street Fighter
description: Capcom's 1987 arcade fighting game that introduced special move inputs and laid the groundwork for Street Fighter II's revolution - even if the original is largely forgotten.
subtitle: The fighter that started it all

title: Streets of Rage
description: Streets of Rage delivered console-exclusive beat-em-up excellence with tight combat, memorable music by Yuzo Koshiro, and cooperative gameplay that rivalled arcade offerings.
subtitle: Genesis brawling

title: Strider
description: Strider delivered acrobatic ninja action across a dystopian world, with Hiryu's plasma sword slicing through enemies as he climbed walls, hung from ceilings, and flipped through the air.
subtitle: Futuristic ninja action

title: Suikoden
description: Suikoden adapted the classical Chinese novel's structure to JRPG form, tasking players with recruiting 108 characters to build an army and headquarters against tyranny.
subtitle: 108 Stars of Destiny

title: Summer Games
description: Summer Games brought Olympic events to home computers with polished presentation, national anthems, and multiplayer competition that defined Epyx's sports game formula.
subtitle: Epyx Olympic excellence

title: Sunset Riders
description: Sunset Riders brought Contra-style action to the Wild West, with four bounty hunters chasing outlaws through saloons, trains, and frontier towns in colourful arcade action.
subtitle: Wild West run-and-gun

title: Super C
description: Super C continued Contra's run-and-gun action with new weapons, overhead stages, and relentless alien battles, maintaining the series' reputation for demanding cooperative gameplay.
subtitle: Contra's intense sequel

title: Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts
description: Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts continued Capcom's legendary difficulty with gorgeous 16-bit visuals, the double-jump, and the requirement to complete the game twice for the true ending.
subtitle: SNES platforming punishment

title: Super Mario 64
description: Super Mario 64 invented 3D platforming with its revolutionary analogue control, dynamic camera system, and open-ended level design that gave players unprecedented freedom of movement.
subtitle: 3D platforming born

title: Super Mario Bros. 3
description: Super Mario Bros. 3 expanded Mario's abilities with suits and power-ups, delivering eight diverse worlds and becoming the NES's defining platformer.
subtitle: NES platforming perfected

title: Super Mario Bros.
description: Bundled with the NES, Super Mario Bros. rescued the American games industry and established the vocabulary of platform game design.
subtitle: The game that defined gaming

title: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins
description: Nintendo R&D1's *Super Mario Land 2* expanded Game Boy Mario with larger sprites, non-linear world selection, and the villainous debut of Wario.
subtitle: Wario's debut

title: Super Mario Land
description: Super Mario Land brought the plumber to Game Boy, adapting the formula for portable play with unique vehicles and Gunpei Yokoi's design sensibility.
subtitle: Mario's handheld debut

title: Super Metroid
description: Nintendo's *Super Metroid* refined the exploration-action formula to near perfection, becoming the template against which all Metroidvanias are measured.
subtitle: The perfect formula

title: Super Robin Hood
description: The Oliver Twins’ *Super Robin Hood* packed platforming, traps, and treasure into a £1.99 cassette that made them household names.
subtitle: Codemasters’ budget swashbuckler

title: Supreme Commander
description: Supreme Commander delivered Total Annihilation's spiritual successor with revolutionary strategic zoom, letting players seamlessly transition from individual units to entire theatre overview.
subtitle: Strategic zoom

title: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night
description: Symphony of the Night transformed Castlevania from linear action to RPG-infused exploration, co-defining the metroidvania genre with its interconnected castle.
subtitle: The metroidvania origin

title: Syndicate
description: Syndicate combined real-time tactics with cyberpunk atmosphere, letting players control a squad of augmented agents in missions of corporate warfare.
subtitle: Corporate dystopia

title: System Shock 2
description: System Shock 2 merged RPG systems with survival horror aboard a derelict starship, influencing BioShock and establishing the template for narrative-driven immersive sims.
subtitle: Horror in space

title: System Shock
description: System Shock combined first-person action with RPG systems and environmental storytelling, creating the 'immersive sim' template that influenced Deus Ex, BioShock, and countless others.
subtitle: Immersive simulation pioneer

title: Tales of Phantasia
description: Tales of Phantasia pioneered real-time JRPG combat with the Linear Motion Battle System, launching a franchise that would span decades with its action-focused approach.
subtitle: Linear Motion Battle

title: Tekken
description: Tekken brought accessible 3D fighting to arcades and PlayStation, with limb-based controls and juggle combos that created an alternative to Virtua Fighter's technical demands.
subtitle: 3D fighting evolution

title: Tempest 2000
description: In 1994 Jeff Minter reimagined Atari’s vector shooter for the Jaguar, delivering a rave-worthy soundtrack and hypnotic visuals.
subtitle: Llamasoft’s neon rebirth of an arcade classic

title: Tempest
description: Tempest pioneered 3D perspective in arcade gaming, sending players down geometric tubes to blast emerging enemies in one of Atari's most visually striking creations.
subtitle: Vector tube shooter

title: Tetris
description: Alexey Pajitnov's falling-block puzzle conquered the world, sold the Game Boy, and proved games could transcend language and culture.
subtitle: The perfect game

title: The Hobbit
description: Melbourne House's 1982 text adventure that pushed the genre forward with independent NPCs, a sophisticated parser, and a living world that changed whether you interacted with it or not.
subtitle: The revolutionary text adventure

title: The Last Ninja
description: System 3's martial arts masterpiece combined isometric exploration, combat, and Ben Daglish's legendary SID soundtrack.
subtitle: Isometric excellence

title: Theme Park
description: Theme Park put players in charge of designing and managing an amusement park, balancing ride construction, staff management, and guest happiness.
subtitle: Build your dream park

title: Thief: The Dark Project
description: Thief invented the first-person stealth genre, making shadows, sound, and patience more important than combat in a dark fantasy world of guards, monsters, and valuable loot.
subtitle: Stealth game pioneer

title: Thrust
description: Jeremy Smith's physics-based game brought Gravitar-style gameplay to home computers with brutal precision requirements.
subtitle: Gravity is a harsh mistress

title: Thunder Force
description: Thunder Force evolved from free-scrolling computer game to Mega Drive showcase, with Thunder Force III and IV delivering some of the finest 16-bit shooting action.
subtitle: Mega Drive shooting excellence

title: Time Crisis
description: Namco's revolutionary 1995 light gun game that introduced the cover mechanic, transforming arcade shooters into tactical experiences.
subtitle: Take cover!

title: TMNT: The Arcade Game
description: Konami's 1989 four-player beat 'em up that became the gold standard for licensed games and arcade co-op, proving that treating licenses seriously produced excellence.
subtitle: Four-player perfection

title: Tomb Raider
description: Tomb Raider sent Lara Croft exploring ancient tombs with athletic platforming and puzzle-solving, creating gaming's first female icon and defining 3D action-adventure.
subtitle: Action archaeology

title: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater
description: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater transformed skateboarding into accessible gaming with intuitive trick systems, iconic level design, and soundtracks that defined a generation.
subtitle: Skateboarding revolution

title: Total Annihilation
description: Total Annihilation introduced true 3D terrain, streaming economy, and unprecedented unit counts, pushing RTS toward grand-scale conflict that StarCraft deliberately avoided.
subtitle: Scale warfare

title: Track & Field
description: Track & Field transformed athletic events into frantic button-mashing competitions, destroying joysticks and creating a multiplayer party game phenomenon.
subtitle: Button-mashing Olympics

title: Transport Tycoon
description: Chris Sawyer's *Transport Tycoon* let players build transport empires across procedural landscapes, inspiring dedicated fans who maintain the game to this day.
subtitle: Build your network

title: Turrican
description: Manfred Trenz's run-and-gun showcased Amiga capabilities with massive levels, smooth scrolling, and Chris Hülsbeck's thunderous soundtrack.
subtitle: German engineering, Amiga power

title: TwinBee
description: TwinBee pioneered the cute-em-up genre with its colourful aesthetic, bell-juggling power-up system, and two-player cooperative shooting featuring adorable bee-shaped ships.
subtitle: Cute vertical shooter

title: Ultima
description: The Ultima series established computer RPG conventions from character creation to open worlds, with Ultima IV pioneering ethical gameplay and virtue systems.
subtitle: The RPG that defined them all

title: Unreal
description: Unreal showcased unprecedented visual technology with vast outdoor environments, coloured lighting, and detailed textures that pushed PC gaming into a new graphical era.
subtitle: Visual spectacle

title: Uridium
description: Andrew Braybrook's metallic dreadnoughts, written for the C64 and converted outward. CRASH gave the Spectrum version 90%; Sinclair User gave it full marks.
subtitle: Side-scrolling speed on the C64

title: Vagrant Story
description: Vagrant Story delivered Shakespearean drama and intricate weapon crafting in a dungeon crawler that demanded mastery, earning perfect scores while remaining defiantly uncommercial.
subtitle: Lea Monde's depths

title: Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines
description: Bloodlines shipped broken but brilliant, capturing the World of Darkness with unprecedented atmosphere and reactivity before patches and mods revealed the masterpiece underneath.
subtitle: Flawed masterpiece

title: Vectorman
description: Vectorman brought pre-rendered 3D graphics to the Mega Drive through a robot hero made of spheres, showcasing impressive visuals in Sega's battle against the next generation.
subtitle: Pre-rendered Mega Drive

title: Virtua Cop
description: Sega's 1994 arcade light gun game that pioneered 3D graphics in the genre and introduced target prioritisation mechanics.
subtitle: The polygon shooter

title: Virtua Fighter
description: Virtua Fighter pioneered 3D polygon fighting games with realistic martial arts, spawning a genre and establishing Sega's arcade dominance in the early 1990s.
subtitle: 3D fighting born

title: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans
description: Warcraft brought real-time strategy to fantasy, establishing Blizzard's flagship universe with humans versus orcs warfare and accessible multiplayer competition.
subtitle: Blizzard's strategy debut

title: Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3
description: Wario Land transformed Mario's antagonist into a playable anti-hero, replacing precision platforming with treasure hunting and shoulder-charging through a greedy adventure.
subtitle: Greed is good

title: Wasteland
description: Interplay's *Wasteland* created the post-apocalyptic RPG template that would later inspire *Fallout*, featuring party-based combat and a persistent, reactive world.
subtitle: Post-nuclear party

title: Way of the Exploding Fist
description: Melbourne House's 1985 fighting game brought martial arts to home computers with smooth animation and precise controls.
subtitle: One-on-one combat perfected

title: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker
description: Wind Waker divided opinion with its cartoon aesthetic but delivered timeless visuals and ocean exploration that endure better than any realistic alternative.
subtitle: Cel-shaded seas

title: Wing Commander
description: Wing Commander combined cinematic storytelling with space combat simulation, pioneering narrative-driven action games and pushing PC hardware to its limits.
subtitle: Space combat cinema

title: Wings of Fury
description: Wings of Fury delivered intense World War II carrier aviation with satisfying bombing runs, strafing attacks, and carrier landings across the Pacific theatre.
subtitle: Pacific carrier combat

title: Winter Games
description: Winter Games brought snow and ice sports to home computers with seven events including ski jumping, bobsled, and figure skating, continuing Epyx's successful Olympic formula.
subtitle: Cold weather Olympics

title: WipEout
description: WipEout combined futuristic anti-gravity racing with designer aesthetics and electronic music, establishing PlayStation's identity as the cool gamer's platform.
subtitle: Anti-gravity cool

title: Wizardry
description: The 1981 Sir-Tech dungeon crawler that defined first-person RPG mechanics and directly inspired Dragon Quest and the entire JRPG genre.
subtitle: JRPG ancestor

title: Wizball
description: Sensible Software's surreal shooter paired innovative gameplay with Martin Galway's dreamy SID soundtrack.
subtitle: Colour restoration odyssey

title: Wonder Boy
description: Wonder Boy combined platforming with constant forward momentum, as the skateboard-riding hero raced through jungle stages collecting fruit to maintain vitality while rescuing his girlfriend.
subtitle: Skateboarding through danger

title: Worms
description: Worms transformed artillery games into a cultural phenomenon, combining destructible terrain, creative weapons, and squeaky-voiced invertebrates into multiplayer mayhem.
subtitle: Artillery warfare

title: Wrecking Crew
description: Wrecking Crew challenged Mario to demolish walls in the correct order, combining puzzle-solving with action as enemies interfered with the destruction.
subtitle: Demolition puzzles

title: X-COM: UFO Defense
description: Julian Gollop's 1994 strategy game for MicroProse — Geoscape above, Battlescape below, permadeath throughout. It shipped under three names: UFO: Enemy Unknown in Britain, X-COM: UFO Defense in America, and X-COM: Enemy Unknown on PlayStation.
subtitle: The 1994 original, and the hyphen that separates it from the reboots

title: XCOM: Enemy Unknown
description: Firaxis's 2012 reboot kept X-COM's two-layer structure and permadeath while replacing Time Units with a two-action turn — a different design sharing a premise, and the game that made XCOM-like a genre label.
subtitle: Firaxis drops the hyphen and rebuilds the game

title: Xenogears
description: Xenogears fused giant robot combat with Jungian psychology, Gnostic mythology, and questions about God, consciousness, and human nature—ambitious beyond its troubled production.
subtitle: Philosophical mecha

title: Xenon 2: Megablast
description: Xenon 2: Megablast combined vertical shooting with upgrade shops and a licensed Bomb the Bass soundtrack, defining the Bitmap Brothers' style.
subtitle: Bitmap Brothers' shooter

title: Xevious
description: Xevious established templates for vertical shooters with its dual weapon system, detailed scrolling landscapes, and mysterious alien aesthetic that influenced countless games.
subtitle: Vertical shooting refined

title: Yakuza
description: Sega's *Yakuza* series blended crime drama with absurdist side content, creating urban sandboxes where brutal combat coexisted with karaoke and arcade games.
subtitle: Like a Dragon

title: Zaxxon
description: Zaxxon pioneered isometric 3D in arcade shooters, challenging players to navigate fortress walls while managing altitude in a visually groundbreaking experience.
subtitle: Isometric space combat

title: Zork
description: Zork defined text adventure gaming with its sophisticated parser, witty writing, and sprawling underground world, establishing Infocom as the master of interactive fiction.
subtitle: The great underground empire

title: Zynaps
description: Dominic Robinson's Hewson shooter held #2 twice and never reached the top — a chart run that shows what it looked like to be the other good game.
subtitle: Second best, for eight months

title: 4X Strategy
description: The strategy genre defined by four key activities: explore the map, expand your territory, exploit resources, and exterminate opponents—epitomised by Civilization.
subtitle: Explore, expand, exploit, exterminate

title: Action RPG
description: Action RPGs combine role-playing progression systems with real-time combat, from *Zelda II* through *Diablo* to the modern looter-shooter.
subtitle: Real-time character growth

title: Arcade Adventure
description: Exploration and puzzle-solving driven by arcade controls, not a text parser: *Atic Atac*, *Knight Lore*, *Head Over Heels*. A category the British press used constantly and which modern taxonomies have quietly dissolved.
subtitle: Britain's own genre, and one with no modern name

title: Arcade Game
description: On home machines, 'arcade game' named a style, not a venue: immediate, reflex-driven, score-chasing action with no reading and no waiting. The broadest genre word in the period press.
subtitle: Not where it was played — how it played

title: Art Games
description: Art games prioritise aesthetic experience, emotional expression, and meaning over traditional gameplay mechanics, challenging definitions of what games can be. Also called experimental games; the two labels were used interchangeably.
subtitle: Games as artistic expression

title: Beat 'em Up
description: Beat 'em ups send players through scrolling stages punching waves of enemies, from *Double Dragon* to *Streets of Rage* to modern revivals.
subtitle: Walk right, punch everyone

title: Console FPS
description: Console first-person shooters adapted PC precision gaming for controllers, creating distinct design philosophies around aim assist, level design, and multiplayer.
subtitle: Shooters on the sofa

title: Console RPG
description: Console RPGs adapted computer role-playing for living room play, prioritising accessibility and storytelling over simulation complexity, becoming Japan's dominant RPG form.
subtitle: Living room adventures

title: Flight Sim
description: Simulated flight, from combat aircraft to trading spacecraft. One of the few home-computer genres that traded reflexes for study, and a genre that made a virtue of complexity when everything else was shedding it.
subtitle: Aircraft, spacecraft, and the pleasure of a long manual

title: First-Person Shooter
description: First-person shooters place players behind the barrel of a gun, creating intimate combat experiences that evolved from Wolfenstein 3D's corridors to modern competitive esports.
subtitle: Through the gun barrel

title: God Games
description: God games place players in positions of supreme power over simulated worlds and populations, from *Populous* to *Black & White*.
subtitle: Divine simulation

title: Graphic Adventure
description: Adventure games that show you the room. Beginning as illustrated text adventures and ending as fully point-and-click, the graphic adventure charts the slow replacement of typing with pointing.
subtitle: The parser gets a picture, then loses the parser

title: Horror Games
description: Horror games evolved from text adventures through survival horror to streaming phenomena, using interactivity's unique properties to create fear that passive media cannot match.
subtitle: Interactive dread

title: Immersive Sim
description: The immersive sim genre prioritises player agency and emergent gameplay, letting systemic interactions create unique solutions rather than prescribing singular paths through designed challenges.
subtitle: Player-driven possibility

title: JRPG
description: JRPGs developed distinct conventions from Western RPGs: linear narratives, turn-based combat, predetermined protagonists, and emotional storytelling that defined a genre loved worldwide.
subtitle: Japanese role-playing games

title: Management Game
description: Running something — a football club, a city, a theme park, a software house — through budgets and decisions, not direct control. Britain's own strand of it turned the football manager into a national institution.
subtitle: Spreadsheets that fight back

title: Maze Game
description: Navigate a maze, collect its contents, avoid what hunts you. *Pac-Man* defined the form so completely that the British 8-bit market produced hundreds of variations, and the press needed a word for all of them.
subtitle: One screen, four ghosts, and a great many imitators

title: Metroidvania
description: Metroidvania describes games combining exploration with ability-gated progression, named after *Metroid* and *Castlevania: Symphony of the Night*.
subtitle: Explore, acquire, return

title: MMORPGs
description: The evolution of massively multiplayer online role-playing games from text-based MUDs through graphical worlds like Ultima Online and EverQuest to the phenomenon of World of Warcraft.
subtitle: From MUDs to millions

title: MUDs
description: Multi-User Dungeons pioneered online multiplayer gaming, creating persistent worlds, social dynamics, and design patterns MMORPGs would later adopt.
subtitle: Text-based multiplayer worlds

title: Music Games
description: Music games evolved from rhythm matching to full-band simulation, creating a genre that made everyone feel like musicians before market saturation caused its dramatic collapse.
subtitle: Play the music

title: Platformer
description: Platform games challenge players to navigate levels through jumping, climbing, and precise movement, defining gaming from Donkey Kong through modern indie revivals.
subtitle: The art of jumping

title: Portable Gaming
description: Portable gaming evolved from simple LCD games through Game Boy dominance to sophisticated handhelds, creating a distinct market with different design priorities.
subtitle: Gaming on the go

title: Racing Game
description: Getting somewhere fast, against a clock or a field. The period press used 'driving game' and 'racing game' more or less interchangeably, covering everything from sprite-scaled coin-ops to serious circuit simulation.
subtitle: Driving games, racing games, and the road that came toward you

title: Racing Simulation
description: Racing simulations prioritise realistic physics and authentic motorsport experience over arcade accessibility, demanding precision and practice.
subtitle: Virtual motorsport

title: Rail Shooters
description: Rail shooters move players through environments automatically while they focus on shooting targets, from light gun arcade games to spectacle-driven modern entries.
subtitle: On-rails action

title: Roguelike
description: The roguelike genre emerged from Rogue's procedural dungeons and permadeath, spawning purist tradition and modern roguelite evolution that influenced countless games.
subtitle: Death and rebirth

title: RTS Genre
description: Real-time strategy emerged from Dune II's template, dominated the 1990s PC landscape, spawned esports, then declined as MOBAs captured competitive audiences.
subtitle: Real-time warfare

title: Shoot 'em Up
description: The dominant action genre of the 8- and 16-bit era: fly, shoot, dodge, repeat. From *Space Invaders* through *R-Type* and *Uridium* to the bullet-hell descendants, and the term the period press reached for more than any other.
subtitle: The most-used genre word in the British computer press

title: Simulation Games
description: Simulation games modelled complex systems—cities, theme parks, civilisations—giving players godlike control and emergent storytelling through interacting mechanics.
subtitle: Systems to master

title: Single-Screen Platformer
description: Single-screen platformers contain entire levels within one fixed view, from *Donkey Kong* to *Bubble Bobble* to modern puzzle-platformers.
subtitle: One screen, infinite challenge

title: Sports Games
description: Sports games evolved from abstract representations to licensed simulations, becoming gaming's most commercially reliable genre through annual releases and real-world authenticity.
subtitle: Virtual athletics

title: Survival Games
description: Survival games challenge players to gather resources, craft tools, and endure hostile environments, from *Minecraft* to *DayZ* to *Valheim*.
subtitle: Fight to live another day

title: Survival Horror
description: Survival horror combined limited resources, vulnerable protagonists, and atmospheric dread to create gaming's most effective horror genre, codified by Resident Evil and evolved through Silent Hill.
subtitle: Terror through scarcity

title: Tactical RPG
description: Tactical RPGs combine grid-based strategy combat with RPG character progression, from *Fire Emblem* to *Final Fantasy Tactics* to *XCOM*.
subtitle: Strategy meets story

title: Text Adventure
description: Text adventures created entire worlds through prose and parser, challenging players to solve puzzles by typing commands in the days before graphics.
subtitle: Worlds built from words

title: Tycoon Games
description: Tycoon games put players in charge of building and managing business empires, from theme parks to railroads to hospitals.
subtitle: Build your empire

title: Walking Simulator
description: Walking simulators prioritise exploration and narrative over traditional gameplay mechanics, sparking debates about what constitutes a game while creating profound interactive experiences.
subtitle: Games without gameplay?

title: Wargame
description: Military conflict simulated at the level of units and terrain, not individual action. The computer wargame inherited its rules, its audience and its typography from the tabletop, and kept them long after the rest of gaming moved on.
subtitle: Hex maps, supply lines, and an unhurried audience

title: Western RPG
description: Western RPGs prioritise player agency and character customisation, letting players define who they are rather than following predetermined protagonists through authored stories.
subtitle: Player-defined heroes

title: 1001 Crew
description: A Dutch C64 group active in the mid-1980s, 1001 Crew pioneered the hardware trickery — including opening the sideborder — that turned intros and demos into technical showcases.
subtitle: The first to open the border

title: Andromeda
description: Andromeda were among the standout Amiga groups of the mid-1990s, their demo Nexus 7 winning The Party 1994 and showcasing what the AGA chipset could do.
subtitle: Danish AGA royalty

title: Booze Design
description: Booze Design proved the C64 scene is no relic: their demo Edge of Disgrace stunned audiences and showed the 8-bit machine still had astonishing work left in it.
subtitle: The modern C64 standard-bearers

title: Censor Design
description: Censor Design's Wonderland demos are among the most celebrated the Commodore 64 ever produced, fusing top-tier code, art, and music into landmark releases.
subtitle: Wonderland on the C64

title: Crest
description: Crest (founded 1988) combined technical audacity and design finesse, setting new records for C64 demos.
subtitle: Viennese precision on the Commodore 64

title: Crionics
description: Crionics were a leading early Amiga group whose collaboration with The Silents on Hardwired produced one of the demoscene's first genuinely cinematic productions.
subtitle: Co-authors of Hardwired

title: Eagle Soft Incorporated
description: Eagle Soft Incorporated dominated North American C64 cracking, and their eagle-logo intros are remembered as some of the most iconic the scene ever produced.
subtitle: The most famous cracktros of all

title: ESI
description: ESI were among the early standard-bearers of the ZX Spectrum demoscene, their megademo The Lyra II helping prove the 8-bit machine belonged in the scene's front rank.
subtitle: Spectrum scene pioneers

title: Fairlight
description: Fairlight became the most legendary cracking group in computing history, spanning C64, Amiga, and PC while defining the aesthetic and ethics of the scene.
subtitle: Legends of the scene

title: Farbrausch
description: Farbrausch revolutionised size-limited demos, creating full games in 96KB and procedural worlds in 4KB through extreme compression and procedural generation.
subtitle: Masters of compression

title: Future Crew
description: Future Crew created Second Reality and established the PC demo scene, with members later founding Remedy Entertainment and shaping the game industry.
subtitle: Defining the PC demo

title: Genesis Project
description: Formed in 1986, Genesis Project cracked, released, and made intros across the C64's whole life — and, unusually, is still active across platforms decades later.
subtitle: The cracking group that wouldn't die

title: Ikari
description: The English C64 group Ikari was voted the world's best cracking group, and its legendary co-operation with Talent is regarded as one of the finest the scene produced.
subtitle: Voted the world's best

title: Kefrens
description: Kefrens were one of the scene's oldest groups, and the vertical sinus-bar effect they popularised still carries their name decades later.
subtitle: The Danes who named an effect

title: Melon Dezign
description: Melon Dezign brought a graphic-design sensibility to the Amiga scene, their distinctive pixel art and clean aesthetic standing apart from the effect-maximalists.
subtitle: The scene's design house

title: Oxyron
description: Oxyron pushed the Commodore 64 into territory others thought impossible, their coders pioneering effects and tricks that became standard scene technique.
subtitle: C64 technique pioneers

title: Paradox
description: Formed in 1989 to crack Amiga software, Paradox outlasted nearly all its rivals, moving from Amiga to consoles to PC and remaining a force in the warez scene for decades.
subtitle: The warez group that wouldn't quit

title: Phenomena
description: One of the most respected Amiga groups of the early scene, Phenomena's Enigma set a bar for music, design, and coding that defined the platform's first golden age.
subtitle: Early Amiga royalty

title: Quartex
description: Quartex were a top-ranked Amiga cracking group of the late 1980s — and a reminder of the scene's real stakes, with members caught up in police busts on two continents.
subtitle: Top of the charts, and on the radar

title: Razor 1911
description: Razor 1911 became one of the longest-running cracking groups in history, active from 1985 through multiple platform generations while maintaining consistent quality.
subtitle: The oldest surviving group

title: Red Sector Inc
description: Red Sector Inc built one of the Amiga's defining early megademos and a demo-construction tool, then merged into TRSI, a powerhouse of cracking and demos.
subtitle: From megademo to TRSI

title: Rgba
description: Rgba pushed the 4K intro into new territory with real-time raymarched graphics, and their member iq carried those techniques into Shadertoy and the wider graphics world.
subtitle: Raymarching in four kilobytes

title: Sanity
description: Sanity were among the most respected Amiga groups of the early 1990s, their productions setting a standard for polish that helped define the platform's golden run.
subtitle: Amiga craft at its peak

title: Scoopex
description: Scoopex helped invent the Amiga megademo, packing dozens of effects into single productions and setting the template the whole scene would follow.
subtitle: Pioneers of the megademo

title: Skid Row
description: Formed in 1990, Skid Row became one of the most dominant Amiga cracking groups, their cracktros — and their motto — a fixture of pirated disks across the platform.
subtitle: Twice the fun, double the trouble

title: Spaceballs
description: The Norwegian group Spaceballs made State of the Art, the rotoscoped-dancer demo whose attitude and design proved the Amiga scene could be cool, not just clever.
subtitle: Style over everything

title: The Black Lotus
description: The Black Lotus (TBL) kept the Amiga demoscene at the cutting edge long past the platform's commercial life, their demo Starstruck a benchmark of what the machine can still do.
subtitle: The modern Amiga's flag-bearer

title: The Silents
description: The Silents spread across national divisions and platforms, and their cinematic 1991 demo Hardwired showed the Amiga could tell a story, not just show off.
subtitle: A scene name across borders

title: Triad
description: Triad became one of the most prolific C64 cracking groups, known for high-quality releases and artistic intros that helped birth the demo scene.
subtitle: Swedish C64 legends

title: Triton
description: Triton made some of the slickest Amiga and PC demos of the early 1990s, then did what many scene groups dreamed of: turned pro, becoming Starbreeze Studios.
subtitle: From Crystal Dream to Starbreeze

title: Commodore 1541
description: The 1541 floppy disk drive was famously slow but contained a complete 6502-based computer, enabling fast loaders and copy protection schemes.
subtitle: The disk drive with its own computer

title: 6502: The People's Processor
description: The MOS 6502 powered the Apple II, Atari 2600, Commodore 64, and NES—making home computing affordable and defining a generation of programmers.
subtitle: Eight bits that changed everything

title: 6510: The C64's Custom Core
description: The MOS 6510 added an integrated I/O port to the 6502, giving the Commodore 64 its signature memory banking and tape control.
subtitle: A 6502 with an I/O trick up its sleeve

title: 68000: The 16-Bit Powerhouse
description: The Motorola 68000 powered the Amiga, Atari ST, Sega Mega Drive, and arcade machines—bringing workstation-class architecture to home computers.
subtitle: Thirty-two bits on the inside where it counts

title: Action Replay
description: The hardware cartridge series that enabled game freezing, cheat creation, and memory manipulation across Commodore 64, Amiga, and consoles - controversial but widely used.
subtitle: The cheat cartridge

title: Agnus: The Amiga's Memory Master
description: Agnus coordinated all memory access on the Amiga, housing the Blitter for fast graphics and the Copper for beam-synchronised effects.
subtitle: DMA controller, Blitter, and Copper in one package

title: The Amiga Custom Chipset
description: Three custom co-processors gave the Amiga capabilities that PCs wouldn't match for years. Read through Commodore's own manual they are not three chips that do graphics, blitting and sound — they are one answer to a single question about who gets the memory, and the 68000 comes last.
subtitle: Agnus, Denise, and Paula

title: APU: The NES Audio Engine
description: The NES Audio Processing Unit delivered two pulse waves, a triangle, noise, and sample playback—creating the iconic sound of 8-bit Nintendo.
subtitle: Five channels of chiptune magic

title: Arcade Hardware
description: Arcade hardware evolved from discrete logic through custom boards to standardised platforms, always pushing graphical boundaries ahead of home systems.
subtitle: Purpose-built gaming machines

title: AY-3-8910: The Sound of the 80s
description: General Instrument's AY-3-8910 brought three-voice synthesis to home computers and arcades—powering the 128K Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, MSX, and countless coin-ops.
subtitle: Three square waves heard around the world

title: AY-3-8912
description: A pin-reduced variant of the AY-3-8910 with identical sound capabilities, commonly found in the ZX Spectrum 128K and other space-constrained designs.
subtitle: The compact cousin

title: Blitter: The Amiga's Graphics Accelerator
description: The Blitter moved, combined, and transformed graphics data faster than any CPU could—making the Amiga's smooth scrolling and complex visuals possible.
subtitle: Hardware-powered block transfers

title: Game Cartridges
description: A cartridge is not storage — it is hardware on the far end of the CPU bus, and the machines that used them could be extended after they shipped by putting new silicon in the slot.
subtitle: ROM on a board, wired to the bus

title: CD-ROM
description: CD-ROM transformed gaming through massive storage capacity, enabling full-motion video, voice acting, and expansive worlds impossible on floppy disks.
subtitle: 650 megabytes of possibility

title: CIA: The C64's Swiss Army Chip
description: The MOS 6526 Complex Interface Adapter handled keyboard scanning, joystick input, serial communication, and timing—the unsung heroes of the Commodore 64.
subtitle: Two chips for I/O, timing, and everything else

title: Copper: The Amiga's Display Coprocessor
description: The Copper synchronised effects to the video beam with just WAIT and MOVE—enabling rainbow gradients, split screens, and per-scanline palette changes.
subtitle: Two instructions that changed everything

title: D-pad
description: The directional control pad invented by Gunpei Yokoi for the 1982 Donkey Kong Game & Watch, which became the universal standard for game controllers.
subtitle: Yokoi's control innovation

title: D-sub connectors
description: D-sub connectors carried game controls, serial communications, printer data and more across generations of computers. Their shared shape made them familiar; their different pinouts made understanding the machine essential.
subtitle: The family of connectors behind games, printers and serial links

title: Dance Mat
description: The floor-based controller that turned rhythm games into physical exercise, defining the Dance Dance Revolution phenomenon.
subtitle: Gaming with your feet

title: Denise: The Amiga's Display Engine
description: Denise transformed raw bitplane data into stunning visuals with dual playfields, eight hardware sprites, and the famous Hold-And-Modify mode.
subtitle: Playfields, sprites, and HAM mode magic

title: DualShock
description: Sony's DualShock controller combined dual analog sticks with rumble feedback, establishing the modern gamepad template still used today.
subtitle: Rumble and precision

title: Flight Stick
description: The specialised joystick for flight and space combat games, evolving from one-button sticks to full HOTAS cockpit setups.
subtitle: Wings for your hands

title: Game Genie
description: Codemasters/Galoob's cheat device for NES, SNES, Genesis, and Game Boy that brought the POKE culture to consoles - and survived Nintendo's legal challenge.
subtitle: Console cheats legitimised

title: Kryoflux
description: A USB-based floppy disk controller that captures raw magnetic flux transitions, enabling preservation of copy-protected and deteriorating disks that standard methods cannot read.
subtitle: Flux-level disk preservation

title: Light Gun
description: The input device category that enabled shooting gallery games from arcades to living rooms, using screen detection technology.
subtitle: Point and shoot gaming

title: Light Pen
description: The forgotten input device that let users draw directly on CRT screens, popular for art software in the 1980s.
subtitle: Draw on your screen

title: MC6847 VDG
description: The Motorola Video Display Generator used in the Dragon and TRS-80 Color Computer, offering text and graphics modes but limited colour flexibility compared to custom chips.
subtitle: Motorola video chip

title: MiSTer FPGA
description: The open-source FPGA project that recreates vintage computers and consoles in hardware, achieving accuracy impossible with software emulation.
subtitle: Hardware-level accuracy

title: MMC1
description: Nintendo's first Multi Memory Controller was the most widely used NES mapper, and the strangest to program: its four control registers loaded serially, a single bit per write.
subtitle: Four registers, one bit at a time

title: MMC3
description: Nintendo's MMC3 mapper chip enabled larger, more sophisticated NES games through bank switching, scanline counting, and expanded capabilities.
subtitle: The NES power expander

title: Motorola 6809
description: The 1978 Motorola processor widely considered the best 8-bit CPU ever designed, featuring clean orthogonal architecture, 16-bit operations, and position-independent code support.
subtitle: The finest 8-bit CPU

title: Multiface
description: Romantic Robot's Multiface — a cartridge that plugged into the Spectrum's expansion port, asserted NMI on a button press, paged its own ROM into low memory, and let the user inspect, modify, and snapshot the running program's state. Released in 1986, the Multiface was the single piece of hardware that turned cheat-finding from specialist work into a community pastime, and was the technical engine behind the magazine POKE columns of the late 1980s.
subtitle: The hardware NMI freezer that made POKE culture possible

title: NES Zapper
description: Nintendo's iconic light gun controller that brought Duck Hunt to millions of living rooms and defined home light gun gaming.
subtitle: The orange light gun

title: Paddle Controller
description: The rotary controller that defined early gaming from Pong to Breakout, offering precise single-axis movement.
subtitle: The original analogue input

title: Paula: The Amiga's Voice
description: Paula delivered four independent 8-bit audio channels with DMA playback—giving the Amiga the most capable sound system of its generation.
subtitle: Four channels of sample-based audio

title: Power Pad
description: Nintendo's floor mat controller for the NES that pioneered physical gaming years before Dance Dance Revolution.
subtitle: Gaming on your feet

title: PPU: The NES Picture Processor
description: The Ricoh 2C02 Picture Processing Unit gave the NES hardware sprites, tile-based backgrounds, and smooth scrolling—defining the look of 8-bit console gaming.
subtitle: Dedicated silicon for smooth scrolling and sprites

title: Raspberry Pi
description: The Raspberry Pi brought affordable single-board computing to education and hobbyists, becoming the platform of choice for retro gaming projects.
subtitle: Computing for everyone

title: R.O.B.
description: Nintendo's robot accessory that helped the NES enter American stores by positioning the console as a toy rather than a video game system.
subtitle: The Robotic Operating Buddy

title: SID: The Sound of the C64
description: The SID 6581/8580 chip gave the Commodore 64 synthesizer-class sound, inspiring composers and hardware hackers alike.
subtitle: Three voices, endless personality

title: Spinner Controller
description: The specialised arcade input device offering continuous 360-degree rotation, essential for games like Tempest and Tron.
subtitle: The arcade's rotary dial

title: Steering Wheel Controller
description: The specialised input device that brought realistic driving control from arcades to living rooms, evolving from bare spinners to force feedback systems.
subtitle: The racing essential

title: Trackball
description: The arcade input device that enabled precise analogue control for games like Centipede and Marble Madness.
subtitle: Rolling precision

title: The ULA
description: The Uncommitted Logic Array (ULA) is the custom Ferranti chip that combined video generation, memory contention, keyboard scanning, tape and beeper I/O, and the border into a single integrated circuit. It is the reason the ZX Spectrum cost £125 instead of £250, and the reason the platform has the visual and acoustic identity it does.
subtitle: One Ferranti gate array — display, keyboard, sound, I/O, and the Spectrum's whole personality

title: Inside the VIC-II
description: Sprites, smooth scrolling, and 16 colours on a budget — the VIC-II (6567/6569) generated everything you saw on a Commodore 64. This entry covers both the historical context and the full programmer's reference.
subtitle: The graphics chip that defined the Commodore 64

title: Video Toaster
description: NewTek's Amiga expansion that turned a home computer into professional broadcast equipment. It sold for $1,595, and Business Week called it as capable as gear normally costing $60,000.
subtitle: Broadcast on a budget

title: VRC II
description: Konami built its own line of NES mapper chips instead of settling for Nintendo's. The VRC II gave eight separately switchable 1 KB character banks and a port for saving to serial EEPROM.
subtitle: Konami's answer to the MMC

title: YM2612
description: Yamaha's YM2612 FM synthesis chip gave the Sega Mega Drive its distinctive sound, enabling complex timbres impossible on competing hardware.
subtitle: The Mega Drive's voice

title: Zilog Z80
description: The Zilog Z80, designed by Federico Faggin after he left Intel, became the dominant 8-bit CPU of European home computing — powering the ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, MSX, Game Boy, Sega Master System, and countless arcade machines. An 8080-compatible superset with shadow registers, block operations, and an instruction set rich enough to feel almost mid-range for a 1976 chip.
subtitle: The 8-bit processor that defined British home computing

title: 576 KByte
description: 576 KByte ran monthly from January 1990 to December 1999 — 140 issues, the only Hungarian title in this library. Its first issue is entirely about Western games, and the transition it was born into can be measured in its own pages: the companies advertising in it are gazdasági munkaközösségek until 1994 and limited companies afterwards.
subtitle: A Hungarian games magazine that starts the month after the system ends

title: ACE Magazine
description: ACE provided multi-format coverage with a mature editorial approach, treating games as legitimate entertainment worthy of serious criticism.
subtitle: Advanced Computer Entertainment

title: Acorn User
description: Launched in August 1982 as the official magazine for Acorn's machines, published by Addison-Wesley for Acorn Computers. Unlike the independent titles this Vault mostly covers, Acorn User was the manufacturer's — which is why Elite launched in it.
subtitle: The manufacturer's own magazine

title: Amiga Action
description: Launched from Sussex by Gollner Publishing in October 1989 against Future, EMAP and Europress, and running to June 1995 — by which time it had been bought by two of them in turn: Europress around mid-1991, then IDG at the end of 1994.
subtitle: Chichester's entry into a crowded market, and what became of it

title: Amiga Computing
description: Database Publications' Amiga magazine ran from June 1988 to October 1997, through three owners. Its own small print traces a line most histories keep separate: Database was a division of Europress, the publisher that picked up CRASH and ZZAP!64 when Newsfield collapsed — and that sold the magazine on to IDG at the end of 1994.
subtitle: Macclesfield's Amiga monthly, and the house that later took CRASH

title: Amiga Format
description: The long-running Amiga magazine (1989-2000) from Future Publishing that provided comprehensive platform coverage with multiple cover disks and professional journalism throughout the Amiga's commercial life.
subtitle: Comprehensive Amiga coverage

title: Amiga Joker
description: Joker Verlag published Amiga Joker from Haar, near Munich, between April 1990 and October 1996. Its masthead states a publishing schedule — ten issues a year, last Friday of the preceding month, double issues for June/July and August/September — that the holdings then confirm month for month across four consecutive years.
subtitle: The German Amiga monthly, and the first German title in this Vault

title: Amiga Power
description: Amiga Power rejected the cosy relationship between magazines and publishers, delivering brutally honest reviews that readers trusted and the industry feared.
subtitle: Uncompromising criticism

title: Amiga Shopper
description: Future Publishing's third Amiga title ran 108 issues from April 1991 to January 1997, positioned at the buying decision rather than the games — the serious end of a market Future already covered twice over.
subtitle: The Amiga magazine for people who wanted to buy things

title: Amiga User International
description: An independent Amiga magazine published by Croftward Limited from Clerkenwell — the same postcode district as EMAP — and running at least from 1987 to 1996. The last British title in this library to get an entry.
subtitle: Croftward's Amiga monthly, and a third publisher in EC1R

title: Amstrad Action
description: 117 issues from October 1985 to June 1995, and the title Future Publishing was founded to print. Its Mastergame award ran from the first issue, and it outlasted the machine it covered.
subtitle: Future Publishing's first magazine, and the CPC's longest run

title: Amstrad Semanal
description: Hobby Press published Amstrad Semanal in Spain from 3 September 1985, weekly, and this library holds a hundred consecutive issues to 1987 — more day-dated issues than any other title held, including Britain's Personal Computer News. Its first cover analyses Knight Lore as the number one program in the world.
subtitle: A weekly Amstrad magazine, and the longest weekly run in this library

title: Amtix!
description: Nineteen issues from October 1985 to April 1987. Newsfield brought the CRASH and ZZAP!64 formula to the Amstrad CPC, gave it the Accolade award, and closed it inside eighteen months.
subtitle: Newsfield's Amstrad title, and the one that did not last

title: Atari Club Magazin
description: Atari ran a members' club in West Germany with its own magazine, held here from 1982 to 1984. Its pages promote E.T. for a December 1982 German release, report survey findings that video games reduce aggression, and apologise for club merchandise selling out — all in the months the American market was collapsing.
subtitle: Atari's German club magazine, selling E.T. while America stopped buying

title: Atari ST User
description: Database Publications' Atari ST monthly ran from March 1986 to October 1994 — the second of three machine-specific titles the Europress group launched, after The Micro User and before Amiga Computing.
subtitle: The middle title in Database's platform sequence

title: Australian Personal Computer
description: APC launched in May 1980 from Carlton, Victoria, with 'AUSTRALIA'S FIRST MICRO MAGAZINE' on the cover — five months after MICRO-80 began publishing in South Australia. Its contributors, columns and cover artist are British, and match a British magazine's, but this library holds nothing from that title early enough to test the connection.
subtitle: Melbourne's general micro monthly, and a claim this library contradicts

title: Bajtek
description: Bajtek launched in September 1985 as a joint monthly supplement to Sztandar Młodych and Odrodzenie, with the stated aim of combating microcomputer illiteracy in Poland. Its first issue covers the ZX Spectrum, LOGO, joysticks, software protection — and Atic Atac.
subtitle: A Polish computer magazine issued as a supplement to the state youth newspaper

title: C= Hacking
description: Founded on Usenet in February 1992 by Craig Taylor to explain what people had worked out about the C64 and C128, and still running a decade later. Pasi 'Albert' Ojala's 'Demo Corner' in it is why FLI, DYCP and sprite stretching are written down at all.
subtitle: The net-magazine that documented the C64's tricks

title: Club Commodore
description: Club Commodore was a bulletin for VIC-20 and CBM users published in Spain from 1982 by Microelectrónica y Control, Commodore's exclusive Spanish distributor. It is the earliest club magazine in this library, its content is technical rather than promotional, and its December 1982 issue wishes readers a happy new year in Spanish, Catalan, Basque and Galician.
subtitle: A Barcelona distributor's bulletin, greeting its readers in four languages

title: Club Nintendo
description: Nintendo of Europe published Club Nintendo from 1989 in English, German and Dutch. The three editions are the same twenty pages in three languages — same features, same page numbers, same jokes — with only the club's return address changed. It was made in cooperation with Tokuma Shoten of Tokyo, under project leads titled national and international.
subtitle: The manufacturer's own magazine, issued page-for-page in three languages

title: Commodore Computer Club
description: Commodore Computer Club ran from September 1982 to December 1991, ninety issues from Milan.
