subtitle: Yokoi's portable revolution

title: Game Boy Advance
description: Nintendo's Game Boy Advance brought 32-bit power to handhelds, delivering SNES-quality gaming on the go with impressive battery life.
subtitle: SNES in your pocket

title: Nintendo Game Boy
description: Gunpei Yokoi's Game Boy chose battery life over power, outlasting technically superior rivals to define handheld gaming. Nintendo's own programming manual shows the choice was not folklore but documented discipline: it tells developers to halt the processor and do nothing at all whenever the machine can afford to.
subtitle: Lateral thinking made portable

title: Sega Game Gear
description: Sega's 1990 colour handheld that was essentially a portable Master System, offering backlit graphics but suffering from poor battery life that limited its success against Game Boy.
subtitle: Portable Master System

title: Jupiter Ace
description: Built in 1982 by the two engineers who had just designed the ZX Spectrum, the Jupiter Ace put Forth in ROM where every other home computer put BASIC — faster, more compact, and commercially fatal. Jupiter Cantab crashed in 1983; the machine outlived the company by years in the hands of its users' club.
subtitle: The home computer that shipped with Forth instead of BASIC

title: MSX
description: MSX attempted to standardise home computers, succeeding spectacularly in Japan while struggling elsewhere, and launching Konami and Metal Gear.
subtitle: The standard that united Japan

title: Nintendo 64
description: Nintendo's 64-bit console delivered groundbreaking 3D experiences with four controller ports that made it the definitive couch multiplayer machine.
subtitle: Four controllers, infinite memories

title: NAOMI
description: Sega's NAOMI arcade board shared Dreamcast architecture, enabling arcade-perfect home ports and efficient cross-platform development.
subtitle: Dreamcast's arcade sibling

title: Neo Geo Pocket Color
description: SNK's 1999 handheld featuring the best portable D-pad ever made and excellent fighting games, cut short by SNK's bankruptcy despite critical acclaim.
subtitle: Fighting game specialist

title: Neo Geo
description: SNK's Neo Geo delivered arcade-identical gaming at home for the price of a used car. Its specification shows why nothing else looked like it: the machine has no tiled background layer at all, and draws almost everything — scenery included — out of sprites.
subtitle: Arcade perfection at home

title: Nintendo Entertainment System
description: Launched as the Famicom in 1983, Nintendo's 8-bit console paired the Ricoh 2A03 CPU with a tile-and-sprite PPU and a strict licensing regime, reviving the crashed console market and selling around 62 million units.
subtitle: The console that rebuilt the games industry

title: Nintendo DS
description: Nintendo's dual-screen handheld combined touchscreen input with traditional controls, enabling innovative gameplay that dominated handheld gaming.
subtitle: Touching is good

title: PC Engine / TurboGrafx-16
description: NEC's PC Engine bridged 8-bit and 16-bit generations, dominated Japan briefly, and introduced the CD-ROM add-on that would reshape gaming. Hudson's chip manuals show how an 8-bit machine kept up: the processor carries a memory manager and the sound hardware on the same die.
subtitle: The compact powerhouse

title: PlayStation 2
description: The PlayStation 2 dominated gaming with 155 million units sold, DVD playback, and a library spanning every genre imaginable.
subtitle: Best-selling console ever

title: PlayStation
description: Sony's PlayStation transformed gaming through CD-ROM capacity, third-party support, and marketing that made consoles mainstream adult entertainment. Sony's developer documentation shows a machine designed by subtraction: the memory manager and the floating-point unit are gone, and what replaces them is a fixed-point geometry coprocessor and a kilobyte of scratch pad.
subtitle: The disc revolution

title: Sega Master System
description: The Sega Master System was technically superior to the NES but couldn't overcome Nintendo's head start and third-party lock-in.
subtitle: The NES challenger

title: Sega Mega Drive / Genesis
description: The Mega Drive broke Nintendo's stranglehold, brought Sonic to life, and made 'Genesis does what Nintendon't' the most aggressive slogan in gaming. Sega's own developer documentation is more careful than the slogan: the headline numbers it is remembered by are each the best case of a pair.
subtitle: Sega's 16-bit champion

title: Sega Saturn
description: Sega's Saturn excelled at 2D and sprite-based games but struggled with 3D, losing the 32-bit console war despite an impressive Japanese library.
subtitle: The 2D powerhouse

title: Sinclair QL
description: Announced in January 1984 at £399 with a 68008, 128K of RAM, two Microdrives and four bundled Psion applications, the Sinclair QL was extraordinary value and barely worked. It shipped months late with part of its operating system in a lump of metal plugged into the back, and by May Sinclair Research was holding £5 million against orders it could not fill — the same sum the whole company sold for two years later.
subtitle: The first 68000-family home computer, and the machine that finished Sinclair Research

title: Super Nintendo Entertainment System
description: The SNES arrived late to the 16-bit war but won through superior software, Mode 7 magic, and the most celebrated game library of any console. In Britain it arrived twice: eighteen months as a grey import at £250–£300, then officially at £149 — Nintendo undercutting the market that had been selling its own machine.
subtitle: Nintendo's 16-bit answer

title: TRS-80 Color Computer
description: The Tandy/Radio Shack 6809-based home computer line (1980-1991), known as the CoCo, which shared architecture with the Dragon and evolved into the capable CoCo 3.
subtitle: Tandy's 6809 line

title: TRS-80
description: The TRS-80 brought personal computing to Radio Shack stores across America, becoming an unexpected bestseller and establishing the home computer market. Tandy's own technical handbook shows a machine built to a price in every detail — including a character code that is only six bits stored, with the seventh worked out by a logic gate.
subtitle: Radio Shack's surprise success

title: Vectrex
description: The 1982 vector graphics game console with built-in monitor, using the Motorola 6809 CPU to create sharp line-based graphics unlike any other home system.
subtitle: Vector graphics console

title: Commodore VIC-20
description: The first computer to sell a million units, the VIC-20 brought colour computing to the masses and paved the way for the C64.
subtitle: The friendly computer

title: Xbox
description: The original Xbox brought PC gaming power to consoles, introduced Xbox Live, and launched the Halo franchise that defined console shooters.
subtitle: Microsoft enters gaming

title: ZX Spectrum Next
description: A community-funded FPGA Spectrum in a Rick Dickinson case: a Z80N at up to 28MHz, 128 hardware sprites, Layer 2 graphics, three AY chips and SD storage — while still running the 1982 machine's software.
subtitle: The Spectrum Sinclair did not build, forty years late

title: Sinclair ZX Spectrum
description: Clive Sinclair's £125 Spectrum brought colour computing to British bedrooms in 1982, igniting the type-in era and a decade of homegrown game development.
subtitle: Rubber-keyed brilliance, on a budget

title: Sinclair ZX81
description: Clive Sinclair's black wedge computer brought programming to Britain's bedrooms, despite its 1KB RAM and membrane keyboard. Its display has no video hardware worth the name: the Z80 generates the picture by running the screen as if it were a program, and FAST mode is the machine offering to stop.
subtitle: Computing for under £70

title: Active Time Battle
description: Active Time Battle is Square's patented combat system: each character has a time gauge, acts only when it fills, and enemies keep attacking while the player decides. Edge defined it for Final Fantasy VII in 1996 and reviewed Final Fantasy Tactics, Parasite Eve and Xenogears as variations on it.
subtitle: Time flows in combat

title: AGI Engine
description: Sierra's Adventure Game Interpreter ran the 3-D Animated Adventures from King's Quest (IBM PCjr, 1984) to Manhunter: San Francisco, at 160×200 with a typed verb-noun parser, until SCI replaced it from King's Quest IV.
subtitle: Sierra's Adventure Game Interpreter

title: AGSP
description: Putting the C64's whole screen anywhere by combining VSP for the horizontal and a line crunch for the vertical - the trick behind full-screen scrolling games and demos, and identifiable by the blanked lines it leaves at the top.
subtitle: Any Given Screen Position

title: Analogue Control
description: Analogue control reads how far a stick is pushed, not just which way. Atari sold it on the 5200 in 1983 with a stick that would not centre; the Nintendo 64 thumb stick made Mario walk or run by degree in 1996, and Sega and Sony followed with analogue pads of their own.
subtitle: Degrees of freedom

title: Arbitrary Code Execution
description: The most powerful speedrunning exploit - manipulating game memory through normal inputs to execute arbitrary code, enabling impossible shortcuts and instant wins.
subtitle: Playing the game's memory

title: Arpeggio
description: Arpeggios rapidly cycled through notes of a chord, simulating polyphony on sound chips limited to single-note channels—a defining technique of chiptune music.
subtitle: Chords from a single channel

title: ASCII Art
description: ASCII art is a picture made of printable text characters. Period magazines trace it from line-printer pictures downloaded from CompuServe around 1980, through the ANSI colour art and smileys of the bulletin boards, to the ASCII logos of the 1990s Amiga scene.
subtitle: Pictures from punctuation

title: Attract Mode
description: Attract mode displayed automated gameplay demonstrations on idle arcade machines, enticing players to insert coins through flashy visuals, high score tables, and gameplay previews.
subtitle: Arcade marketing display

title: Attribute-Aware Design
description: How Spectrum designers and programmers worked with the platform's two-colours-per-cell rule: monochrome rooms, block alignment, colour pushed to the border, transparent printing, masking, and the attribute byte reused as the level map.
subtitle: Designing for the ZX Spectrum's two-colours-per-cell rule

title: Audio Programming
description: Audio programming on vintage hardware demanded intimate knowledge of sound chips, precise timing, and clever techniques to achieve musical results.
subtitle: Sound from code

title: Bank Switching
description: Bank switching allows systems with limited address space to access more memory by swapping different memory regions into the same address range.
subtitle: Expanding memory through hardware tricks

title: Base Building
description: Base building is the construction half of real-time strategy: structures that gather a resource, produce units and defend the plot. Reviewers described Dune II in 1992 as Sim City with a war attached, called Warcraft and Command & Conquer copies of it, and by 1998 used "base-building game" as a genre label.
subtitle: Construction strategy

title: BASIC Curricula
description: BASIC curricula in schools introduced millions of students to programming concepts through hands-on coding on classroom computers.
subtitle: Teaching code in schools

title: BASIC V2 Reference
description: Complete command reference for Commodore 64 BASIC V2
subtitle: Complete command reference

title: Battery Backup
description: A lithium cell in the cartridge keeps its work RAM powered while the console is off, so a game can save without a disk or a password. Family BASIC had it in 1984; The Legend of Zelda's gold cartridge made it famous in 1987; a CR2032 still does the job.
subtitle: Cartridge save memory

title: Beeper Music
description: How the 48K Spectrum's single speaker bit produced continuous in-game tunes and three-voice harmony: Matthew Smith's interleaved game loop, Tim Follin's multi-channel routines, and what they cost the rest of the program.
subtitle: Single-channel melody on the Sinclair ZX Spectrum's one-bit speaker

title: Blast Processing
description: Blast Processing was Sega of America's 1992-93 marketing term for the Genesis. Sega's own magazine defined it as displaying one image while loading another; the developer manual never names it; the word came from a Mega-CD interview.
subtitle: Marketing meets hardware

title: BOBs: Blitter Objects
description: BOBs used the Amiga's Blitter to draw sprites into the playfield—offering unlimited objects at the cost of CPU coordination and flicker-free rendering.
subtitle: Software sprites on the Amiga

title: Branching Narrative
description: A branching narrative is a story whose path depends on what the player does. Period sources trace it through the Fighting Fantasy gamebooks, adventures with several endings (Deadline had ten), Wing Commander's performance-branched campaign, Chrono Trigger's alternate endings and Blade Runner's randomised suspects.
subtitle: Your story, your choices

title: BSP Trees
description: A BSP tree sorts a level's walls in advance so the renderer can draw them in order from any viewpoint. John Carmack learned it from Bruce Naylor's papers in April 1993 while squeezing Wolfenstein 3D onto the SNES, rebuilt Doom around it, and took it into 3D with the PVS for Quake.
subtitle: 3D rendering optimisation

title: How a Cassette Becomes a Game
description: Cassettes were slow, cheap, and everywhere. Here's how data marched from tape to RAM, one bit at a time.
subtitle: From magnetic stripes to moving sprites

title: Cel Shading
description: Cel shading draws 3D models in flat colour bands with heavy outlines to look hand-drawn. The name came from LightWave's Cel Shader in 1997; Sega applied it to Jet Set Radio in 2000, Nintendo's cel-shaded Link stunned Spaceworld 2001, and by 2003 magazines called it a fad.
subtitle: 3D with cartoon style

title: Character Graphics
description: Character graphics used redefined text characters as game graphics, enabling colourful displays with minimal memory on systems designed primarily for text.
subtitle: Building worlds from 8×8 blocks

title: Character-Shift Parallax
description: The C64 has one background layer, so its games faked a second by rolling the pixel definitions of a few characters against the direction of the scroll. Achim traces it to Bounder, Parallax and Marauder; John Rowlands added it to Mayhem in Monsterland in an hour.
subtitle: Parallax by redrawing the font

title: Client-Side Prediction
description: Client-side prediction lets a networked game act on the player's input before the server confirms it, then corrects the result when the answer arrives. Magazines in 1996-97 describe id Software introducing it in QuakeWorld, its PUSHLATENCY command, and the rubber-band corrections that came with it.
subtitle: Making lag invisible

title: Code Wheels
description: A code wheel is a pair of printed discs a game asks the player to consult before it runs, so the disk itself could ship unprotected. In print from Starflight in 1987 to Monkey Island's Dial-A-Pirate, with reviewers recording both the jokes and the black-on-black wheels.
subtitle: Analog DRM

title: Collision Detection
description: Collision detection determined when game objects touched, using techniques from simple bounding boxes to pixel-perfect checks, each trading accuracy for performance.
subtitle: When objects meet

title: Colour Clash
description: The ZX Spectrum stores colour per 8×8 cell, not per pixel, so anything drawn into a cell shares its two colours with whatever is already there. The period press called it "attribute problems" and reviewed games on how they handled it.
subtitle: The Spectrum's curse

title: Data Compression
description: Compression techniques allowed game developers to fit larger games into limited ROM and RAM by encoding data more efficiently, from simple RLE to sophisticated algorithms.
subtitle: Fitting more into less

title: Copy Protection
description: Copy protection evolved from simple disk tricks to elaborate physical manuals and hardware dongles, creating an ongoing battle between publishers and crackers.
subtitle: The anti-piracy arms race

title: Copylock
description: Rob Northen's disk protection system that became the industry standard on Amiga and Atari ST, using sophisticated techniques to detect original disks and resist cracking.
subtitle: The protection standard

title: Crafting Systems
description: A crafting system lets the player make items from gathered ingredients. In the magazines held here it runs from Secret of Evermore's alchemy in 1995 through the trade skills of Ultima Online and EverQuest to the recipes, forges and crafting stations reviewers judged in the MMORPGs of 2003-04.
subtitle: Making from materials

title: Cycle Accuracy
description: Cycle-accurate emulation reproduces what the hardware does on each clock cycle. The sources here show why: games that hang when timing is approximate, chips that steal bus cycles from the CPU by documented rules, and emulator authors who set "cycle-exact" as the goal.
subtitle: Emulation timing tiers

title: Destructible Terrain
description: The technique of modifying bitmap landscapes in real-time, famously used in Worms to create satisfying explosions that reshape the battlefield.
subtitle: Worms' secret weapon

title: Dialogue Trees
description: A dialogue tree offers the player a short list of replies, each opening another. The magazines here trace it from Law of the West's four replies in 1985 through Sierra's "conversation tree" of 1992 to the statistic-gated dialogue of Fallout and Planescape: Torment.
subtitle: Branching conversation

title: Difficulty Design
description: Difficulty design is the choice of how hard a game is and who can change it. The sources here run from the arcade trade's "easy to learn, hard to play" rule and the Atari VCS difficulty switches to GoldenEye's objective-changing modes and The Lost Levels.
subtitle: Balancing challenge and accessibility

title: Digitised Sprites
description: Digitised sprites are video frames of real actors reduced to a machine's palette. In use on the C64 by 1988, made famous by Pit-Fighter and Mortal Kombat; not to be confused with Rare's rendered sprites.
subtitle: Real actors, pixel form

title: Dirty Rectangles
description: Dirty rectangle rendering optimised screen updates by tracking and redrawing only the areas that changed, saving CPU cycles when most of the display remained static.
subtitle: Efficient screen updates

title: Disk Fastloaders
description: The 1541 is slow because its bus protocol is bit-banged in software around the VIC-II's DMA; fastloaders replace both ends of it. Epyx claimed five times, Datel's Warp 25 two hundred blocks in six seconds, and JiffyDOS printed the stopwatch figures.
subtitle: Cutting load times on the Commodore 1541

title: Disk Protection
description: Disk protection techniques prevented casual copying of floppy disks through intentional errors, non-standard formatting, and hardware tricks.
subtitle: Copy prevention on floppy

title: Dithering
description: Dithering created the illusion of additional colours by interleaving pixels of different shades, expanding limited palettes through optical mixing.
subtitle: More colours from fewer

title: Double Buffering
description: Double buffering drew to an off-screen buffer while displaying another, eliminating visual tearing and enabling smooth animation even on slow hardware.
subtitle: Smooth, tear-free graphics

title: DYCP
description: The C64 scroller where each letter bobs up and down on its own sine as it crosses the screen. Explained in print by Pasi 'Albert' Ojala in 1991, whose article is why the technique is documented at all.
subtitle: Different Y Character Position

title: Emulation Techniques
description: An emulator makes one machine's software run on another by imitating its hardware. The magazines here give the method in Chris Hardy's words, the interpreter-versus-recompiler choice in Simon Goodwin's, MAME's growth from 1997, and the UltraHLE and Connectix cases of 1999.
subtitle: Software becoming hardware

title: Enemy Design
description: Enemy design is the choice of what opposes the player and how it behaves. Nishikado, Iwatani, Jarvis, Miyamoto and Bungie's Jaime Griesemer describe their choices here, from invaders that shoot back to Grunts that panic.
subtitle: Making meaningful opposition

title: Falling Block
description: A falling-block game drops pieces into a well and clears filled rows or matched groups. Tetris defined it, and the 1988-94 reviews here describe the rules, the Game Boy pack-in, and how Columns, Dr. Mario and Puyo Puyo varied them.
subtitle: Puzzle game foundation

title: Fast Loaders
description: Fast loaders accelerated tape and disk loading on 8-bit computers, reducing frustrating wait times through optimised data transfer routines.
subtitle: Beating the bottleneck

title: Fatalities
description: A Fatality is the finishing move Mortal Kombat lets the winner perform on a beaten opponent. The moves sold the game, were renamed and replaced on the Super NES in 1993, were named in the US Senate hearings that winter, and multiplied into Babalities, Friendships and Animalities in the sequels.
subtitle: Finish them

title: Filmation Engine
description: Ultimate Play the Game's Filmation engine gave 8-bit isometric games solid, masked, flicker-free objects — and set the template that a hundred Spectrum arcade adventures followed.
subtitle: Isometric illusion

title: Filter Sweeps
description: Filter sweeps create dynamic timbral changes by gradually adjusting filter cutoff frequency, a signature effect of the C64's SID chip.
subtitle: Moving through the frequency spectrum

title: First-Person Horror
description: First-person horror frightens a player who sees through the character's eyes. The 1997-2004 PC reviews here describe the method: sound before sight, scarce light, set-pieces at the moment of false safety, and suspense over gore.
subtitle: Through terrified eyes

title: Fixed-Point Maths
description: Fixed-point arithmetic gives 8-bit systems sub-pixel precision for smooth movement, physics, and animation—all with fast integer operations.
subtitle: Smooth movement without floating point

title: FLD
description: A C64 trick that inserts gaps between character lines, pushing the graphics below them down the screen. Unusually for a scene effect, it appeared in commercial games before it appeared in demos.
subtitle: Flexible Line Distance

title: FLI
description: A C64 trick that re-triggers the VIC-II's colour fetch on every pixel line instead of every eighth, multiplying the colours available in a bitmap — at the cost of a permanent grey scar down the left of the screen.
subtitle: Flexible Line Interpretation

title: FM Synthesis
description: FM synthesis makes complex timbres by letting one oscillator vary another's frequency. Chowning's method became Yamaha's chip family: the YM2151 in arcades, the YM3812 on the Ad Lib and Sound Blaster, the YM2413 in MSX-MUSIC, the YM2612 in the Mega Drive.
subtitle: Frequency modulation music

title: Full Motion Video
description: Full motion video played filmed actors from CD. Sega called Night Trap the first interactive movie in 1992, The 7th Guest shipped 36 minutes of it, Wing Commander III put Mark Hamill on four CDs, and by 1998 Computer Gaming World was writing its obituary.
subtitle: Live action in games

title: Fog of War
description: Fog of war hides what the player has not scouted. Computer wargames argued about it from 1982, Empire painted the unexplored world black, and Warcraft II split the black shroud from the fog that returns when your units leave.
subtitle: Strategic information hiding

title: Force Feedback
description: Force feedback puts motors in a controller so the game can push back. Hard Drivin' had a motorised steering column in 1989, Immersion's Louis Rosenberg pitched the modelled version in 1996, and by 1998 Microsoft and Logitech were shipping wheels and sticks the games had yet to catch up with.
subtitle: Feel the game

title: FPP
description: The most permissive of the C64 vertical tweaks: every single pixel line of graphics placed anywhere on screen, independently of every other — so graphics can be reversed, repeated or stretched at will.
subtitle: Flexible Pixel Position

title: Frame Animation
description: Frame animation creates movement by displaying sequences of pre-drawn sprite images, with quality determined by frame count, timing, and artistic principles borrowed from traditional animation.
subtitle: Sprite-based motion

title: Frameskipping and Interpolation
description: When a C64 game runs out of raster time, it can render less often than it thinks (frameskipping) or think less often than it renders, filling the gaps with linear interpolation. Cadaver set out both in his Rant 9 and shipped the second in Metal Warrior 4.
subtitle: Running the logic slower than the screen

title: Freescape
description: Incentive's engine gave 8-bit micros a real three-dimensional world — filled polygons, free movement, looking up and down — four years before consumer 3D hardware existed. CRASH gave the first game built on it 97%.
subtitle: Solid 3D on a machine with no maths

title: Game Design
description: Game design is deciding what a game asks of its player and what it gives back. The 1982-97 sources here are designers on their own method: Chris Crawford's advice to beginners and his revision of it, a 1984 designers' panel, Sid Meier on the player's role, and Miyamoto's miniature garden.
subtitle: The craft of creating play

title: The Game Loop
description: Every game runs on the same fundamental pattern: read input, update state, render graphics, repeat. Understanding the game loop is the first step to building anything interactive.
subtitle: The heartbeat of every game

title: Ghost AI
description: Pac-Man's four ghosts each hunt by a different rule so the pack comes from all directions. Toru Iwatani's own account of why, the chase-and-disperse waves, the power-pellet reversal, and the pattern play the rules made possible.
subtitle: Pac-Man's four personalities

title: Hard restart
description: Every C64 music driver silences and resets a SID voice two frames before each note, because the chip's envelope generator can otherwise stall for 1.7 frames. The workaround is older than the explanation.
subtitle: Working around the SID's ADSR bug

title: Hardware Scrolling
description: Hardware scroll registers let the display shift smoothly pixel-by-pixel without copying memory—essential for fast, smooth side-scrolling games.
subtitle: Smooth movement without moving data

title: Havok
description: Havok was the Dublin physics middleware that released beta code in 1999, merged with Ipion in 2001, aimed version 2.0 at ragdoll characters in 2003, and by 2005 was, in Edge's words, the standard by which the others were judged, with Half-Life 2 and Halo 2 to show for it.
subtitle: Physics middleware

title: Hitboxes
description: Hitboxes define the invisible collision boundaries around game objects, determining when attacks connect, pickups are collected, and characters collide with the world.
subtitle: Collision boundaries

title: Interrupt-Driven Music
description: Interrupt-driven music used timer interrupts to update sound chips at regular intervals, allowing music playback while the CPU handled game logic.
subtitle: Sound without blocking

title: Isometric Projection
description: Isometric projection created the illusion of three-dimensional space on 2D screens, enabling exploration games impossible with flat side-views.
subtitle: 3D from 2D

title: KERNAL I/O Routines
description: The C64’s KERNAL ROM exposes a patchable API for keyboard, screen, tape, disk, and serial I/O—perfect for BASIC and assembly alike.
subtitle: The Commodore 64’s built-in service desk

title: Lenslok
description: The physical copy protection device that required players to decode on-screen codes through a plastic prism - launched on Elite in late 1985 and disliked from the first month.
subtitle: The hated prism

title: Linecrunch
description: A C64 trick that crushes character lines down to a single pixel row, pulling the screen upward. Unlike FLD it can move bitmap graphics — and it first appeared not in a demo but in a cracktro.
subtitle: Squeezing eight pixel rows into one

title: Link Cable
description: The Game Boy's link cable came in the 1989 box as the Video Link Cable, joined two machines for two-player Tetris, grew a Four Player Adapter in 1991, and became the point of Pokémon's two editions in 1998.
subtitle: Wired multiplayer

title: Lookup Tables
description: Lookup tables pre-calculated expensive operations like trigonometry and multiplication, storing results for instant retrieval on processors too slow for real-time maths.
subtitle: Trading memory for speed

title: Manual Protection
description: Manual protection required players to consult physical documentation to play games, deterring piracy through information unavailable on copied disks.
subtitle: Look it up to play

title: Memory Management
description: Memory management techniques enabled complex games on hardware with kilobytes of RAM, from bank switching to compression to careful data structure design.
subtitle: Making the most of limited RAM

title: Memory Mapping
description: Memory-mapped I/O places hardware registers at specific addresses, allowing software to control graphics, sound, and input by reading and writing memory locations.
subtitle: Addresses for everything

title: MOD Format
description: The MOD format combined samples with pattern-based sequencing in a single self-contained file, becoming the standard for game and demo music on the Amiga and across the chiptune scene.
subtitle: The tracker music revolution

title: Mode 7
description: Background mode 7 of the Super NES PPU rotates, enlarges and reduces a single 1024×1024-dot layer through a 2×2 matrix in registers $211B–$211E; changed every scanline by HDMA it becomes the perspective floor of F-Zero and Pilotwings.
subtitle: SNES rotation and scaling

title: Model 2
description: Model 2 was Sega's Model 1 polygon engine with texture-mapping hardware from General Electric's flight-simulator division, co-developed from August 1992. It debuted with Daytona USA in 1994 at 300,000 textured polygons a second and was succeeded by the unrelated Model 3.
subtitle: Arcade 3D revolution

title: Motion Capture
description: Motion capture records a performer's movement as data for a 3D character; Sega AM2 used a magnetic system on Virtua Fighter by 1994, Acclaim, Gremlin and Psygnosis built optical studios in 1995, and by 1998 it was standard practice and already being argued against.
subtitle: Recording reality

title: Multidirectional Scrolling
description: The C64 shifts 1,000 bytes of screen memory by hand every time the hardware scroll register wraps, so multidirectional scrolling is a scheduling problem: spread the shift over frames, hide it behind a second screen, and decide whether the scroll is locked to eight directions or free.
subtitle: Eight ways, or any way

title: Object Pooling
description: Object pooling pre-allocates and reuses game objects instead of creating and destroying them, avoiding memory fragmentation and allocation overhead.
subtitle: Reuse, don't reallocate

title: Opening the borders
description: Tricking the C64's VIC-II into never starting its border, so sprites and graphics can occupy the frame around the screen. The first C64 trick to become a competitive sport, and the one whose priority is most disputed.
subtitle: Drawing outside the frame the VIC-II reserves

title: Open World Design
description: A game space crossed at will, its tasks taken in any order while the world carries on. Described for Elite in 1984, weighed against Elite for Mercenary in 1986, and sold as a city that "breathes" for Grand Theft Auto in 1997; the phrase itself appears in 2000.
subtitle: Freedom to explore

title: Palette Cycling
description: Palette cycling created animation effects by rotating colour values rather than redrawing graphics, enabling flowing water, glowing effects, and pulsing lights without CPU overhead.
subtitle: Animation without redraw

title: Parallax Scrolling
description: Parallax scrolling moved background layers at different speeds to create an illusion of depth, transforming flat 2D games into seemingly three-dimensional spaces.
subtitle: Depth through motion

title: Password Systems
description: A password packs the game's state — level, weapons, tanks — into characters or a dot grid the player writes down and types back in, so a cartridge can save without a battery. Metroid's 24 characters, Mega Man II's 5×5 grid, and the JUSTIN BAILEY code that fell out of one.
subtitle: Save without battery

title: Permadeath
description: The rule that a dead character's save is deleted. The 1986-87 reviews of Epyx's Rogue explained the rule and printed the disk-copy workaround; Antic's type-in A-Rogue kept it; Edge named it "permadeath" in 2013.
subtitle: Death means death

title: PETSCII Character Chart
description: PETSCII codes, screen codes, and control characters—the complete reference for displaying text and graphics on the Commodore 64.
subtitle: Every character code the C64 knows about

title: Physics Engines
description: Physics engines became a separable component of games between Trespasser's muscle-driven dinosaurs in 1997 and the physics-card pitch of 2005, with MathEngine and Havok licensing the first realtime engines at the end of the 1990s and racing games as the first customers.
subtitle: Simulating the real world

title: Pixel Art
description: Drawing by hand in the dots of a low-resolution, fixed-palette display. Antic used the phrase in 1984 for Lucasfilm's Gary Winnick; Amiga Action put "pixel artists" in quotes in 1989; Bullfrog, Domark and Psygnosis artists explained the 16-colour craft in 1992; by 1994 it was a job title.
subtitle: Painting with squares

title: Point and Click
description: Point-and-click adventures replaced the typed parser with a cursor: ICOM's Deja Vu on the Mac in 1985, Lucasfilm's on-screen verb menu from Maniac Mansion, and Sierra's icon bar from King's Quest V.
subtitle: Mouse-driven adventure

title: Portable Game Design
description: Handheld design worked inside a fixed budget of screen, battery and pocket. Nintendo chose LCD over fancier parts for cost and battery life (Retro Gamer, 2008, on Yokoi); the 1989-90 press weighed the Game Boy's 20 hours and jacket-pocket size against the Lynx's colour screen and three hours.
subtitle: Constraints breed creativity

title: Position-Independent Code
description: Code that runs correctly wherever it is loaded, because every reference is relative to the program counter. The 6809's architects made it their highest-priority design goal (BYTE, 1979), Motorola's manual made it a rule, OS-9 made it a requirement; 6502 programmers managed it by effort.
subtitle: Code that runs anywhere

title: Pre-Rendered Backgrounds
description: A pre-rendered background is a picture of a place with polygon characters drawn over it from a fixed camera. Reviewers traced the formula from Alone in the Dark through Myst to Resident Evil, and Final Fantasy VII made it the look of the PlayStation's biggest game.
subtitle: Static beauty

title: PRINT vs POKE
description: Performance comparison of PRINT and POKE for screen output—and why understanding the difference makes you a better C64 programmer.
subtitle: Why games don't use PRINT statements

title: Procedural Generation
description: Procedural generation created game content through algorithms rather than manual design, enabling vast worlds, endless replayability, and experiences that fit in kilobytes.
subtitle: Algorithmic content creation

title: Pseudo-3D Road
description: A perspective road drawn as horizontal strips bent for corners and shifted for hills, with sprites scaled by distance. Sega's Turbo had it in 1982, Out Run perfected it in 1986, and conversion programmers wrote the road routine first.
subtitle: OutRun's famous perspective

title: Pulse Width Modulation
description: Pulse width modulation varied the duty cycle of square waves, transforming simple bleeps into rich, evolving tones that defined the sound of chip music.
subtitle: Shaping square waves

title: Puzzle Game Design
description: How puzzle games are made: few elements, abstract presentation, felt progress. Stated by Computer Gaming World in 1988 ("simple in concept and play, but also addictively challenging"), by Edge in 2001 ("Accessibility alone determines whether a puzzle game lives or dies"), and at length by Alexey Pajitnov in 2007.
subtitle: Elegant rules, emergent depth

title: Ragdoll Physics
description: Ragdoll physics hands a jointed character to the physics engine so it falls as the forces dictate; described by Chris Hecker in Edge in 1998, shipped in Unreal Tournament 2003 via MathEngine's Karma, and dismissed by Gabe Newell as flopping-around corpses once Half-Life 2 had made physics a tool instead.
subtitle: Dynamic death

title: Random Numbers
description: RND() internals, techniques, and patterns for game development
subtitle: RND() internals and techniques

title: Raster Effects
description: Raster effects change graphics parameters during screen drawing, creating colour bars, split screens, and effects beyond normal hardware limits.
subtitle: Per-scanline graphics tricks

title: Raster Interrupts
description: Raster interrupts trigger code at exact screen positions, enabling split-screen effects, colour bars, and multiplexed sprites that defined 8-bit graphics.
subtitle: Precision timing with the video beam

title: Raster Tricks
description: Raster tricks push hardware beyond specifications by precisely timed manipulation during screen display, achieving impossible-seeming effects.
subtitle: Exploiting the electron beam

title: RenderWare
description: RenderWare began in 1994 as Criterion Software's software-only 3D library for 386 and 486 PCs, was rewritten from scratch as RenderWare3 for the PlayStation 2 generation, powered Grand Theft Auto III after DMA Design lost most of its staff, and went to Electronic Arts with Criterion in 2004.
subtitle: Cross-platform 3D middleware

title: Rhythm Matching
description: Judging button presses against a music track. PaRappa the Rapper (1996) switched between four CD audio tracks by score; the Japanese press named the genre "rhythm action" in 1997; Konami's Bemani division built the scrolling chart and the peripherals; Harmonix's founder credits PaRappa for Guitar Hero.
subtitle: Play to the beat

title: Ring Buffer
description: A fixed block of memory used as a queue, with read and write indexes that wrap. BYTE explained it to hobbyists in 1977; Tim Follin's Agent X II engine uses a 16-entry one, wrapped with AND 15, for its echo; Amiga Exec's interrupt handlers fed device tasks through them.
subtitle: Circular data, fixed memory

title: Rotoscoping
description: Rotoscoping traced real human movement frame by frame, creating fluid animation in games like Prince of Persia and Another World that felt remarkably lifelike.
subtitle: Animation from life

title: Rumble Pak
description: Nintendo's Rumble Pak plugged into the N64 controller and shook it on cue. Announced as the Jolt Pak and shipped with Star Fox 64 in spring 1997, it was retrofitted to Mario 64 and Wave Race in Japan, sold for £15 in Britain, and answered by Sony's DualShock in 1998.
subtitle: Feel the game

title: Run-Length Encoding
description: Run-length encoding compressed data by storing repeated values as count-value pairs, dramatically reducing storage for graphics with large uniform areas.
subtitle: Simple compression

title: SCI Engine
description: Sierra's Creative Interpreter replaced AGI from King's Quest IV (1988): an object-oriented scripting language on a virtual machine, 320×200 graphics, MT-32 and AdLib music, and from 1990 an icon interface in place of the parser.
subtitle: Sierra's Creative Interpreter

title: Screen Memory
description: Screen RAM, colour RAM, and the VIC-II—understanding how 1000 bytes create 40×25 characters of colourful text.
subtitle: How the C64 displays text and graphics

title: Scrolling
description: Scrolling techniques expanded game worlds beyond single screens, from smooth hardware-assisted movement to creative software solutions that defined platformers and shooters.
subtitle: Moving through game worlds

title: SCUMM
description: SCUMM powered LucasArts adventure games from Maniac Mansion through The Curse of Monkey Island, providing tools that let designers focus on puzzles and dialogue rather than low-level code.
subtitle: Script Creation Utility for Maniac Mansion

title: Self-Modifying Code
description: Self-modifying code changed its own instructions at runtime, enabling impossible optimisations on 8-bit systems by treating code as data.
subtitle: Code that rewrites itself

title: Sequence Breaking
description: A speedrunner's term for taking a route the game's makers did not intend: the ice beam before the bombs in Metroid. Edge defined it in 2007 as "the use of a route other than that intended by the game creators"; Retro Gamer used it unexplained the same year. No earlier use is held.
subtitle: Playing out of order

title: Size Coding
description: Size coding emerged from demo scene competitions with strict byte limits, pushing programmers to achieve impossible effects in 64KB, 4KB, or even 256 bytes.
subtitle: The art of compression

title: Software Scrolling
description: The ZX Spectrum has no scroll hardware, so scrolling means moving screen bytes: character steps, one-pixel rotates, or the stack-pointer "push-scroll" Software Creations used for Ghosts 'n' Goblins. The choice shaped how Spectrum games moved.
subtitle: When hardware won't help

title: Sound Drivers
description: Sound drivers were the software engines that controlled audio hardware, translating composer's music data into the bleeps, samples, and synthesised sounds that defined each platform's acoustic character.
subtitle: Audio engine software

title: Speedcode
description: Replacing a loop with thousands of straight-line instructions to strip out the cost of looping. On the C64 it was the technique that broke raster-split and DYCP records — and it is usually generated, not written.
subtitle: Loop unrolling, taken to its conclusion

title: Split-Screen
description: Split-screen gives each player their own view of one display. Reviewers traced it from Spy vs Spy and Pitstop II on the C64 through Lotus on the Amiga and Super Mario Kart to the four-way splits of Mario Kart 64 and GoldenEye, naming the cost each time: less to see, and slower with four.
subtitle: Sharing the view

title: Sprite Animation
description: Frame-by-frame sprite animation creates the illusion of movement by cycling through carefully designed images at controlled intervals.
subtitle: Bringing pixels to life

title: Sprite crunching
description: A cycle-exact C64 trick that corrupts the VIC-II's internal sprite counter to make sprites shorter than the hardware allows — documented byte by byte by Crossbow of Crest, who got them down to 17 lines and left the record open.
subtitle: Shrinking a sprite by abusing a VIC-II glitch

title: Sprite Flicker
description: Sprite flicker rapidly alternated which sprites displayed each frame, allowing games to show more objects than hardware supported at the cost of visible flickering.
subtitle: Exceeding hardware limits

title: Sprite Multiplexing
description: By repositioning hardware sprites mid-frame as the raster beam passes, programmers displayed far more objects than the hardware officially supported.
subtitle: More sprites than hardware allows

title: Sprite Scaling
description: Sprite scaling created the illusion of 3D depth by drawing sprites at different sizes based on distance, enabling racing games, shooters, and flight simulators on 2D hardware.
subtitle: Pseudo-3D depth

title: Sprite stretching
description: Holding the C64's sprite graphics pointer still for a raster line so the same row of sprite data is drawn again, stretching a sprite to any height. The forgiving half of a pair whose other half needs cycle-exact timing.
subtitle: Telling the VIC-II to read the same line twice

title: Sprites
description: Sprites are hardware-supported graphical objects that move independently of the background, fundamental to 2D game graphics across platforms.
subtitle: Hardware-accelerated game objects

title: Stable Raster
description: The double-IRQ technique that achieves cycle-exact synchronisation with the VIC-II raster beam, enabling perfect mid-screen effects on the Commodore 64.
subtitle: Cycle-exact timing

title: State Machines
description: State machines bring order to complex game logic—managing title screens, gameplay, pauses, and game-overs through clear transitions and isolated behaviour.
subtitle: Organising game logic cleanly

title: Stealth Mechanics
description: Stealth mechanics make the enemy something to avoid. The 1981-2002 sources here follow the idea from Castle Wolfenstein's patrols and Nazi uniform, through Metal Gear Solid's alert states, to Thief's light gem and the disguises of Hitman.
subtitle: Unseen and unheard

title: Super FX Chip
description: Argonaut's Graphic Support Unit for Super NES cartridges: a 10.74 MHz RISC-style processor sharing the game pak's ROM and RAM, plotting pixels into PPU character format so that Star Fox (1993) could draw polygons. The Super FX 2 ran at 21.477 MHz.
subtitle: Cartridge silicon

title: Tank Controls
description: Tank controls steer a character by turning on the spot and walking the way it faces, whatever the camera does. The 1993-2012 sources here cover the fixed cameras of Alone in the Dark, the slow retreats of Resident Evil, the side-step Resident Evil 4 refused, and the late arrival of the name.
subtitle: Character-relative movement

title: Tech-tech
description: The C64 effect where a logo ripples horizontally, each raster line offset along a sine. Documented by Pasi 'Albert' Ojala, and later rebuilt on FLI by Compyx/Focus after a 25-year gap.
subtitle: Making a logo wave a line at a time

title: Texture Mapping
description: Texture mapping wraps a flat picture onto a polygon. Named on the PC for Strike Commander in 1991, it defined Doom and Ridge Racer, gave the PlayStation its warping textures, and came built into the Nintendo 64 with mip-mapping.
subtitle: Images on polygons

title: Tile-Based Collision
description: By checking which tiles a character overlaps rather than testing every object, tile collision provides fast, memory-efficient collision detection for platform games.
subtitle: Efficient collision detection for platformers

title: Tile-Based Graphics
description: Tile-based graphics build screens from small reusable images, enabling memory-efficient game worlds on limited hardware.
subtitle: Building worlds from small pieces

title: Tile Maps
description: Tile maps constructed game worlds from small reusable graphic blocks, enabling large levels within tight memory constraints while simplifying collision detection and level design.
subtitle: Building worlds from blocks

title: Trainers
description: A trainer is a set of cheats patched into a game — infinite lives, energy, time — offered from a menu before it starts. Crackers added them to releases (Retro Gamer, 2005; a Medway Boys cracker's recollection of 1986-90); Datel sold a "TRAINER MODE" on the Action Replay (1992); Silkworm's own cheat used the word (1989).
subtitle: +5 and counting

title: Turn-Based Combat
description: Combat resolved in rounds after the player commits every character's action. Described for Wizardry in 1982 ("Encounters are fought in turns"), sold with Dragon Warrior in 1989, and named "turn-based" by the British press in 1994-95 to say what Secret of Mana and Super Mario RPG were not.
subtitle: Strategic pacing

title: Twister
description: The rotating-column effect and its relatives - x-rotators, waving carpets - built on the C64 by running FLI on every second line, which buys back 63 cycles to spend on the effect itself.
subtitle: Rotating a shape by rebuilding it from pre-drawn line fragments

title: User Defined Graphics (UDGs)
description: Twenty-one programmer-supplied 8×8 patterns, codes 144 to 164, that the Spectrum's print routine treats as ordinary letters: the manual's route from BASIC into pixel graphics.
subtitle: Custom 8×8 character glyphs on the Sinclair ZX Spectrum

title: Unit Pathfinding
description: How a game moves a unit from A to B on its own. Wargames were finding the cheapest route across terrain by 1983, Paradroid ran its robots on hand-keyed patrol routes, and by the late 1990s the 'pathfinding problem' was the standing complaint against real-time strategy.
subtitle: Navigation intelligence

title: Variables and Memory
description: How variables work internally and memory management for BASIC programs
subtitle: BASIC memory management

title: Vector Graphics
description: A vector monitor draws lines by steering the beam, not by scanning pixels. Cinematronics' Space Wars brought it to arcades in 1978, Atari's Quadrascan games made it famous, Sega's Space Fury added colour, and the Vectrex took it home.
subtitle: Lines of light

title: VSP
description: A C64 trick that shifts the whole screen horizontally by deliberately delaying the VIC-II's DMA. It has at least four names, none of them agreed, and it can crash real hardware.
subtitle: Variable Screen Positioning, or HSP, or DMA delay, or Wanker

title: VSync
description: VSync synchronised game updates with the monitor's vertical refresh, preventing screen tearing and providing consistent timing for game logic.
subtitle: Synchronising with the display

title: Y-Depth Sorting
description: The technique of sorting sprites by their Y position to create correct depth ordering in top-down and isometric games, essential for beat 'em ups and action RPGs.
subtitle: Sprite ordering by position

title: Z-Machine
description: The virtual computer Infocom's text adventures ran on: a game compiled once, an interpreter per machine. Lebling described it in BYTE in 1980 with four interpreters; Infocom advertised twenty formats by 1984.
subtitle: The portable text adventure engine

title: Z80 Instruction Set Reference
description: Reference for the most common Z80 assembly instructions with T-states, bytes, and flag effects, as Zilog's Z80 CPU User Manual gives them.
subtitle: Selected CPU instruction reference

title: ZX Spectrum hardware ports
description: The Spectrum's I/O port map: port $FE for keyboard, border, beeper, and tape on every model; port $1F for the Kempston joystick; ports $7FFD and $1FFD for 128K and +2A/+3 memory paging; ports $FFFD and $BFFD for the AY-3-8912 sound chip on the 128K models; the +3's disk and printer ports. Bit assignments as the Sinclair and Amstrad manuals and Chris Smith's ULA book give them.
subtitle: Talking to the ULA, the AY chip, and the joystick — one port at a time

title: ZX Spectrum ROM disassembly
description: Reference for the ZX Spectrum's 16 KB ROM at $0000-$3FFF — the restart vectors, the interrupt routine, the character set, the system variables, and the ROM routines a game is most likely to call, each checked against Logan and O'Hara's 1983 disassembly.
subtitle: The 16 KB ROM that boots the machine, runs BASIC, and quietly underpins every Spectrum game

title: 3D Construction Kit
description: Having shipped four games on Freescape, Incentive packaged the engine as a product: build your own 3D world, compile it to a stand-alone program, and sell it. Domark published it at £24.99 in 1991.
subtitle: Incentive sold the engine itself

title: AMOS
description: François Lionet's revolutionary game creation language for the Amiga that made sprite-based game development accessible to anyone who could learn BASIC.
subtitle: Amiga game creation

title: Arcade Game Designer
description: Jonathan Cauldwell's authoring system for the ZX Spectrum: the tool behind most modern Spectrum homebrew, letting people who cannot write Z80 assembly ship real games — with a Spectrum Next version reported in development.
subtitle: The Quill's descendant, forty years on

title: Aseprite
description: The industry-standard pixel art editor and animation tool used by indie developers worldwide, combining professional features with a workflow designed specifically for sprite creation.
subtitle: Modern pixel art standard

title: Beta BASIC
description: Andy Wright's comprehensive BASIC extension for the ZX Spectrum that added procedures, toolkit features, and graphics commands missing from Sinclair BASIC.
subtitle: Spectrum BASIC enhanced

title: Blitz Basic 2
description: Mark Sibly's compiled BASIC for the Amiga that produced machine-code-fast games, proving BASIC could compete with assembly - the language that built Worms.
subtitle: Compiled BASIC power

title: DefleMask
description: A cross-platform tracker supporting multiple vintage sound chips, enabling composers to create authentic music for Genesis, NES, Game Boy, C64, and more from a single interface.
subtitle: Multi-system chiptune tracker

title: Deluxe Paint
description: Electronic Arts' Deluxe Paint defined pixel art creation on the Amiga and became the standard tool for game graphics throughout the 16-bit era.
subtitle: The pixel artist's brush

title: FamiTracker
description: FamiTracker brought tracker-style composition to NES audio, enabling musicians to create authentic 8-bit soundtracks on modern PCs.
subtitle: NES music for the modern age

title: GameMaker
description: GameMaker enabled game creation through visual programming, lowering barriers to development and spawning hits like *Undertale* and *Hotline Miami*.
subtitle: Games without code

title: GameBase
description: GameBase catalogued Commodore 64 and Amiga game libraries with integrated emulation, providing one-click access to thousands of preserved titles.
subtitle: Commodore game database

title: GFA BASIC
description: The powerful structured BASIC for the Atari ST that combined BASIC accessibility with modern programming features, becoming the platform's most popular programming language.
subtitle: Structured BASIC

title: Graphic Adventure Creator
description: Sean Ellis and Brendan Kelly's authoring system for Incentive Software combined a text adventure generator with a drawing package. It won its reputation on the Amstrad before reaching the Spectrum in 1986, where Sinclair User gave it 5/5.
subtitle: Incentive's answer, and it arrived on the Amstrad first

title: HVSC
description: The High Voltage SID Collection preserves over 50,000 Commodore 64 music files, becoming the definitive archive of SID chip music history.
subtitle: High Voltage SID Collection

title: id Tech
description: id Tech engines powered Doom, Quake, and countless licensed games, with source releases educating generations of programmers.
subtitle: Engines that built genres

title: Imagine
description: The feature-rich 3D modelling and animation package that became one of the most powerful creative tools on the Amiga, used for professional and demo scene work alike.
subtitle: Advanced Amiga 3D

title: LightWave 3D
description: The 3D software bundled with NewTek's Video Toaster that became an industry standard, powering the CGI for Babylon 5, Star Trek, and countless other productions.
subtitle: From Toaster to Hollywood

title: Logo
description: Seymour Papert's educational programming language that used turtle graphics to make coding accessible to children.
subtitle: The turtle that taught programming

title: PAW
description: Gilsoft's 1987 successor to The Quill added a real parser — adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, pronouns and multiple objects per command — plus 128K support and object weights. CRASH scored it 97% and said it would matter more than everything else in adventures put together.
subtitle: The Professional Adventure Writer, and a 97% for a utility

title: ProTracker
description: ProTracker became the standard tool for Amiga music creation, establishing the tracker interface and MOD format that influenced music production software for decades.
subtitle: The sound of the Amiga

title: RPG Maker
description: The Japanese game creation series that let hobbyists create their own role-playing games, launching countless indie developers.
subtitle: JRPG creation for everyone

title: Scratch
description: MIT's Scratch teaches programming through visual block-based coding, introducing millions of children to computational thinking.
subtitle: Programming through play

title: Sculpt 3D
description: One of the first 3D modelling and rendering packages for the Amiga, created by Eric Graham and proving that home computers could produce ray-traced imagery.
subtitle: Early Amiga 3D

title: SID Wizard
description: A cross-platform tracker for creating SID chip music, allowing modern composers to create authentic Commodore 64 soundtracks that run on real hardware.
subtitle: Modern C64 music creation

title: Simons' BASIC
description: The Commodore-published BASIC extension that added 114 commands for graphics, sprites, and sound to the C64, transforming its limited BASIC into a viable game development tool.
subtitle: C64 BASIC extended

title: Sinclair BASIC
description: Sinclair BASIC gave ZX Spectrum users an accessible programming environment, teaching a generation of British developers despite its quirks and limitations.
subtitle: The Spectrum's programming language

title: SoundTracker
description: Karsten Obarski's 1987 Amiga program that invented the tracker interface for music creation, spawning ProTracker and influencing all sample-based music software that followed.
subtitle: The first tracker

title: Steam
description: Valve's Steam transformed PC game distribution from retail boxes to digital downloads, becoming the dominant storefront while enabling indie developers and creating new business models.
subtitle: The platform that changed PC gaming

title: STOS
description: François Lionet's game creation language for the Atari ST that preceded AMOS, bringing accessible game development to the ST platform.
subtitle: Atari ST game creation

title: The Quill
description: Graeme Yeandle's 1983 authoring system for Gilsoft let people who could not program write and sell text adventures. It reviewed at 9/10 in Sinclair User three times, charted alongside games, and defined a decade of British amateur adventure publishing.
subtitle: The Welsh Wizards of Adventure

title: Unity
description: Unity made professional game development accessible to individuals and small teams, powering countless indie hits and mobile games with its approachable workflow.
subtitle: Game development democratised

title: Unreal Engine
description: Epic's Unreal Engine evolved from a shooter's technology into the world's most widely used game engine, powering everything from indie games to films.
subtitle: Powering worlds

title: World of Spectrum
description: World of Spectrum became the definitive online archive for ZX Spectrum software, preserving thousands of games, utilities, and documents for future generations.
subtitle: The Spectrum archive

title: Worldmaker and Grax
description: Bo Jangeborg wrote his own graphics tooling before he wrote Fairlight. Grax drew rooms; Worldmaker assembled them into a world. The Edge described it in 1985 as a Quill-style utility for 3D adventures and intended to sell it as a product — the same tools-before-games pattern that runs through the whole Spectrum story.
subtitle: The room-design tools behind Fairlight, built from an adventure-illustration utility

title: ZXAS
description: A 5K Z80 assembler for the 16K ZX81, published by Bug-Byte in 1981. Source was typed into REM statements; output went straight into RAM. Sinclair User called using it 'the single biggest step to proficiency in machine code programming' — two years before the same publisher released Manic Miner.
subtitle: Bug-Byte's ZX81 assembler, and the first rung of the ladder

title: ZZT
description: The 1991 ASCII game creation system that launched Epic Games and spawned a creative community of young game makers.
subtitle: Tim Sweeney's first game
